author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy
title: Accessibility strategy
statement: This accessibility strategy outlines the current principles and work needed to improve the accessibility of the GOV.UK Design System. The primary goals of this strategy are to inform decision-making and enhance the success of accessibility-related activities within the GOV.UK Design System team. Given the continuous and iterative nature of accessibility work, this strategy will continue to change and adapt over time. Using the GOV.UK Design System in a service does not immediately make that service accessible. Additional research, design, development and testing work is needed to make any service accessible, even when using accessible styles, components and patterns.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Accessibility and design systems
title: Accessibility strategy: Accessibility and design systems
statement: At least 1 in 5 people report having a disability in the UK, making accessibility an essential consideration for all UK Government services and websites. The GOV.UK Design System supports hundreds of services, which receive millions of views every month. Embedding web accessibility within a central design system allows us to influence baseline accessibility across these hundreds of services. To learn more about why accessibility is essential when building digital services, read the ‘understanding accessibility requirements’ guidance for public sector bodies.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Accessibility and design systems).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Principles for increasing accessibility
title: Accessibility strategy: Principles for increasing accessibility
statement: The GOV.UK Design System team follows 3 sets of principles to increase the accessibility of government services.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Principles for increasing accessibility).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Principles for increasing accessibility > Web accessibility
title: Accessibility strategy: Web accessibility
statement: We follow the 4 principles of web accessibility upon which WCAG is based: 1. Perceivable – Information and user interface components must be presentable to users in ways they can perceive. 2. Operable – User interface components and navigation must be operable. 3. Understandable – Information and the operation of the user interface must be understandable. 4. Robust – Content must be robust enough that it can be interpreted reliably by a wide variety of user agents, including assistive technologies.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Principles for increasing accessibility > Web accessibility).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Principles for increasing accessibility > Universal design
title: Accessibility strategy: Universal design
statement: When designing accessible styles, components and patterns, we aim to follow the 7 principles of universal design: 1. Equitable use – The design is useful and marketable to people with diverse abilities. 2. Flexibility in use – The design accommodates a wide range of individual preferences and abilities. 3. Simple and intuitive use – The design is easy to understand, regardless of the user's experience, knowledge, language skills, or current concentration level. 4. Perceptible information – The design communicates necessary information effectively to the user, regardless of ambient conditions or the user's sensory abilities. 5. Tolerance for error – The design minimises hazards and the adverse consequences of accidental or unintended actions. 6. Low physical and cognitive effort – The design can be used efficiently and comfortably and with minimum fatigue. 7. Size and space for approach and use – The design provides appropriate sizing and spacing of elements, allowing the user to interact successfully. Modifications to principles 6 and 7 are to make sure they apply to web-based designs rather than physical spaces.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Principles for increasing accessibility > Universal design).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Principles for increasing accessibility > Progressive enhancement
title: Accessibility strategy: Progressive enhancement
statement: We use progressive enhancement when building styles, components and patterns and encourage service teams to use the same approach. Progressive enhancement assists in web accessibility by encouraging teams to build resilient services. 1. Start with proper semantic HTML. The semantic structure helps build an organised and accurate accessibility tree for assistive technologies like screen readers. 2. Ensure the main content is available without CSS. This availability helps accommodate custom user stylesheets and forced colour modes. 3. Build an experience that works well without JavaScript. Offer accessible JavaScript enhancements when it improves the user experience. Even in cases where this is not achieved, provide fallback options for interactive elements that use JavaScript. Learn more about progressive enhancement in the Service Manual.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Principles for increasing accessibility > Progressive enhancement).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Prioritising accessibility concerns
title: Accessibility strategy: Prioritising accessibility concerns
statement: An ‘accessibility concern’ is our umbrella term for any question about the accessibility of a portion of a product. Accessibility concerns can surface in any product, including: - GOV.UK Frontend - the GOV.UK Design System website - the GOV.UK Prototype Kit - the GOV.UK Frontend technical documentation website - other content produced by the GOV.UK Design System team The GOV.UK Design System’s top focus for accessibility is on styles and components included in GOV.UK Frontend and patterns built using GOV.UK Frontend. When the team encounters multiple accessibility concerns across multiple products, we prioritise work based on the impact on users of government services. Due to the broad reach of GOV.UK Frontend, the team are likely to prioritise accessibility concerns above concerns in other products they manage. Our goal is to focus first on high-risk and high-impact accessibility concerns in the products that directly impact end-users and the public.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Prioritising accessibility concerns).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Prioritising accessibility concerns > Accessibility concern types
title: Accessibility strategy: Accessibility concern types
statement: The team puts accessibility concerns in 2 categories: 1. Theoretical: A question or statement regarding the accessibility of an implementation within the Design System without evidence of real-world impact. 2. Evidenced: Sharing new research, data or evidence showing that an implementation within the Design System could cause barriers for disabled people. The team will usually prioritise evidenced issues and queries over theoretical ones. Feedback from users and other proof of real-world impact provides much stronger evidence for the team, especially when determining priority and urgency. When resolving an accessibility concern involves a solution that causes a breaking change, strong evidence helps justify the change.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Prioritising accessibility concerns > Accessibility concern types).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Prioritising accessibility concerns > Theoretical accessibility concerns
title: Accessibility strategy: Theoretical accessibility concerns
statement: Theoretical issues and queries are more difficult to address as they do not provide new evidence or relevant research. For accessibility concerns about the theoretical accessibility of an implementation, the team will check for: - existing decisions documented regarding the current implementation - overlap with other raised issues and queries - additional community resources related to the accessibility concern If there is no documentation or confirmation that the current implementation is an evidenced accessibility concern, the team may: - check for existing evidence or research within the GOV.UK Design System - request additional evidence or research from the group who submitted the accessibility concern - assume that the reasoning behind existing decisions and implementations was sound until further evidence is found - assume that previous decisions for the GOV.UK Design System were made in good faith - wait for new evidence or factors to emerge before questioning previous decisions This approach supports the team closing accessibility concerns which do not include enough evidence to be meaningfully acted upon, allowing the team to focus on evidenced accessibility concerns.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Prioritising accessibility concerns > Theoretical accessibility concerns).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Prioritising accessibility concerns > Evidenced accessibility concerns
title: Accessibility strategy: Evidenced accessibility concerns
statement: Many types of evidence can indicate an evidenced accessibility concern, but some of the most common examples are: - new findings from user research - service team usability testing results - new global best-practises or standards - direct feedback from users of a service or product - a demonstration of unintended behaviour from an assistive technology - results from an internal or external accessibility audit When presented with new evidence of a potential accessibility concern, the team will analyse and determine whether the concern: - has been addressed or assessed before - breaks WCAG AA compliance - is high-severity (as defined in the section below)
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Prioritising accessibility concerns > Evidenced accessibility concerns).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Prioritising accessibility concerns > Determining severity of an accessibility concern
title: Accessibility strategy: Determining severity of an accessibility concern
statement: There are 3 factors to determine a high-severity concern: - there is reasonable evidence that it makes it difficult or impossible for some people to complete certain tasks - it affects the accessibility of essential services or critical infrastructure - individual service teams cannot efficiently resolve it on their own If the accessibility concern does not meet all 3 factors listed, the team will determine the severity on a case-by-case basis. Low and medium severity are not defined in this document and will be determined by the team as needed.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Prioritising accessibility concerns > Determining severity of an accessibility concern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Prioritising accessibility concerns > Disagreement on accessibility concerns
title: Accessibility strategy: Disagreement on accessibility concerns
statement: Sometimes, the existence, urgency or strength of evidence for an accessibility concern is not universally agreed. In these cases, we follow 3 increasing levels for escalation.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Prioritising accessibility concerns > Disagreement on accessibility concerns).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Prioritising accessibility concerns > Level 1 for disagreement escalation
title: Accessibility strategy: Level 1 for disagreement escalation
statement: If the GOV.UK Design System team can confirm the accessibility concern internally, then work can continue normally.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Prioritising accessibility concerns > Level 1 for disagreement escalation).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Prioritising accessibility concerns > Level 2 for disagreement escalation
title: Accessibility strategy: Level 2 for disagreement escalation
statement: If the GOV.UK Design System team is unable to confirm the accessibility concern or disagrees with the raised concern, then the following steps are taken to resolve the disagreement: 1. Assess the severity of the accessibility concern (as defined in the section above) 2. If the accessibility concern is not determined to be high-severity, continue to hold discussions within the team and any frontend and accessibility communities where applicable
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Prioritising accessibility concerns > Level 2 for disagreement escalation).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Prioritising accessibility concerns > Level 3 for disagreement escalation
title: Accessibility strategy: Level 3 for disagreement escalation
statement: If the severity is high and the GOV.UK Design System is still unable to confirm the accessibility concern or disagrees with the raised concern, then check with the GDS accessibility monitoring team for a second opinion. If the GDS accessibility monitoring team confirms the accessibility concern, set a priority level for the concern. When disagreement involves multiple parties, the decision-making hierarchy is: - Top: GDS accessibility monitoring team - Second: GOV.UK Design System team (including any accessibility specialists on the team) - Third: External auditing groups and teams It is not regularly the role of the GDS accessibility monitoring team to make decisions like these, and this decision-making process is unique to the GOV.UK Design System team. This is due to the centralised nature of the GOV.UK Design System and the limited capacity of the GDS accessibility monitoring team. Other service teams will need to determine their decision-making method when disagreements over accessibility concerns arise.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Prioritising accessibility concerns > Level 3 for disagreement escalation).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Baseline WCAG accessibility compliance
title: Accessibility strategy: Baseline WCAG accessibility compliance
statement: We aim to meet level AA WCAG for: - styles, components and patterns - the GOV.UK Design System website - the GOV.UK Frontend technical documentation website - other content produced by the GOV.UK Design System team We aim to maintain this level AA rating for the version of WCAG which: - is considered the ‘latest published version’ - has been published for at least a year For example, in August 2022, we would follow the WCAG 2.1 recommendation from 05 June 2018. The one year gap between a WCAG version’s release and when we support it allows our team the necessary time to update the GOV.UK Design System’s styles, components and patterns, and the team’s other products. If regulations require updates to occur at an earlier date or to meet a newer version of WCAG, the regulatory requirement will take precedence.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Baseline WCAG accessibility compliance).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Baseline WCAG accessibility compliance > Improving baseline compliance
title: Accessibility strategy: Improving baseline compliance
statement: Where feasible, the team aims to identify areas where they can surpass WCAG AA guidelines to provide a more accessible design system. WCAG does not cover all aspects of accessibility, and when the team identifies an opportunity to go beyond compliance to improve accessibility, they will explore that opportunity. The team initially releases changes to the GOV.UK Design System at baseline WCAG AA compliance. Releasing a baseline WCAG-compliant version allows service teams to implement components sooner. After the initial release, the GOV.UK Design System team will prioritise further accessibility improvements where possible. There are some AAA criteria and other accessibility improvements that the team can consistently deliver during our normal contribution processes. However, meeting AAA criteria is not a requirement nor guarantee for any portion of the GOV.UK Design System and its products. When working on individual styles, components and patterns, the team may determine that it is possible and feasible to meet additional AAA criteria. When feasible, the team aims to pursue the additional level of AAA compliance when the following factors are met: 1. There is team capacity for the time and effort needed to implement a solution. 2. The solution will not negatively affect any competing higher-priority accessibility activities. 3. The solution doesn't begin failing several previously-met AAA criteria in an effort to pass a single AAA criterion. 4. The solution continues to pass all A and AA WCAG criteria. 5. The solution is easy or practical for service teams to implement. 6. Service teams can consistently implement the solution without significant risk of inaccessible implementation. 7. The solution works across the versions of browsers and assistive technologies supported by GOV.UK Frontend. If the factors above are not met, the team should document which AAA criteria were discussed, but not pursued and which factors led to the decision.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Baseline WCAG accessibility compliance > Improving baseline compliance).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Testing accessibility concerns
title: Accessibility strategy: Testing accessibility concerns
statement: The team uses the GOV.UK Service Manual guidance on testing for accessibility and tests the accessibility of each component using a mix of testing tools, automated testing during deployment and manual testing.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Testing accessibility concerns).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Testing accessibility concerns > Testing tools
title: Accessibility strategy: Testing tools
statement: The team uses a variety of tools during the development process, including, but not limited to: - WAVE browser plugin - Axe browser plugin - browser accessibility reports The team also uses general inspection techniques, including: - sensory inspection (visual, auditory, etc.) - HTML inspection using browser developer tools - accessibility tree inspection
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Testing accessibility concerns > Testing tools).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Testing accessibility concerns > Automated testing
title: Accessibility strategy: Automated testing
statement: The team currently uses jest-axe as part of our deployment process, along with @axe-core/puppeteer. These tools test the example code snippets in the GOV.UK Design System against axe-core. The team does not solely rely on automated testing processes, as a 2017 study from GDS concluded that only about 30% of issues are found by automated testing tools, such as axe-core. As of May 2023, we have improved our automated accessibility testing processes: 1. We now run JavaScript in our test example code snippets. 2. We now test every example code snippet for each component, instead of just the first example per component. 3. We now run our tests in @axe-core/puppeteer to include colour contrast checks, but we still use jest-axe to report issues. 4. We added html-validate to our automated tests. This helps us test for HTML compliance, including various WCAG 2.1 checks available through html-validate. We have an accessibility activity issue in GitHub where we track our efforts to enhance automated testing in our development pipeline.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Testing accessibility concerns > Automated testing).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Testing accessibility concerns > Manual testing
title: Accessibility strategy: Manual testing
statement: Manual testing for a style, component or pattern follows our own guidance on establishing accessibility acceptance criteria. Additionally, the team follows the GOV.UK Service manual guidance on testing with assistive technologies. The team records results on our accessibility testing template spreadsheet (Google Sheet), which lists the specific browser and assistive technology combinations with which we test. Currently, the team uses desktop-type devices to access assistive technologies in the following ways: - screen readers through Assistiv Labs and macOS - screen magnifiers through Assistiv Labs and macOS - high contrast and other display modes through Assistiv Labs and browsers - speech recognition software through Windows testing computers and macOS As of November 2022, there are limitations to how the team performs and records manual testing. These limitations may be addressed by the proposed ‘Standardise and improve our manual testing methodology activity’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Testing accessibility concerns > Manual testing).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Testing accessibility concerns > User research and usability testing
title: Accessibility strategy: User research and usability testing
statement: Accessibility user research often includes activities such as: - usability testing of prototypes - user interviews - surveys To ensure services are accessible, user research must include disabled people and should also include people with a variety of access needs and impairment types. The majority of accessibility user research results are contributed by service teams and the broader communities that use the GOV.UK Design System. The team does not do additional user research for every new contribution as standard. The team might determine that further accessibility user research is necessary for complex or sensitive components and design patterns. If further research is needed, the team will decide if it’s best to handle the research internally or in partnership with one or more service teams. Examples of when the team and other service teams have completed additional accessibility user research include: - Making the focus state more accessible - Externally testing our components with a research prototype - Exit this page accessibility research
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Testing accessibility concerns > User research and usability testing).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Recording accessibility concerns
title: Accessibility strategy: Recording accessibility concerns
statement: Individuals and teams can raise an accessibility concern as either a GitHub issue or a query from any other supported channel. If an incoming query is more than a quickly-answered question, it will be recorded as a GitHub issue. By keeping accessibility concerns in the same place as all our GitHub issues, the team can more easily identify accessibility concerns related to other items. Addressing and storing accessibility concerns separate from GitHub issues could lead to them receiving less attention. If an accessibility concern turns out to be a bug the team cannot quickly fix, the team will determine whether it should be recorded in the GOV.UK Design System accessibility statement. We also will record relevant accessibility concerns for specific styles, components or patterns in their corresponding guidance pages.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Recording accessibility concerns).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Recording accessibility concerns > Recording WCAG compliance status
title: Accessibility strategy: Recording WCAG compliance status
statement: If the GOV.UK Design System does not meet the requirements of level AA accessibility compliance, the team will update the GOV.UK Design System accessibility statement and keep the records of changes required until compliance is met.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Recording accessibility concerns > Recording WCAG compliance status).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Proposed accessibility activities
title: Accessibility strategy: Proposed accessibility activities
statement: One of the goals of this strategy is to outline the work needed to improve the accessibility of the GOV.UK Design System. We document this work as a set of proposed activities, presented in a GitHub project. View the Accessibility strategy: proposed activities GitHub project. This GitHub project allows service teams to see the areas of work under consideration, and is intended to enhance the success of the included activities. The project will be reviewed quarterly, to align with quarterly planning.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Proposed accessibility activities).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Proposed accessibility activities > Priority levels
title: Accessibility strategy: Priority levels
statement: We identify the priority of each proposed activity based on the following levels: 1. what we must do legally 2. what only we are positioned to do 3. what reduces the risk of inaccessible implementations 4. what improves accessibility for many services 5. what makes it easier for service teams to do their jobs 6. what is good to do without adding risk to the priorities above The team will need to decide how much time and effort to spend on activities since work is dependent on finite team capacity. Higher priority activities should receive a more significant share of the team’s time and effort. Lower priority activities can still receive time and effort, but focusing on lower priority activities should not compromise the completion or success of higher priority activities.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Proposed accessibility activities > Priority levels).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Proposed accessibility activities > Activity categories
title: Accessibility strategy: Activity categories
statement: To help the team manage the number of activities, there are 4 main areas where the team has proposed activities: 1. Design system fundamentals 2. Areas the team is best-positioned to handle 3. Processes in the UK government 4. Tools and training in GDS
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Proposed accessibility activities > Activity categories).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Performance measurement
title: Accessibility strategy: Performance measurement
statement: Three of the goals of this strategy are to: - inform decision-making and prioritisation of accessibility-related matters within the GOV.UK Design System team - improve the success, speed, and scope of accessibility-related issues within the GOV.UK Design System team - increase awareness, understanding, transparency and participation in accessibility-related cases within government communities and service teams
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Performance measurement).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Performance measurement > Performance indicators
title: Accessibility strategy: Performance indicators
statement: Initially, the team will assess the performance of this accessibility strategy by measuring the: - increase in community engagement with the accessibility strategy’s content - use of the strategy to guide and improve the GOV.UK Design System team’s decision-making - progress and completion of activities mentioned in the strategy - number of accessibility concerns recorded as GitHub issues in the team’s repositories - number of accessibility concerns listed in the GOV.UK Design System accessibility statement
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Performance measurement > Performance indicators).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Performance measurement > Additional indicators
title: Accessibility strategy: Additional indicators
statement: If capacity is available to expand measurement efforts, additional performance indicators might include: - accessibility testing template use – completion rate, regularity and consistency - accessible implementation by service teams – accessibility audit result patterns, service accessibility statement patterns, service team satisfaction - service team satisfaction – responses to accessibility-specific questions in surveys and research - accessibility concern average time to resolution – the time it takes from the initial recording or reporting of an accessibility concern to its resolution - the number of accessibility regressions – checking the robustness of our quality assurance / testing process by measuring how many accessibility bugs make it into a release - number of accessibility concerns raised by service teams versus concerns raised internally – to gauge how heavily we rely on users to surface accessibility concerns - overall impact of the GOV.UK Design System or the strategy on web accessibility across UK government services – this would require additional resources and expertise, or collaboration with other teams who have the necessary resources and expertise
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Performance measurement > Additional indicators).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Performance measurement > Recording performance measurement results
title: Accessibility strategy: Recording performance measurement results
statement: The team will gather performance measurement results every 6 months and record them in the team’s internal documentation. The team will also review the GOV.UK Design System accessibility statement every 6 months and update as needed. The team will use the results of performance measurement and accessibility statement reviews to help inform quarterly planning.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Performance measurement > Recording performance measurement results).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Terms used in this strategy
title: Accessibility strategy: Terms used in this strategy
statement: This section defines terms particular to this accessibility strategy and to the GOV.UK Design System team.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Terms used in this strategy).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Terms used in this strategy > Accessibility
title: Accessibility strategy: Accessibility
statement: For the GOV.UK Design System, accessibility specifically refers to web accessibility. We focus on developing styles, components and patterns that, when combined, can create services that disabled people can use. The Web Accessibility Initiative (WAI) comprehensively defines web accessibility in their Introduction to Web Accessibility. To learn more about why accessibility is essential when building digital services, read the ‘understanding accessibility requirements’ guidance for public sector bodies.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Terms used in this strategy > Accessibility).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Terms used in this strategy > Accessibility concerns
title: Accessibility strategy: Accessibility concerns
statement: For this document, an ‘accessibility concern’ is any question about the accessibility of a portion of a product. Accessibility concerns are those surfaced as either a GitHub issue or a query from any other source. Some, but not all, accessibility concerns will turn out to be bugs or feature requests. Confirmed accessibility bugs will be recorded as GitHub issues, regardless of how reports surfaced them. Most high-priority accessibility concerns will be found in styles and components included in GOV.UK Frontend and patterns built using GOV.UK Frontend. That’s because hundreds of services incorporate these elements.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Terms used in this strategy > Accessibility concerns).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Terms used in this strategy > Breaking releases and breaking changes
title: Accessibility strategy: Breaking releases and breaking changes
statement: A ‘breaking release’ is a numbered version of the GOV.UK Frontend repository that breaks compatibility with previous versions of the code. A breaking release only occurs when some service teams must make changes to their service code for their service to keep working correctly. Individual changes in the release that break compatibility are called ‘breaking changes’. Breaking releases for GOV.UK Frontend are identified by an increment in the first digit of the release version number. For example, going from 5.X.X to 6.0.0 is a breaking release. Learn more about release versioning for GOV.UK Frontend.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Terms used in this strategy > Breaking releases and breaking changes).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Terms used in this strategy > Service teams
title: Accessibility strategy: Service teams
statement: Throughout this document, ‘service teams’ refers to all individuals, teams, organisations and groups that directly use any GOV.UK Design System products, including: - the GOV.UK Design System - GOV.UK Frontend code - the Prototype Kit The term ‘service teams’ is intended to be inclusive of all groups that use GOV.UK Design System products, even if those groups are not specifically working on a service or structured as a distinct team. We rely on service teams to build accessible services for end-users.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Terms used in this strategy > Service teams).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Terms used in this strategy > Support
title: Accessibility strategy: Support
statement: For the GOV.UK Design System and Prototype Kit teams, ‘support’ has a specific meaning. Support is a service provided to users of the GOV.UK Design System, GOV.UK Frontend repository and the Prototype Kit. Generally, one team member is assigned to be on support each workday. We provide support to users through 3 channels: - email - slack - GitHub issues The team member assigned to support on a given workday will help triage requests and gather information from the team to answer questions.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Terms used in this strategy > Support).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility strategy > Terms used in this strategy > The team
title: Accessibility strategy: The team
statement: Throughout this document, ‘the team’, ‘our team’ and ‘we’ refer to the GOV.UK Design System team. This team is inclusive of members of the Prototype Kit team.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility strategy" (Terms used in this strategy > The team).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addressing accessibility issues in your service
title: Addressing accessibility issues in your service
statement: We're always looking to improve the accessibility of the Design System. To decide the best way to address an accessibility issue, you should: 1. Gather relevant information. 2. Try to reproduce the issue. 3. Check if it's a known issue. Accessibility issues in your service can happen for different reasons. These could include: - an issue in the GOV.UK Design System - an issue with the service due to changes made to components - an issue with an assistive technology - a false positive from an accessibility checker - a misunderstood result from a user research session
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addressing accessibility issues in your service" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addressing accessibility issues in your service > Gather information
title: Addressing accessibility issues in your service: Gather information
statement: First, gather all relevant information and any useful context. If the issue came from a user or auditor, include which software the user was using, specifically: - which type of assistive technology (if any) and its version - which operating system and its version - which browser and its version - the page on which the issue appeared Or if the issue came from an accessibility testing tool, include: - which tool it was - its version - the page on which the issue appeared Add anything else that's important to reproduce the issue.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addressing accessibility issues in your service" (Gather information).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addressing accessibility issues in your service > Reproduce the issue in your service
title: Addressing accessibility issues in your service: Reproduce the issue in your service
statement: Try to reproduce the issue in your own service, ideally using the same set of technologies as reported. If you do not know the set of technologies used, at least test with standard tools. If the issue came from someone using assistive tech, test with the combinations mentioned in the Service Manual. If the issue was from an accessibility testing tool, test with the most common testing tools. If you cannot test with all the relevant technologies, you can test with a single set of technologies that you do have available. If you cannot reproduce it at this point, you can test in other combinations of browsers and assistive tech or testing tools. If you still cannot reproduce the issue, investigating it will be very difficult. However, if you’re sure it's a valid issue, it’s still worth sharing it with us.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addressing accessibility issues in your service" (Reproduce the issue in your service).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addressing accessibility issues in your service > Reproduce the issue on the GOV.UK Design System website
title: Addressing accessibility issues in your service: Reproduce the issue on the GOV.UK Design System website
statement: If you can reproduce it in your own service, try to reproduce it on the GOV.UK Design System website. Open the examples on the component’s page and test it with the same set of technologies. If you cannot reproduce it here, this probably means there's an issue with changes you've made to the component or how the component is used in your service. In this case, you'll have to fix this yourself. Make sure you're using the latest version of GOV.UK Frontend. It's possible the issue was fixed in a previous version and updating to the latest version might fix it in your service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addressing accessibility issues in your service" (Reproduce the issue on the GOV.UK Design System website).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addressing accessibility issues in your service > Check if it's a known issue
title: Addressing accessibility issues in your service: Check if it's a known issue
statement: If you can reproduce it on our website, check that it’s not an issue we already know about. We track accessibility-related issues in a few different places: - the list of issues in the GOV.UK Frontend repo - discussions for each component in our community backlog - our list of known issues flagged by validators or automated testing tools, if the issue came from an accessibility checking tool - our list of reported vendor bugs, if the issue came from an assistive technology or browser
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addressing accessibility issues in your service" (Check if it's a known issue).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addressing accessibility issues in your service > Report the issue
title: Addressing accessibility issues in your service: Report the issue
statement: If the issue already exists but you have more information, you can add a comment to it. Any new information can help us better understand the issue. If the issue does not exist, you can create a new issue.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addressing accessibility issues in your service" (Report the issue).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility
title: Accessibility
statement: Our work to make the GOV.UK Design System meet public sector accessibility regulations is a continuous and iterative process. Using the GOV.UK Design System in a service does not immediately make that service accessible. You’ll need additional research, design, development and testing work to make sure your service is accessible, even when using accessible styles, components and patterns.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility > Accessibility strategy
title: Accessibility: Accessibility strategy
statement: Read our accessibility strategy for more information on our current principles and work needed to improve the accessibility of the GOV.UK Design System.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility" (Accessibility strategy).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility > Accessibility statement
title: Accessibility: Accessibility statement
statement: Our accessibility statement helps not just end users but also service teams to understand how accessibile GOV.UK Frontend, its documentation website and this website are.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility" (Accessibility statement).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility > Addressing accessibility issues
title: Accessibility: Addressing accessibility issues
statement: Find out how to investigate accessibility issues in your service and work out the best way to address them.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility" (Addressing accessibility issues).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accessibility > Accessibility in the Service Manual
title: Accessibility: Accessibility in the Service Manual
statement: The Accessibility and assisted digital guidance in the Service Manual outlines what you need to know and what you need to do to ensure your service is accessible.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accessibility" (Accessibility in the Service Manual).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Changes to the Design System to meet WCAG 2.2
title: Changes to the Design System to meet WCAG 2.2
statement: We have retired WCAG 2.2 callouts and guidance across the Design System website. The callouts were designed to make teams aware of the changes to WCAG 2.2 and help them make necessary adjustments to their services before October 2024. This was the date that public sector bodies needed to be compliant with the WCAG 2.2 updates to the accessibility regulations. Now that this date has passed we have removed the callouts and brought specific messages into our overall guidance where it’s useful. Let us know if you are missing any particular information in our announcement of the WCAG 2.2 callout retirement.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Changes to the Design System to meet WCAG 2.2" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accordion
title: Accordion
statement: The accordion component lets users show and hide sections of related content on a page.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accordion" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accordion > When to use this component
title: Accordion: When to use this component
statement: Only use an accordion if there's evidence it’s helpful for the user to: - see an overview of multiple, related sections of content - choose to show and hide sections that are relevant to them - look across information that might otherwise be on different pages For example, an accordion can work well if the user needs to reveal and compare information that’s relevant to them. Accordions can also work well for people who use a service regularly. For example, users of caseworking systems who need to do familiar tasks quickly. Test with users to decide if using an accordion outweighs the potential problems with hiding content.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accordion" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accordion > When not to use this component
title: Accordion: When not to use this component
statement: Accordions hide content from the user. Not all users will notice them or understand how they work. For this reason, you should only use them in specific situations and if user research supports it. Do not use an accordion for content that all users need to see. Test your content without an accordion first. Well-written and structured content, as shown in GOV.UK writing standards, can remove the need to use an accordion. It’s usually better to: - simplify and reduce the amount of content - split the content across multiple pages - keep the content on a single page, separated by headings - use a list of links at the start of the page (known as 'anchor links') to take the user to particular sections of a page Accordions work best for simple content and links. Do not use accordions to split up a series of questions. Use separate pages instead. Do not put accordions within accordions, as it will make content difficult to find. Do not use the accordion component if the amount of content inside will make the page slow to load.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accordion" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accordion > Decide between using accordions, tabs and details
title: Accordion: Decide between using accordions, tabs and details
statement: The Accordion component, Tabs component and Details component all work by hiding sections of content which a user can choose to reveal. Avoid using any of these components within one another. If you decide to use one of these components, consider if: - the user needs to look at more than one section at a time – an accordion can show multiple sections at a time, unlike tabs - the user needs to switch quickly between sections – tabs can show content without pushing other sections down the page, unlike accordions - there are many sections of content – accordions can fit more sections as they’re arranged vertically, unlike tabs which are arranged horizontally - there’s only one or two pieces of short, less important content – the details component is more suitable as it’s visually smaller and less prominent than an accordion or tabs
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accordion" (Decide between using accordions, tabs and details).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accordion > How it works
title: Accordion: How it works
statement: There are 2 ways to use the accordion component. You can use HTML or, if you’re using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro. The accordion component uses JavaScript. When JavaScript is not available, users will see all the content displayed with the section labels as headings. If you are using HTML, you must add an 'id' attribute to the tag with the govuk-accordion class. It must be unique across the service's domain to maintain the persistent expanded state of the accordion.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accordion" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accordion > How it works > Section heading buttons
title: Accordion: Section heading buttons
statement: An accordion will usually start with all sections hidden. To show a section, the user can interact anywhere in the heading button. The heading button includes all of these areas: - heading text - summary line (if you decide to add one) - call-to-action text to 'show' or 'hide' For users of screen readers, all the text in the button will be read as a single statement (separated by commas to allow for slight pauses). There’s also some visually hidden content in the heading text to help announce the call-to-action as 'show this section' or 'hide this section'.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accordion" (How it works > Section heading buttons).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accordion > How it works > Write clear button text
title: Accordion: Write clear button text
statement: Write the heading and summary line like any other button text. Use sentence case, describe the content that will show, and keep it short. Users of screen readers might find it difficult to navigate the accordion if the button text is too long. If you struggle to come up with clear button text, it might be because the way you’ve separated the content is not clear. Organise sections in a way that makes sense to users, based on their needs.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accordion" (How it works > Write clear button text).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accordion > How it works > Adding a summary line
title: Accordion: Adding a summary line
statement: Only add a summary line if it’s actually needed, as it's likely to make the button text too long. If you’ve decided that you need the summary line, you must make it as short as possible.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accordion" (How it works > Adding a summary line).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accordion > How it works > Structure section headings with the rest of the page
title: Accordion: Structure section headings with the rest of the page
statement: The accordion component shows section headings as headings. If needed, change the heading level of the section headings to make them fit within the other headings on the page.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accordion" (How it works > Structure section headings with the rest of the page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accordion > How it works > Starting with sections open
title: Accordion: Starting with sections open
statement: Users might need some sections to be open from the start. If they leave and then return to the page, they might also need sections they opened to stay open. By default, if the user leaves and then returns to the page within the same page session, the accordion component will use 'session storage' to remember which sections were open. This functionality can be turned off by adding rememberExpanded: false to the Nunjucks macro. To see the changes you've made, you may need to create a new 'session'. For example, by opening a page in a new tab or window. Add the govuk-accordionsection--expanded class to the govuk-accordionsection div to make individual sections open from the start. You can also do this using nunjucks macro options, if you are using the nunjucks macro by setting the expanded option to true on the individual accordion items you want to be expanded. You can configure sections to start and stay open, but not stay closed.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accordion" (How it works > Starting with sections open).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Accordion > How it works > Do not disable sections
title: Accordion: Do not disable sections
statement: Disabling controls is normally confusing for users. If there is no content for a section, either remove the section or, if this would be confusing for your users, explain why there is no content when the section is opened.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Accordion" (How it works > Do not disable sections).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Back link
title: Back link
statement: Use the back link component to help users go back to the previous page in a multi-page transaction. Although browsers have a back button, some sites break when you use it - so many users avoid it, instead of losing their progress in a service. Also, not all users are aware of the back button.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Back link" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Back link > When to use this component
title: Back link: When to use this component
statement: Always include the Back link component on GOV.UK Question pages in your service. You can include a back link on other pages within a multi-page transaction, if it makes sense to do so.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Back link" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Back link > When not to use this component
title: Back link: When not to use this component
statement: Never use the back link component together with the Breadcrumbs component. If necessary, you should do research with your users to learn which they find more helpful in your service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Back link" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Back link > How it works
title: Back link: How it works
statement: Always place back links at the top of a page, before the element. Placing them here means that the 'Skip to main content' link allows the user to skip all navigation links, including the back link. Make sure the link takes users to the previous page they were on, in the state they last saw it. Where possible, ensure the back link works even when JavaScript is not available. If this is not possible, you should hide the back link when JavaScript is not available. There are 2 ways to use the back link component. You can use HTML or, if you are using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro. Using the default link text ('Back') is ideal for services with a simple journey. For example, applying for a National Insurance number. Users will only ever go back to the previous page in the service. For more complex user journeys, consider using different link text, like 'Go back to [page]'. For example, in an admin system with many different areas. In this case, if you used 'Back', it might not be clear to users what they are going back to.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Back link" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Back link > How it works > Back links on dark backgrounds
title: Back link: Back links on dark backgrounds
statement: Use the govuk-back-link--inverse modifier class to show a white link on a dark background – for example, in headers, custom components, and patterns with darker backgrounds. Make sure all users can see the back link – the background colour must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 with white to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (minimum), level AA.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Back link" (How it works > Back links on dark backgrounds).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Breadcrumbs
title: Breadcrumbs
statement: The breadcrumbs component helps users to understand where they are within a website’s structure and move between levels.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Breadcrumbs" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Breadcrumbs > When to use this component
title: Breadcrumbs: When to use this component
statement: Use the breadcrumbs component when you need to help users understand and move between the multiple levels of a website.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Breadcrumbs" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Breadcrumbs > When not to use this component
title: Breadcrumbs: When not to use this component
statement: Do not use the breadcrumbs component on websites with a flat structure, or to show progress through a linear journey or transaction. If you’re using other navigational elements on the page, such as a sidebar, consider whether your users need the additional support of breadcrumbs.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Breadcrumbs" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Breadcrumbs > How it works
title: Breadcrumbs: How it works
statement: Always place breadcrumbs at the top of a page, before the element. Placing them here means that the 'Skip to main content' link allows the user to skip all navigation links, including breadcrumbs. The breadcrumbs should start with your 'home' page and end with the parent section of the current page. There are 2 ways to use the breadcrumbs component. You can use HTML or, if you are using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Breadcrumbs" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Breadcrumbs > How it works > Collapsing breadcrumbs on mobile devices
title: Breadcrumbs: Collapsing breadcrumbs on mobile devices
statement: If you have long breadcrumbs you can configure the component to only show the first and last items on mobile devices. To do this, add a govuk-breadcrumbs--collapse-on-mobile class to the outer element of the component HTML. Or if you’re using Nunjucks, add collapseOnMobile: true to the Nunjucks macro as shown in this example.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Breadcrumbs" (How it works > Collapsing breadcrumbs on mobile devices).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Breadcrumbs > How it works > Breadcrumbs on dark backgrounds
title: Breadcrumbs: Breadcrumbs on dark backgrounds
statement: Use the govuk-breadcrumbs--inverse modifier class to show white links and arrows on dark backgrounds – for example, in headers, custom components, and patterns with darker backgrounds. Make sure all users can see the breadcrumbs – the background colour must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 with white to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (minimum), level AA.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Breadcrumbs" (How it works > Breadcrumbs on dark backgrounds).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Button > When to use this component
title: Button: When to use this component
statement: Use the button component to help users carry out an action like starting an application or saving their information.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Button" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Button > How it works
title: Button: How it works
statement: Write button text in sentence case, describing the action it performs. For example: - ‘Start now’ at the start of your service - ‘Sign in’ to an account a user has already created - ‘Continue’ when the service does not save a user’s information - ‘Save and continue’ when the service does save a user’s information - ‘Save and come back later’ when a user can save their information and come back later - ‘Add another’ to add another item to a list or group - ‘Pay’ to make a payment - ‘Confirm and send’ on a Check answers page that does not have any legal content a user must agree to - ‘Accept and send’ on a Check answers page that has legal content a user must agree to - ‘Sign out’ when a user is signed in to an account You may need to include more or different words to better describe the action. For example, ‘Add another address’ and ‘Accept and claim a tax refund’. Align the primary action button to the left edge of your form. There are 2 ways to use the Button component. You can use HTML or, if you are using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Button" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Button > How it works > Default buttons
title: Button: Default buttons
statement: Use a default button for the main call to action on a page. Avoid using multiple default buttons on a single page. Having more than one main call to action reduces their impact, and makes it harder for users to know what to do next.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Button" (How it works > Default buttons).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Button > How it works > Start buttons
title: Button: Start buttons
statement: Use a start button for the main call to action on your service’s Start page. Start buttons do not usually submit form data, so use a link tag instead of a button tag.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Button" (How it works > Start buttons).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Button > How it works > Secondary buttons
title: Button: Secondary buttons
statement: Use secondary buttons for secondary calls to action on a page. Pages with too many calls to action make it hard for users to know what to do next. Before adding lots of secondary buttons, try to simplify the page or break the content down across multiple pages. You can also group default and secondary buttons together.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Button" (How it works > Secondary buttons).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Button > How it works > Warning buttons
title: Button: Warning buttons
statement: Warning buttons are designed to make users think carefully before they use them. They only work if used very sparingly. Most services should not need one. Only use warning buttons for actions with serious destructive consequences that cannot be easily undone by a user. For example, permanently deleting an account. When letting users carry out an action like this, it's a good idea to include an additional step which asks them to confirm it. In this instance, use another style of button for the initial call to action, and a warning button for the final confirmation. Do not only rely on the red colour of a warning button to communicate the serious nature of the action. This is because not all users will be able to see the colour or will understand what it signifies. Make sure the context and button text make clear what will happen if the user selects it.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Button" (How it works > Warning buttons).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Button > How it works > Buttons on dark backgrounds
title: Button: Buttons on dark backgrounds
statement: Use the govuk-button--inverse modifier class to show white buttons on dark backgrounds – for example, in headers, custom components, and patterns with darker backgrounds. Make sure all users can see the button – the white button and background colour must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (minimum), level AA.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Button" (How it works > Buttons on dark backgrounds).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Button > How it works > Disabled buttons
title: Button: Disabled buttons
statement: Disabled buttons have poor contrast and can confuse some users, so avoid them if possible. Only use disabled buttons if research shows it makes the user interface easier to understand.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Button" (How it works > Disabled buttons).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Button > How it works > Grouping buttons
title: Button: Grouping buttons
statement: Use a button group when two or more buttons are placed together. Any links within a button group will automatically align with the buttons.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Button" (How it works > Grouping buttons).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Button > How it works > Stop users from accidentally sending information more than once
title: Button: Stop users from accidentally sending information more than once
statement: Sometimes, users double click buttons because they: - have used operating systems where they have to double click items to make them work - are experiencing a slow connection which means they are not given feedback on their action quickly enough - have motor impairments such as hand tremors which cause them to click the button involuntarily In some cases, this can mean their information is sent twice. For example, the GOV.UK Notify team discovered that a number of users were receiving invitations twice, because the person sending them was double clicking the 'send' button. If you are working in production and research shows that users are frequently sending information twice, you can configure the button to ignore the second click. To do this, set the data-prevent-double-click attribute to true. You can do this directly in the HTML or, if you’re using Nunjucks, you can use the Nunjucks macro as shown in this example. This feature will prevent double clicks for users that have JavaScript enabled, however you should also think about the issue server-side to protect against attacks. In the case of slow connections, aim to give the user information about what’s happening, for example, by showing a loading spinner or a modal, before using data-prevent-double-click.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Button" (How it works > Stop users from accidentally sending information more than once).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Character count
title: Character count
statement: Help users know how much text they can enter when there is a limit on the number of characters.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Character count" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Character count > When to use this component
title: Character count: When to use this component
statement: Always test your service without a character count first. Only use the character count component when there is a good reason for limiting the number of characters users can enter. For example, if there is: - evidence that users are likely to enter more information than they need to - a legal or technical reason that means an entry must be no more than a certain number of characters
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Character count" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Character count > When not to use this component
title: Character count: When not to use this component
statement: If your users keep hitting the character limit imposed by the backend of your service then try to increase the limit rather than use a character count.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Character count" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Character count > How it works
title: Character count: How it works
statement: It tells users how many characters they have remaining as they type into a Textarea component with a character limit. Users will get updates at a pace that works best for the way they interact with the textarea. This means: - sighted users will see a count message that updates as they type - screen reader users will hear the count announcement when they stop typing. This component does not restrict the user from entering information. The user can enter more than the character limit, but are told they've entered too many characters. This lets them type or copy and paste their full answer, then edit it down. The count message appears below the textarea so that: - it’s clearly separate from any hint text or error message above the textarea - if it’s below the visible screen area, users will still see it again when they scroll down to send their response This component uses JavaScript. If JavaScript is not available, users will see a static message in place of the count message, telling them how many characters they can enter. There are 2 ways to use the character count component. You can use HTML or, if you’re using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Character count" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Character count > How it works > If you’re asking more than one question on the page
title: Character count: If you’re asking more than one question on the page
statement: If you're asking more than one question on the page, do not set the contents of the as the page heading. Read more about asking multiple questions on Question pages.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Character count" (How it works > If you’re asking more than one question on the page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Character count > How it works > Consider if a word count is more helpful
title: Character count: Consider if a word count is more helpful
statement: In some cases it may be more helpful to show a word count. For example, if your question requires a longer answer. Do this by setting data-count-type="words" and then data-maxlength in the component markup. For example, for a word limit of 150 set these options as: data-count-type="words" data-maxlength="150".
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Character count" (How it works > Consider if a word count is more helpful).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Character count > How it works > Avoid narrow limits
title: Character count: Avoid narrow limits
statement: When using a character count, try to set the limit higher than most users will need. Find out what this is by doing user research and data analysis.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Character count" (How it works > Avoid narrow limits).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Character count > How it works > If the limit is far higher than users are likely to reach
title: Character count: If the limit is far higher than users are likely to reach
statement: You can choose to display a character count message when the length of text within the textarea passes a certain 'threshold' of characters. This is useful when a character limit is needed due to the technical limitations of the service, but users are unlikely to reach that limit. To do this, set the threshold in the component markup as a percentage. For example, data-threshold="75" will show the count message only when the user has entered a length of text that's 75% of the limit or more. Screen reader users will hear the character limit when they first interact with a textarea using the threshold option. Sighted users will not see anything until the count message is shown – though you might choose to include the character limit in the hint text.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Character count" (How it works > If the limit is far higher than users are likely to reach).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Character count > How it works > Error messages
title: Character count: Error messages
statement: Error messages should be styled like this: If a user tries to send their response with too many characters, you must show an error message above the field as well as the count message below it. The error message tells users what went wrong and how to fix it. The count message provides live feedback and updates as a user types. The input shows a red border only when the user tries to enter more than the character limit. If the number of characters is within the limit, the input does not show this border even when there's been an error. We felt it might cause the user difficulty if the border disappeared once they started typing. Make sure errors follow GOV.UK guidance on writing error messages and have specific error messages for specific error states.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Character count" (How it works > Error messages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Character count > How it works > If the input is empty
title: Character count: If the input is empty
statement: Say ‘Enter [whatever it is]’. For example, ‘Enter a summary’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Character count" (How it works > If the input is empty).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Character count > How it works > If the input is too long
title: Character count: If the input is too long
statement: Say ‘[whatever it is] must be [number] characters or less’. For example, ‘Summary must be 400 characters or less’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Character count" (How it works > If the input is too long).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Checkboxes
title: Checkboxes
statement: Let users select one or more options by using the checkboxes component.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Checkboxes" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Checkboxes > When to use this component
title: Checkboxes: When to use this component
statement: Use the checkboxes component when you need to help users: - select multiple options from a list - toggle a single option on or off
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Checkboxes" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Checkboxes > When not to use this component
title: Checkboxes: When not to use this component
statement: Do not use the checkboxes component if users can only choose one option from a selection. In this case, use the Radios component.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Checkboxes" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Checkboxes > How it works
title: Checkboxes: How it works
statement: Always position checkboxes to the left of their labels. This makes them easier to find, especially for users of screen magnifiers. Unlike with radios, users can select multiple options from a list of checkboxes. Do not assume that users will know how many options they can select based on the visual difference between radios and checkboxes alone. If needed, add a hint explaining this, for example, 'Select all that apply'. Do not pre-select checkbox options as this makes it more likely that users will: - not realise they’ve missed a question - submit the wrong answer Order checkbox options alphabetically by default. In some cases, it can be helpful to order them from most-to-least common options. For example, you could order options for ‘What is your nationality?’ based on population size. Group checkboxes together in a with a that describes them, as shown in the examples on this page. This is usually a question, like ‘How would you like to be contacted?’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Checkboxes" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Checkboxes > How it works > If you’re asking one question on the page
title: Checkboxes: If you’re asking one question on the page
statement: If you're asking just one question per page as recommended, you can set the contents of the as the page heading. This is good practice as it means that users of screen readers will only hear the contents once. Read more about why and how to set legends as headings. There are 2 ways to use the checkboxes component. You can use HTML or, if you’re using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Checkboxes" (How it works > If you’re asking one question on the page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Checkboxes > How it works > If you’re asking more than one question on the page
title: Checkboxes: If you’re asking more than one question on the page
statement: If you're asking more than one question on the page, do not set the contents of the as the page heading. Read more about asking multiple questions on Question pages.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Checkboxes" (How it works > If you’re asking more than one question on the page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Checkboxes > How it works > Checkbox items with hints
title: Checkboxes: Checkbox items with hints
statement: You can add hints to checkbox items to provide additional information about the options. Keep each hint to a single short sentence, without any full stops. Screen readers will read out the entire text when users interact with an item. This could frustrate users if the text is long. Do not use links in hint text.
