While screen readers will read out the link text when describing the item, they usually do not tell users the text is a link.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Checkboxes" (How it works > Checkbox items with hints).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Checkboxes > How it works > Add an option for ‘none’
title: Checkboxes: Add an option for ‘none’
statement: When 'none' would be a valid answer, give users the option to check a box to say none of the other options apply to them – without this option, users would have to leave all of the boxes unchecked. Giving users this option also makes sure they do not skip the question by accident. Remember to start by asking one question per page in your service. You might be able to remove the need for a 'none' option by asking the user a better question or filtering them out with a ‘filter question’ beforehand. The GOV.UK Service Manual has guidance on designing good questions. Show the ‘none’ option last. Separate it from the other options using a divider. The text is usually the word ‘or’. Write a label that repeats the key part of the question. For example, for the question 'Will you be travelling to any of these countries?', say 'No, I will not be travelling to any of these countries.' To enable some JavaScript that unchecks all other checkboxes when the user clicks 'None', add the exclusive behaviour to the 'none' checkbox. If JavaScript is unavailable, and a user selects both the ‘none’ checkbox and another checkbox, display an error message.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Checkboxes" (How it works > Add an option for ‘none’).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Checkboxes > How it works > Smaller checkboxes
title: Checkboxes: Smaller checkboxes
statement: Use standard-sized checkboxes in most cases. However, smaller checkboxes work well on pages where it’s helpful to make them less visually prominent. For example, on a page of search results, the main user need is to see the results. Using smaller checkboxes lets users see and change search filters without distracting them from the main content. Small checkboxes can work well on information dense screens in services designed for repeat use, like caseworking systems. In services like these, the risk that they will not be noticed is lower because users return to the screen multiple times.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Checkboxes" (How it works > Smaller checkboxes).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Checkboxes > How it works > Error messages
title: Checkboxes: Error messages
statement: Error messages should be styled like this: Make sure errors follow the guidance in the Error message component and have specific error messages for specific error states.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Checkboxes" (How it works > Error messages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Checkboxes > How it works > If users check both a 'none' checkbox and another checkbox
title: Checkboxes: If users check both a 'none' checkbox and another checkbox
statement: Say: Select [option label text] or select ‘[none of the above label text]’ For example: Select countries you will be travelling to, or select ‘No, I will not be travelling to any of these countries’
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Checkboxes" (How it works > If users check both a 'none' checkbox and another checkbox).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookie banner
title: Cookie banner
statement: Allow users to accept or reject cookies which are not essential to making your service work.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookie banner" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookie banner > When to use this component
title: Cookie banner: When to use this component
statement: Use this component if your service sets any cookies on a user’s device. Remember, you must: - tell users about the cookies your service sets on their device - let users accept or reject any cookies that are not essential to providing your service The term ‘non-essential cookies’ includes: - HTML5 local storage - service workers - any other technologies that store files on the user’s device This cookie banner and the Cookies page pattern are based on the approach to getting cookie consent used on the GOV.UK website. This component page shows several options for using a cookie banner, based on the types of cookies you’re using in the service. We also tell you what to cover in your cookie banner, with some text examples.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookie banner" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookie banner > When to use this component > Before you start
title: Cookie banner: Before you start
statement: Audit and categorise your cookies as shown in the cookies page pattern to help you choose the best option for your service. You must not take the information on this page as legal advice. Your organisation is responsible and accountable for what they do to comply with data protection legislation, such as: - Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations (PECR) - General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) Check with your organisation's privacy expert to see how data protection legislation affects your website and service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookie banner" (When to use this component > Before you start).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookie banner > How it works
title: Cookie banner: How it works
statement: Show the cookie banner every time the user accesses your service until they either: - accept or reject cookies using the buttons in the cookie banner - save their cookie preferences on your service’s Cookies page Once the user has accepted or rejected cookies, the cookie banner should: - hide the cookie banner message - show a confirmation message – and a 'hide' button to let the user close the banner - set a cookie to save the user’s preferences for 1 year Make sure the cookie banner does not: - show when the user visits again, once their preferences have been saved - set any non-essential cookies unless the user accepted them on a previous visit Position the cookie banner after the opening tag and before the ’skip to main content‘ link. If you're using the Nunjucks page template, use the bodyStart block. Do not make the Cookie banner component ‘sticky’ to the top of the page by using position: fixed or any other method. This is to make sure it does not cover or obscure any content which has a focus applied. This is to comply with WCAG 2.2 success criterion 2.4.11 Focus not obscured (minimum).
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookie banner" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookie banner > How it works > Option 1: If you’re only using essential cookies
title: Cookie banner: Option 1: If you’re only using essential cookies
statement: You can choose not to have a cookie banner if the service only sets essential or 'strictly necessary' cookies, as these do not need user consent. However, you must tell users that you set essential cookies. You can do this with a cookies page – link to this page in the footer.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookie banner" (How it works > Option 1: If you’re only using essential cookies).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookie banner > How it works > Option 2: If you set non-essential cookies for users (with or without JavaScript)
title: Cookie banner: Option 2: If you set non-essential cookies for users (with or without JavaScript)
statement: You can choose this option if your service sets non-essential cookies on the server – your service may also set non-essential cookies on the client. To get consent from the user, display the cookie banner inside a form that lets them submit their choice to accept or reject cookies. All users will be able to see the banner as this approach does not rely on JavaScript. Here's an example of a cookie banner inside a form: Once the user has accepted or rejected cookies and set their cookie preferences, reload the page to show a confirmation message. Here's an example of a confirmation message inside a form:
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookie banner" (How it works > Option 2: If you set non-essential cookies for users (with or without JavaScript)).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookie banner > How it works > Show the same message to all users
title: Cookie banner: Show the same message to all users
statement: In the cookie banner, tell the user about all the cookies you’re using in the service – whether they've enabled JavaScript or not. This way, you will not need to ask the user to give their consent again on their next visit.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookie banner" (How it works > Show the same message to all users).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookie banner > How it works > Help users keep their place using progressive enhancement
title: Cookie banner: Help users keep their place using progressive enhancement
statement: If the user is entering information into a form as part of the service, they might lose their place when they submit their choice to accept or reject cookies. To help users running JavaScript on their device, you can write some JavaScript code to let them submit their choice and prevent the page from reloading. Include all possible messages that the user could see in the cookie banner when the page loads. Hide these with the hidden HTML attribute where needed. Here's an example of a progressively enhanced cookie banner that includes all possible messages which are hidden using HTML – the cookie banner message is shown using JavaScript to remove the hidden attribute: Here's the same example of a progressively enhanced cookie banner, with the confirmation message shown instead:
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookie banner" (How it works > Help users keep their place using progressive enhancement).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookie banner > How it works > Option 3: If you set non-essential cookies, but only using client-side JavaScript
title: Cookie banner: Option 3: If you set non-essential cookies, but only using client-side JavaScript
statement: You can choose to make your banner only work with JavaScript if your service only needs to set non-essential cookies on the client. When the page loads, the hidden html attribute hides the component, as well as all the cookie banner messages it contains, which the user might otherwise see.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookie banner" (How it works > Option 3: If you set non-essential cookies, but only using client-side JavaScript).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookie banner > How it works > Show the cookie banner only to users that have enabled JavaScript
title: Cookie banner: Show the cookie banner only to users that have enabled JavaScript
statement: Use JavaScript to show cookie banner messages to users that have not accepted or rejected cookies by removing the hidden attribute as needed. Write your own JavaScript code so that when the user accepts or rejects cookies, the cookie banner will: - hide the cookie message by adding the hidden attribute - show a confirmation message by removing its hidden attribute - give the confirmation message the tabindex="-1" and role="alert" attributes – this will allow the element to be focused so assistive technology can read the message - shift focus to the confirmation message Here’s an example:
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookie banner" (How it works > Show the cookie banner only to users that have enabled JavaScript).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookie banner > How it works > When the user has accepted cookies
title: Cookie banner: When the user has accepted cookies
statement: Show a confirmation message confirming that the user has either accepted or rejected cookies by removing the hidden attribute.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookie banner" (How it works > When the user has accepted cookies).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookie banner > What to cover in your cookie banner
title: Cookie banner: What to cover in your cookie banner
statement: Include the name of the service in the banner heading to help users understand that the cookies you’re talking about are different from the ones set by the main GOV.UK platform. You’ll need to change the example cookie banner text if your service: - allows third parties to set cookies (tell the user that both your organisation and other organisations will be setting cookies) - uses cookies for reasons other than collecting analytics information or remembering the user’s settings Keep the text as short as possible while making sure it’s an accurate description of how you use cookies. For example, if you use more than one ‘functional’ cookie and there’s not enough space to mention what each of them does, you could ask for permission to set cookies so ‘you can use as many of the service’s features as possible’. See the Cookies page pattern for more advice on writing about cookies.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookie banner" (What to cover in your cookie banner).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookie banner > What to cover in your cookie banner > If you’re using essential cookies and analytics cookies
title: Cookie banner: If you’re using essential cookies and analytics cookies
statement: You can use this example text for a service which sets essential and analytics cookies. Analytics cookies are those set by your organisation to collect information about how people are using your digital service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookie banner" (What to cover in your cookie banner > If you’re using essential cookies and analytics cookies).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookie banner > What to cover in your cookie banner > If you’re using more than one type of non-essential cookie
title: Cookie banner: If you’re using more than one type of non-essential cookie
statement: You can use this example text for a service that set: - essential cookies - analytics cookies - functional cookies to remember the user’s settings but are not essential
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookie banner" (What to cover in your cookie banner > If you’re using more than one type of non-essential cookie).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookie banner > Creating a cookies page
title: Cookie banner: Creating a cookies page
statement: You’ll need a Cookies page in your service as well as a cookie banner.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookie banner" (Creating a cookies page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookie banner > Brand refresh of the Cookie banner component
title: Cookie banner: Brand refresh of the Cookie banner component
statement: In June 2025, we updated this component to support a wider refresh of the GOV.UK brand. You should now use the refreshed GOV.UK branding. If your service has updated to GOV.UK Frontend v6.0.0 or later, you no longer need to use the govukRebrand feature flag and should remove it.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookie banner" (Brand refresh of the Cookie banner component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input
title: Date input
statement: Use the date input component to help users enter a memorable date or one they can easily look up.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input > When to use this component
title: Date input: When to use this component
statement: Use the date input component when you’re asking users for a date they’ll already know, or can look up without using a calendar.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input > When not to use this component
title: Date input: When not to use this component
statement: Do not use the date input component if users are unlikely to know the exact date of the event you’re asking about. Read more in the Ask users for dates pattern.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input > How it works
title: Date input: How it works
statement: The date input component consists of 3 fields to let users enter a day, month and year. The 3 date fields are grouped together in a with a that describes them, as shown in the examples on this page. This is usually a question, like ‘What is your date of birth?’. If you’re asking one question per page in your service, you can set the contents of the as the page heading. This is good practice as it means that users of screen readers will only hear the contents once. Read more about why and how to set legends as headings. Make sure that any example dates you use in hint text are valid for the question being asked. Accept month names written out in full or abbreviated form (for example, ‘january’ or ‘jan’) as some users may enter months in this way. There are 2 ways to use the date input component. You can use HTML or, if you’re using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro. Never automatically tab users between the fields of the date input because this can be confusing and may clash with normal keyboard controls.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input > How it works > If you’re asking more than one question on the page
title: Date input: If you’re asking more than one question on the page
statement: If you're asking more than one question on the page, do not set the contents of the as the page heading. Read more about asking multiple questions on question pages.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" (How it works > If you’re asking more than one question on the page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input > How it works > Use the autocomplete attribute for a date of birth
title: Date input: Use the autocomplete attribute for a date of birth
statement: Use the autocomplete attribute on the date input component when you're asking for a date of birth. This lets browsers autofill the information on a user's behalf if they’ve entered it previously. To do this, set the autocomplete attribute on the 3 fields to bday-day, bday-month and bday-year. See how to do this in the HTML and Nunjucks tabs in the following example. If you are working in production you’ll need to do this to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.3.5: Identify input purpose, level AA.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" (How it works > Use the autocomplete attribute for a date of birth).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input > How it works > Error messages
title: Date input: Error messages
statement: If you’re highlighting the whole date, style all the fields like this: If you’re highlighting just one field - either the day, month or year - only style the field that has an error. The error message must say which field has an error, like this: Make sure errors follow the guidance in the Error message component and have specific error messages for specific error states. If there’s more than one error, show the highest priority error message. In order of priority, show error messages about: - missing or incomplete information - information that cannot be correct (for example, the number ‘13’ in the month field) - information that fails validation for another reason
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" (How it works > Error messages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input > How it works > If nothing is entered
title: Date input: If nothing is entered
statement: Highlight the date input as a whole. Say ‘Enter [whatever it is]’. For example, ‘Enter your date of birth’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" (How it works > If nothing is entered).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input > How it works > If the date is incomplete
title: Date input: If the date is incomplete
statement: Highlight the day, month or year field where the information is missing or incomplete. If more than one field is missing information, highlight the fields the user needs to fill in. Say ‘[whatever it is] must include a [whatever is missing]’. For example, ‘Date of birth must include a month’, ‘Date of birth must include a day and month’ or ‘Year must include 4 numbers’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" (How it works > If the date is incomplete).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input > How it works > If the date entered cannot be correct
title: Date input: If the date entered cannot be correct
statement: For example, ‘13’ in the month field cannot be correct. Highlight the day, month or year field with the incorrect information. Or highlight the date as a whole if there’s incorrect information in more than one field, or it's not clear which field is incorrect. Say ‘[Whatever it is] must be a real date’. For example, ‘Date of birth must be a real date’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" (How it works > If the date entered cannot be correct).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input > How it works > If the date is in the future when it needs to be in the past
title: Date input: If the date is in the future when it needs to be in the past
statement: Highlight the date input as a whole. Say ‘[whatever it is] must be in the past’. For example, ‘Date of birth must be in the past’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" (How it works > If the date is in the future when it needs to be in the past).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input > How it works > If the date is in the future when it needs to be today or in the past
title: Date input: If the date is in the future when it needs to be today or in the past
statement: Highlight the date input as a whole. Say ‘[whatever it is] must be today or in the past’. For example, ‘Date of birth must be today or in the past’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" (How it works > If the date is in the future when it needs to be today or in the past).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input > How it works > If the date is in the past when it needs to be in the future
title: Date input: If the date is in the past when it needs to be in the future
statement: Highlight the date input as a whole. Say ‘[whatever it is] must be in the future’. For example, ‘The date your course ends must be in the future’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" (How it works > If the date is in the past when it needs to be in the future).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input > How it works > If the date is in the past when it needs to be today or in the future
title: Date input: If the date is in the past when it needs to be today or in the future
statement: Highlight the date input as a whole. Say ‘[whatever it is] must be today or in the future’. For example, ‘The date your course ends must be today or in the future’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" (How it works > If the date is in the past when it needs to be today or in the future).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input > How it works > If the date must be the same as or after another date
title: Date input: If the date must be the same as or after another date
statement: Highlight the date input as a whole. Say ‘[whatever it is] must be the same as or after [date and optional description]’. For example, ‘The date your course ends must be the same as or after 1 September 2017 when you started the course’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" (How it works > If the date must be the same as or after another date).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input > How it works > If the date must be after another date
title: Date input: If the date must be after another date
statement: Highlight the date input as a whole. Say ‘[whatever it is] must be after [date and optional description]’. For example, ‘The day your course ends must be after 1 September 2017’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" (How it works > If the date must be after another date).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input > How it works > If the date must be the same as or before another date
title: Date input: If the date must be the same as or before another date
statement: Highlight the date input as a whole. Say ‘[whatever it is] must be the same as or before [date and optional description]’. For example, ‘The date of Gordon’s last exam must be the same as or before 31 August 2017 when they left school’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" (How it works > If the date must be the same as or before another date).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input > How it works > If the date must be before another date
title: Date input: If the date must be before another date
statement: Highlight the date input as a whole. Say ‘[whatever it is] must be before [date and optional description]’. For example, ‘The date of Gordon’s last exam must be the same as or before 31 August 2017’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" (How it works > If the date must be before another date).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Date input > How it works > If the date must be between two dates
title: Date input: If the date must be between two dates
statement: Highlight the date input as a whole. Say ‘[whatever it is] must be between [date] and [date and optional description]’. For example, ‘The date your contract started must be between 1 September 2017 and 30 September 2017 when you were self-employed’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Date input" (How it works > If the date must be between two dates).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Details
title: Details
statement: Make a page easier to scan by letting users reveal more detailed information only if they need it.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Details" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Details > When to use this component
title: Details: When to use this component
statement: Use the details component to make a page easier to scan when it contains information that only some users will need.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Details" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Details > When not to use this component
title: Details: When not to use this component
statement: Do not use the details component to hide information that the majority of your users will need.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Details" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Details > Decide between using details, accordions and tabs
title: Details: Decide between using details, accordions and tabs
statement: The Details component, Accordion component, and Tabs component all hide sections of content which a user can choose to reveal. Use the details component instead of tabs or an accordion if you only have 1 section of content. The details component is less visually prominent than tabs and accordions, so tends to work better for content which is not as important to users.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Details" (Decide between using details, accordions and tabs).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Details > How it works
title: Details: How it works
statement: The details component is a short link that shows more detailed help text when a user clicks on it. There are 2 ways to use the details component. You can use HTML or, if you are using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Details" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Details > How it works > Write clear link text
title: Details: Write clear link text
statement: Make the link text short and descriptive so users can quickly work out if they need to click on it.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Details" (How it works > Write clear link text).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Error message
title: Error message
statement: This guidance is for government teams that build online services. To find information and services for the public, go to GOV.UK. Follow the Validation pattern and show an error message when there is a validation error. In the error message explain what went wrong and how to fix it.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Error message" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Error message > When to use this component
title: Error message: When to use this component
statement: Show an error message next to the field and in the Error summary component when there is a validation error. Use standard messages for different components.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Error message" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Error message > When not to use this component
title: Error message: When not to use this component
statement: Do not use error messages to tell a user that they are not eligible or do not have permission to do something. Or to tell them about a lack of capacity or other problem the user cannot fix - because the problem is with the service rather than with the information the user has provided. Instead, take the user to a page that explains the problem (for example, telling them why they’re not eligible) and provides useful information about what to do next. There are separate patterns for: - 'There is a problem with the service' pages - 'Page not found' pages - 'Service unavailable' pages
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Error message" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Error message > How it works
title: Error message: How it works
statement: For each error: - put the message in red after the question text and hint text - use a red border to visually connect the message and the question it belongs to - if the error relates to a specific field within the question, give it a red border and refer to that field in the error message - for example: "you must enter a year" Do not clear any form fields when showing the Error message component. Keep both passing and failing answers. Keeping information that caused errors helps users to: - see what went wrong - edit their previous answer - avoid re-entering information To help screen reader users, the error message component includes a hidden 'Error:' before the error message. These users will hear, for example, "Error: The date your passport was issued must be in the past". If your error message is written in another language, you can change the prefix as needed, as shown in this example. Summarise all errors at the top of the page the user is on using an Error summary component. There are 2 ways to use the error message component. You can use HTML or, if you are using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Error message" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Error message > How it works > Match up error messages to labels
title: Error message: Match up error messages to labels
statement: Error messages should directly include language from the question or fieldset label. This helps match up the error message with the relevant form field. Here are some examples of label and error message pairs. Example 1: - Label: ‘How many hours do you work a week?’ - Error message: ‘Enter how many hours you work a week’ Example 2: - Label: ‘Address line 1’ - Error message: ‘Enter address line 1, typically the building and street’
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Error message" (How it works > Match up error messages to labels).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Error message > How it works > Be clear and concise
title: Error message: Be clear and concise
statement: Describe what has happened and tell them how to fix it. The message must be in plain English, use positive language and get to the point. Do not use: - technical jargon like ‘form post error’, ‘unspecified error’ and ‘error 0x0000000643’ - words like ‘forbidden’, ‘illegal’, ‘you forgot’ and ‘prohibited’ - ‘please’ because it implies a choice - ‘sorry’ because it does not help fix the problem - ‘valid’ and ‘invalid’ because they do not add anything to the message - humourous, informal language like ‘oops’ Do not give an example in the error message if there is an example on the screen. For example, if you are asking for a National Insurance number and include ‘QQ 12 34 56 C’ as hint text, do not include an example in the error message. Above all, aim for clarity. Read the message out loud to see if it sounds like something you would say.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Error message" (How it works > Be clear and concise).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Error message > How it works > Be consistent
title: Error message: Be consistent
statement: Use the same message next to the field and in the Error summary component so they: - look, sound and mean the same - make sense out of context - reduce the cognitive effort needed to understand what has happened
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Error message" (How it works > Be consistent).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Error message > How it works > Be specific
title: Error message: Be specific
statement: General errors are not helpful to everyone. They do not make sense out of context. Avoid messages like: - ‘An error occurred’ - ‘Answer the question’ - ‘Select an option’ - ‘Fill in the field’ - ‘This field is required’ Different errors need different messages. For example, text fields may be: - empty - too long - too short - using characters that are not allowed - in the wrong format An error for a specific situation is more helpful. It will tell someone what has happened and how to fix it.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Error message" (How it works > Be specific).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Error message > How it works > Use instructions and descriptions
title: Error message: Use instructions and descriptions
statement: Some errors work better as instructions and some work better as descriptions. For example: - ‘Enter your first name’ is clearer, more direct and natural than ‘First name must have an entry’ - ‘Enter a first name that is 35 characters or less’ is wordier, less direct and natural than ‘First name must be 35 characters or less’ - ‘Enter a date after 31 August 2017 for when you started the course’ is wordier, less direct and natural than ‘Date you started the course must be after 31 August 2017’ Use both instructions and descriptions, but use them consistently. For example, use an instruction for empty fields like ‘Enter your name’, but a description like ‘Name must be 35 characters or less’ for entries that are too long.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Error message" (How it works > Use instructions and descriptions).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Error message > How it works > Use error message templates
title: Error message: Use error message templates
statement: Use template messages for common errors on: - Addresses pattern - Character count component - Checkboxes component - Date input component - Email address pattern - File upload component - Names pattern - National Insurance numbers pattern - Radios component - Phone numbers pattern - Text input component - Textarea component
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Error message" (How it works > Use error message templates).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Error message > How it works > Track errors
title: Error message: Track errors
statement: Find out how often people see them. This will let you: - improve content - A/B test variations - redesign a journey
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Error message" (How it works > Track errors).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Error summary
title: Error summary
statement: Use this component at the top of a page to summarise any errors a user has made. When a user makes an error, you must show both an error summary and an Error message component next to each answer that contains an error.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Error summary" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Error summary > When to use this component
title: Error summary: When to use this component
statement: Always show an error summary when there is a validation error, even if there’s only one.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Error summary" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Error summary > How it works
title: Error summary: How it works
statement: You must: - move keyboard focus to the error summary (the govuk-frontend javascript will do this for you) - include the heading ‘There is a problem’ - link to each of the answers that have validation errors - make sure the error messages in the error summary are worded the same as those which appear next to the inputs with errors As well as showing an error summary, follow the Validation pattern - for example, by adding ‘Error: ’ to the beginning of the page so screen readers read it out as soon as possible. And make your error messages clear and concise. There are 2 ways to use the error summary component. You can use HTML or, if you are using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Error summary" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Error summary > How it works > Linking from the error summary to each answer
title: Error summary: Linking from the error summary to each answer
statement: You must link the errors in the error summary to the answer they relate to. For questions that require a user to answer using a single field, like a file upload, select, textarea, text input or character count, link to the field. When a user has to enter their answer into multiple fields, such as the day, month and year fields in the date input component, link to the first field that contains an error. If you do not know which field contains an error, link to the first field. For questions that require a user to select one or more options from a list using radios or checkboxes, link to the first radio or checkbox.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Error summary" (How it works > Linking from the error summary to each answer).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Error summary > How it works > Where to put the error summary
title: Error summary: Where to put the error summary
statement: Put the error summary at the top of the main container. If your page includes breadcrumbs or a back link, place it below these, but above the .
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Error summary" (How it works > Where to put the error summary).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Exit this page
title: Exit this page
statement: Give users a way to quickly and safely exit a service, website or application. For service journeys, you must use this component with the Exit a page quickly pattern.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Exit this page" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Exit this page > When to use this component
title: Exit this page: When to use this component
statement: Use the component on pages with sensitive information that could: - put someone at risk of abuse or retaliation - reveal someone’s plans to avoid or escape from harm For example, when a potential victim is using a service to help them leave a domestic abuser. You can use this component on either: - all the pages in a service - parts of the journey with sensitive information You can also use this component for standalone content pages, such as dashboards and guidance.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Exit this page" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Exit this page > When not to use this component
title: Exit this page: When not to use this component
statement: Do not use this component if the service or content is unlikely to put a user at risk. See the Exit a page quickly pattern for examples of at-risk and sensitive topics. The 'Exit this page' component is a Button component that has been marked up with additional CSS and JavaScript functionality, to make it work in a specific way. Keep in mind that seeing this component might discourage certain users from using your service. If the user does not identify themselves as being at risk, they might see the button on a service and decide it’s not relevant to them.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Exit this page" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Exit this page > How it works
title: Exit this page: How it works
statement: There are 2 ways to use this component. You can use HTML or, if you're using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Exit this page" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Exit this page > How it works > Adding the button
title: Exit this page: Adding the button
statement: Position the component at the top of your page, above the beginning of the grid ( ) but still within the width container ( ).
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Exit this page" (How it works > Adding the button).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Exit this page > How it works > Choosing a different website to load
title: Exit this page: Choosing a different website to load
statement: When activated, the component by default will take the user to the homepage of BBC Weather. You can change this if there’s a more appropriate site for your users. Avoid websites that might show personalised pages (such as frequently visited, last visited or suggested links), as this content could put the user at risk.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Exit this page" (How it works > Choosing a different website to load).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Exit this page > How it works > Adding the secondary link
title: Exit this page: Adding the secondary link
statement: Add the code for the 'secondary link' into the layout file of your service. The 'secondary link' is an additional govuk-skip-link that works in a similar way. Place it under the page template's default skip link at the very top of the body. When the user interacts with the 'secondary link', it will perform the same action as pressing the button to activate Exit this Page. The href for the 'secondary link' should be the same as the URL used for the button. The component will still work if the 'secondary link' is not added, but it'll be less accessible overall.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Exit this page" (How it works > Adding the secondary link).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Exit this page > Consider what to do with user session data
title: Exit this page: Consider what to do with user session data
statement: You’ll need to decide if your service will store the user’s session data after they’ve activated the Exit this page component and left your service. For example, you could do this in 2 steps: 1. replace the default website link to a URL in your service, that when visited, will clear the user's session data 2. redirect the user to another website, such as BBC Weather
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Exit this page" (Consider what to do with user session data).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Exit this page > Enhancement features
title: Exit this page: Enhancement features
statement: These features are included in the component and should work automatically, as long as the user has enabled Javascript in their browser. You do not need to do anything to make these work.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Exit this page" (Enhancement features).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Exit this page > Enhancement features > Loading overlay
title: Exit this page: Loading overlay
statement: The 'loading overlay' will appear immediately when the user activates Exit this page. The overlay helps users with slow connections clear their screen until the browser loads the next page.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Exit this page" (Enhancement features > Loading overlay).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Exit this page > Enhancement features > Showing progress for 'shift key' presses
title: Exit this page: Showing progress for 'shift key' presses
statement: To show the user the number of times they’ve pressed the shift button, there’s a series of 3 progress dots under the button, provided as a visual enhancement. Each time the shift key is pressed, one of the dots will be filled. The user has 5 seconds to press the shift key 3 times. After that, the sequence and progress dots will reset.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Exit this page" (Enhancement features > Showing progress for 'shift key' presses).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Exit this page > Accessibility features and considerations
title: Exit this page: Accessibility features and considerations
statement: In addition to the Exit this page button itself, users have 2 other options to activate the component. We've tested and iterated both of these options to be accessible, reliable and as discreet as possible for users. The keyboard option, where the user can press shift 3 times, gives users a discreet way to activate the component, particularly keyboard-only users. We considered options that used a single key press (such as the 'esc' key), but we could not be confident that this would not interfere with other user actions. The 'secondary link' option is a hidden link in the tab order of the page. This gives users of assistive technology an easier way to reliably activate the component. To help users of speech recognition software activate the 'secondary link' more discreetly, we considered changing the link text to something else that hid its real purpose. However, we decided this was more likely to confuse users. We're also confident about the other ways users can use speech recognition software to activate the 'secondary link' without saying the text out loud, such as choosing the link as an item number on a list.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Exit this page" (Accessibility features and considerations).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Feedback
title: Feedback
statement: Ask users to give feedback about their experience using your service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Feedback" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Feedback > When to use this component
title: Feedback: When to use this component
statement: Use the Feedback component to give users the opportunity to give feedback at any point in their journey. This helps you gather a wide range of feedback to understand how well your service performs and improvements you can make.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Feedback" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Feedback > How it works
title: Feedback: How it works
statement: Show the Feedback component on as many pages of your service as you can. The component is designed to allow users to give feedback at any time without distracting them.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Feedback" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Feedback > How it works > Ask for feedback at the end of each page
title: Feedback: Ask for feedback at the end of each page
statement: Place the Feedback component just before the GOV.UK footer component. If your service is using Nunjucks, you can use the GOV.UK Frontend page template to add the Feedback component by placing it in the footerStart template block.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Feedback" (How it works > Ask for feedback at the end of each page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Feedback > How it works > Asking users for feedback
title: Feedback: Asking users for feedback
statement: The heading and message in the Feedback component should tell users: - why you want feedback - what you'll do with their feedback Also try to give users some idea about: - how long it'll take to give feedback - the difference between giving feedback and asking for support You must include a link to a feedback page, which could be either: - a GOV.UK feedback page - a feedback page page of your own, if you need to ask specific questions
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Feedback" (How it works > Asking users for feedback).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Fieldset > When to use this component
title: Fieldset: When to use this component
statement: Use the fieldset component when you need to show a relationship between multiple form inputs. For example, you may need to group a set of text inputs into a single fieldset when asking for an address in your service. If you’re using the examples or macros for a Radios component, Checkboxes component or Date input component, the fieldset will already be included.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Fieldset" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Fieldset > How it works
title: Fieldset: How it works
statement: The first element inside a fieldset must be a legend which describes the group of inputs. This could be a question, such as ‘What is your current address?’ or a statement like ‘Personal details’. If you’re asking just one question per page in your service as recommended, you can set the contents of the as the page heading, as shown in the example below. This is good practice as it means that users of screen readers will only hear the contents once. Read more about why and how to set legends as headings. On Question pages in your service containing a group of inputs, including the question as the legend helps users of screen readers to understand that the inputs are all related to that question. Include general help text in the legend if it would help the user fill in the form, and you cannot write it as hint text. However, try to keep it as short as possible.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Fieldset" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: File upload
title: File upload
statement: This guidance is for government teams that build online services. To find information and services for the public, go to GOV.UK. Help users select and upload a file.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "File upload" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: File upload > When to use this component
title: File upload: When to use this component
statement: You should only ask users to upload something if it’s critical to the delivery of your service. We improved the component in March 2025, so you’ll need to enable the improved File upload component as a new feature. Read a blog post about design tips for helping users upload things.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "File upload" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: File upload > How it works
title: File upload: How it works
statement: To upload a file, the user can either: - use the ‘Choose file’ button - drag and drop a file into the file upload input area
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "File upload" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: File upload > How it works > Let users reuse uploaded files
title: File upload: Let users reuse uploaded files
statement: Make sure users can easily reuse a previously uploaded file within a single journey, unless doing so would be a major security or privacy concern. For example, a user might need to upload a photo of their driving licence to prove their identity, and again to prove their address. You can make it easier for the user to reuse a file by showing it as an option for the user to select so they do not need to upload it again. Consider users on public devices before choosing to make the file available to preview or download. There are 2 ways to use the file upload component. You can use HTML or, if you’re using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "File upload" (How it works > Let users reuse uploaded files).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: File upload > How it works > Error messages
title: File upload: Error messages
statement: Error messages should be styled like this: Make sure errors follow the guidance in the Error message component and have specific error messages for specific error states.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "File upload" (How it works > Error messages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: File upload > How it works > If no file has been selected
title: File upload: If no file has been selected
statement: Say ‘Select a [whatever they need to select]’. For example, ‘Select a report’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "File upload" (How it works > If no file has been selected).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: File upload > How it works > If the file is the wrong file type
title: File upload: If the file is the wrong file type
statement: Say ‘The selected file must be a [list of file types]’. For example, ‘The selected file must be a CSV or ODS’ or ‘The selected file must be a JPG, BMP, PNG, TIF or PDF’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "File upload" (How it works > If the file is the wrong file type).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: File upload > How it works > If the file is too big
title: File upload: If the file is too big
statement: Say ‘The selected file must be smaller than [largest file size]’. For example, ‘The selected file must be smaller than 2MB’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "File upload" (How it works > If the file is too big).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: File upload > How it works > If there is a limit on how many files the user can select
title: File upload: If there is a limit on how many files the user can select
statement: Say ‘You can only select up to [highest number] files at the same time’. For example, ‘You can only select up to 10 files at the same time’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "File upload" (How it works > If there is a limit on how many files the user can select).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: File upload > Using the improved File upload component
title: File upload: Using the improved File upload component
statement: In March 2025, we introduced changes to the File upload component that service teams can opt in to as part of GOV.UK Frontend 5.9.0. The improved component is intended to: - fix accessibility issues - improve the user experience - allow text in the component to be translated We recommend service teams start using the latest component to improve the experience for users. However, it's a visual change from the previous component and might affect existing designs and layouts. To let teams migrate at their own pace, the improvements are only enabled if you use the javascript macro option or extra markup in your HTML. This example shows you how to enable the improved File upload component:
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "File upload" (Using the improved File upload component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: File upload > Using the improved File upload component > Changes in the improved component
title: File upload: Changes in the improved component
statement: To make it easier for users to drag and drop files, we’ve made the drop zone: - bigger - visible at all times - more visually responsive to user interactions We’ve also changed the ‘Choose file’ button to be more consistent with the secondary button in the Button component. Service teams can change the text on the button and in the ‘No file chosen’ message. We decided to make this text changeable for translation purposes and to let teams be specific about the file to upload. However, teams should aim to keep the text as short as possible for accessibility purposes. For example, screen reader users might find it difficult to use the component if the text is too long. All the text in the component can now be translated to match the language of the page content when JavaScript is running.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "File upload" (Using the improved File upload component > Changes in the improved component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: File upload > Using the improved File upload component > Improvements for assistive technology users
title: File upload: Improvements for assistive technology users
statement: Users of Dragon, a speech recognition tool, cannot activate their browser’s native file inputs by using commands for interacting with web page controls. They have to rely on mouse commands or keyboard commands, which take multiple steps to activate the component. With the improved File upload component, users can say commands for interacting with web page controls to choose files. However, due to browser security features, this may not work right away or on subsequent interactions on the same page. If users cannot interact with the component, they'll first need to perform another action, such as a mouse click.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "File upload" (Using the improved File upload component > Improvements for assistive technology users).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: GOV.UK footer
title: GOV.UK footer
statement: The GOV.UK footer provides copyright, licensing and other information about your service. If you use the page template, you'll also get the footer without having to add it, as it's included by default. However, if you want to customise the default footer, read the page template guidance about customising components.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "GOV.UK footer" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: GOV.UK footer > How it works
title: GOV.UK footer: How it works
statement: Add a copyright notice to the footer to clarify who owns the copyright. For GOV.UK services, add the coat of arms to keep things consistent with the rest of GOV.UK. Make it clear whether content is available for re-use - and if it is, under what sort of licence. Use an Open Government Licence unless you have permission from the National Archives to use a different type of licence.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "GOV.UK footer" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: GOV.UK footer > Adding links
title: GOV.UK footer: Adding links
statement: You can add links to: - your service's privacy notice - your service's accessibility statement - your service's Cookies page - terms and conditions - help content Use ‘Privacy’, ‘Accessibility’, ‘Cookies’ and ‘Terms and conditions’ for the link text. If you include links to ‘help’ pages within the GOV.UK footer component, make sure to place those links consistently within the footer content. Also make sure that ‘help’ links always function in a similar way across each page. This is to comply with WCAG 2.2 success criterion 3.2.6 Consistent help.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "GOV.UK footer" (Adding links).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: GOV.UK footer > Adding secondary navigation
title: GOV.UK footer: Adding secondary navigation
statement: Only add secondary GOV.UK navigation if you’re creating a GOV.UK service, and you want users to be able to navigate away from the service to somewhere else on the GOV.UK website. For example, you probably don’t want to encourage a user to navigate away from a linear, form-type service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "GOV.UK footer" (Adding secondary navigation).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: GOV.UK footer > Brand refresh of the GOV.UK footer component
title: GOV.UK footer: Brand refresh of the GOV.UK footer component
statement: In June 2025, we updated this component to support a wider refresh of the GOV.UK brand. You should now use the refreshed GOV.UK branding. If your service has updated to GOV.UK Frontend v6.0.0 or later, you no longer need to use the govukRebrand feature flag and should remove it. With these changes, the GOV.UK header and GOV.UK footer components should now only be used by services on the GOV.UK website. Services outside of the GOV.UK proposition should stop using the header and footer components and instead create their own.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "GOV.UK footer" (Brand refresh of the GOV.UK footer component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Generic header
title: Generic header
statement: Use this generic version of the header to tell users they’re using a government service that’s not part of the GOV.UK website.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Generic header" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Generic header > When to use this component
title: Generic header: When to use this component
statement: Use the Generic header component if your service is both: - a public-facing government service - not on the GOV.UK website (meaning that your service is not part of the GOV.UK proposition) This is to bring consistency and maintain user trust in journeys that move between the GOV.UK website and other government websites and services. This component also helps ensure your non-GOV.UK service does not: - identify itself as being part of GOV.UK - use the crown or GOV.UK logotype in the header - use the GDS Transport typeface - use the GOV.UK brand colours See the guidance on if your service is not on GOV.UK in the Service manual.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Generic header" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Generic header > When not to use this component
title: Generic header: When not to use this component
statement: If your service is hosted on one of these gov.uk domains, you must use the GOV.UK header component instead: - gov.uk/[myservice] - [myservice].service.gov.uk - [myblog].blog.gov.uk
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Generic header" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Generic header > How it works
title: Generic header: How it works
statement: If you use the page template, you’ll first need to replace the default GOV.UK header in the page template with the Generic header component. Use the Generic header component to display your own: - brand logo - homepage link - font for your service name (instead of GDS Transport) You must also follow the steps in the Using GOV.UK Frontend without GOV.UK branding guidance to remove other GOV.UK brand elements elsewhere in your service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Generic header" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Generic header > How it works > Using your own brand logo
title: Generic header: Using your own brand logo
statement: Follow your organisation’s guidelines and best practice to show your brand logo. To make your logo image as accessible and optimised as possible, also see: - Design System guidance on using images - Image guidance for GOV.UK content and publishers
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Generic header" (How it works > Using your own brand logo).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Generic header > How it works > Homepage link
title: Generic header: Homepage link
statement: By default, the homepage link points to /, which is the top level of your service’s domain. You should customise the link to point to wherever makes the most sense for your service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Generic header" (How it works > Homepage link).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Generic header > How it works > Do not show navigation links in the Generic header component
title: Generic header: Do not show navigation links in the Generic header component
statement: As with the GOV.UK header component, you should not use the Generic header component to show navigation links. Use the Service navigation component instead to let users navigate to different parts of your service and find useful links and tools.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Generic header" (How it works > Do not show navigation links in the Generic header component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: GOV.UK header
title: GOV.UK header
statement: The GOV.UK header component tells users they’re using a service on GOV.UK and lets them use GOV.UK-wide tools. Also known as the GOV.UK masthead. If you use the page template, you'll also get the GOV.UK header without having to add it, as it's included by default. However, if you want to customise the default GOV.UK header, read the page template guidance about customising components.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "GOV.UK header" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: GOV.UK header > When to use this component
title: GOV.UK header: When to use this component
statement: If your service is being hosted on one of these domains, use the GOV.UK header component: - gov.uk/[myservice] - [myservice].service.gov.uk - [myblog].blog.gov.uk You must use the GOV.UK header component at the top of every page. This is to maintain user trust as they move around the GOV.UK website and other government websites and services. The Service Manual explains why it’s important for you to make your service look like GOV.UK.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "GOV.UK header" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: GOV.UK header > When not to use this component
title: GOV.UK header: When not to use this component
statement: If your service is not hosted on one of the gov.uk domains outlined, you must not use the GOV.UK header component as it’s not considered part of GOV.UK. Use the Generic header component instead to show your own organisation’s branding.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "GOV.UK header" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: GOV.UK header > How it works
title: GOV.UK header: How it works
statement: Together, the GOV.UK header and Service navigation component both ensure users get a consistent experience on GOV.UK. This also assures users that they’re in the right place to use your service and to understand that GOV.UK functions as one website. For guidance on how to plan your header and navigation, see the Help users navigate a service pattern.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "GOV.UK header" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: GOV.UK header > How it works > Default GOV.UK header
title: GOV.UK header: Default GOV.UK header
statement: Most services on GOV.UK should use the default GOV.UK header. It should only show the GOV.UK logo and any GOV.UK-wide links and tools to help your users. Do not add the menu of GOV.UK topic links to your service’s GOV.UK header.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "GOV.UK header" (How it works > Default GOV.UK header).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: GOV.UK header > How it works > Do not show service name or navigation links in the GOV.UK header
title: GOV.UK header: Do not show service name or navigation links in the GOV.UK header
statement: You can no longer use the GOV.UK header to show service name or navigation links. Use the Service navigation component instead. The Help users navigate a service pattern shows how the GOV.UK header and Service navigation components work together to help users know they’re using your service and navigate around it.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "GOV.UK header" (How it works > Do not show service name or navigation links in the GOV.UK header).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: GOV.UK header > How it works > GOV.UK header with One Login
title: GOV.UK header: GOV.UK header with One Login
statement: GOV.UK One Login maintains their own header on the Let users navigate to their GOV.UK One Login and sign out easily page.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "GOV.UK header" (How it works > GOV.UK header with One Login).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: GOV.UK header > Brand refresh of the GOV.UK header component
title: GOV.UK header: Brand refresh of the GOV.UK header component
statement: In June 2025, we updated this component to support a wider refresh of the GOV.UK brand. You should now use the refreshed GOV.UK branding. If your service has updated to GOV.UK Frontend v6.0.0 or later, you no longer need to use the govukRebrand feature flag and should remove it. With these changes, the GOV.UK header and GOV.UK footer components should now only be used by services on the GOV.UK website. Services outside of the GOV.UK proposition should stop using the header and footer components and instead create their own.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "GOV.UK header" (Brand refresh of the GOV.UK header component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Inset text > When to use this component
title: Inset text: When to use this component
statement: Use the inset text component to differentiate a block of text from the content that surrounds it, for example: - quotes - examples - additional information about the page
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Inset text" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Inset text > When not to use this component
title: Inset text: When not to use this component
statement: Some users do not notice inset text if it’s used on complex pages or near to other visually prominent elements. For this reason, avoid using inset text as a way of highlighting very important information that users need to see. If you need to draw attention to very important content, like legal information, use the Warning text component instead.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Inset text" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Inset text > How it works
title: Inset text: How it works
statement: Use inset text very sparingly - it’s less effective if it’s overused. There are 2 ways to use the inset text component. You can use HTML or, if you’re using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Inset text" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Language navigation
title: Language navigation
statement: The Language navigation component helps users choose and switch between languages when using a service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Language navigation" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Language navigation > When to use this component
title: Language navigation: When to use this component
statement: Use the Language navigation component when you can provide your service in more than one language. For example, to help users switch from a page in English to a version of the same page in Welsh. How you use this component will depend on whether you offer a choice of languages for: - specific pages within your service - your whole service
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Language navigation" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Language navigation > When not to use this component
title: Language navigation: When not to use this component
statement: Do not use this component unless you can provide all the same key information on a page in another language.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Language navigation" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Language navigation > How it works
title: Language navigation: How it works
statement: The Language navigation component shows users a choice of languages and helps the user choose and switch between them. Use the native name of each language, such as Cymraeg for Welsh. This helps speakers of that language recognise the link. The component does not translate content. You'll need to create, test and maintain content for all the languages you offer your service in. See some of the other things you might need to do as part of designing services that offer multiple languages. Make sure the user does not lose any data they've entered when they navigate to another language. Do not ask the user to re-enter information they've already given.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Language navigation" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Language navigation > How it works > Placement on pages
title: Language navigation: Placement on pages
statement: Where you place the Language navigation component helps users understand whether they can use your entire service or only specific pages in another language. Choose a single consistent location that works best for your users. Use the same placement throughout your service in all languages. This helps users in many ways. For example, some users often switch languages throughout their journey as a way to check their understanding of a page.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Language navigation" (How it works > Placement on pages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Language navigation > How it works > If you only offer specific pages in another language
title: Language navigation: If you only offer specific pages in another language
statement: You could place the language navigation at the top of a page, after the h1 element. If you choose to place the language navigation elsewhere on a page, it should be in a sensible place in the page heading structure with its own visible or hidden heading.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Language navigation" (How it works > If you only offer specific pages in another language).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Language navigation > How it works > If you offer your whole service in another language
title: Language navigation: If you offer your whole service in another language
statement: If users can change the language for your whole service, you can place the Language navigation component into the Service navigation component. The Service navigation component includes options to align the language navigation with navigation items as shown in this example.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Language navigation" (How it works > If you offer your whole service in another language).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Language navigation > How it works > Ensure hidden text and attributes are in the correct languages
title: Language navigation: Ensure hidden text and attributes are in the correct languages
statement: The code in this component contains a navigation landmark and some hidden text to help users, including users of assistive technology. Make sure to translate these attributes as needed. aria-label (or ariaLabel in Nunjucks) labels the component's navigation landmark. By default the label is 'language', which will be announced by a screen reader as 'language navigation'. Translate this label to the language of the page it's on. Hidden text within the link for each language option (or languageDescriptionText in Nunjucks) explains what the link will do. For example, 'Change the language to English'. Translate these to the language you're linking to.
