citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Language navigation" (How it works > Ensure hidden text and attributes are in the correct languages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Language navigation > How it works > Language navigation on dark backgrounds
title: Language navigation: Language navigation on dark backgrounds
statement: Use the govuk-language-navigation--inverse modifier class to show white links and text on a dark background – for example, inside a Service navigation with a dark background. Make sure all users can see the language navigation – the background colour must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 with white to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (minimum), level AA.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Language navigation" (How it works > Language navigation on dark backgrounds).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Language navigation > Designing services that offer multiple languages
title: Language navigation: Designing services that offer multiple languages
statement: GOV.UK Content and publishing guidance gives some advice on things you need to consider when translating content. Test your service with users in your intended language to spot potential issues such as word inaccuracies and cultural differences. The Service Manual for Wales shows how you can consider bilingualism in your research.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Language navigation" (Designing services that offer multiple languages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Language navigation > Designing services that offer multiple languages > Internationalisation and localisation
title: Language navigation: Internationalisation and localisation
statement: If you choose to show larger parts of your service in another language, consider if you need to translate the text within components such as navigation, buttons and accordions. Our components use English by default but include methods to translate text within them. Follow our documentation on how to localise GOV.UK Frontend. For some languages, you’ll need to modify components to make sure text displays well and is understandable by users of assistive technologies. For example, to show languages using scripts that read from right to left, such as Arabic, you’ll need to make changes to components and layouts. See W3C’s introduction to internationalisation for more about some of the things you might need to consider. Keep in mind that language and regional differences can affect the format users expect to see and enter information such as names, numbers and addresses.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Language navigation" (Designing services that offer multiple languages > Internationalisation and localisation).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Notification banner
title: Notification banner
statement: Use a notification banner to tell the user about something they need to know about, but that’s not directly related to the page content.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Notification banner" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Notification banner > When to use this component
title: Notification banner: When to use this component
statement: A notification banner lets you tell the user about something that’s not directly relevant to the thing they’re trying to do on that page of the service. For example: - telling the user about a problem that’s affecting the service as a whole (for example, delays in processing applications because of an emergency) - telling the user about something that affects them in particular (for example, an approaching deadline they need to meet) - telling the user about the outcome of something they've just done on a previous page (for example, confirming that an email has been sent)
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Notification banner" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Notification banner > When not to use this component
title: Notification banner: When not to use this component
statement: Use notification banners sparingly. There’s evidence that people often miss them, and using them too often is likely to make this problem worse. If the information is directly relevant to the thing the user is doing on that page, put the information in the main page content instead. Use an Inset text component or Warning text component if it needs to stand out. Do not: - use a notification banner to tell the user about validation errors - use an Error message component and Error summary component instead - show a notification banner and an Error summary component on the same page - just show the error summary
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Notification banner" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Notification banner > How it works
title: Notification banner: How it works
statement: Position a notification banner immediately before the page h1. The notification banner should be the same width as the page's other content, such as components, headings and body text. For example, if the other content takes up two-thirds of the screen on desktop devices, then the notification banner should also take up two-thirds. Read about how to lay out pages. Use role="region" and aria-labelledby="govuk-notification-banner-title" (with id="govuk-notification-banner-title" on ) so that screen reader users can navigate to the notification banner. Avoid showing more than one notification banner on the same page. Instead, combine the messages in a single notification banner. If the messages are too different to combine, only show the highest priority notification banner.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Notification banner" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Notification banner > How it works > Notification banner headings
title: Notification banner: Notification banner headings
statement: You can use headings in the govuk-notification-bannercontent to help structure your content. Avoid using headings for single-line notifications that do not need them.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Notification banner" (How it works > Notification banner headings).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Notification banner > Telling the user about a problem that affects the whole service
title: Notification banner: Telling the user about a problem that affects the whole service
statement: Use a ‘neutral’ blue notification banner if the user needs to know about a problem with the service as a whole. For example: - in a service that lets the user register or apply for something, they might need to know that it’s taking longer than usual to process applications because of an emergency - in an account-type service, the user might need to know that the service will be down for scheduled maintenance If your service is on GOV.UK and it’s affected by an emergency, ask your department’s content team to make a request to add a downtime message on GOV.UK content that links to it. If your service is getting more demand than usual, check that you’ve set up There is a problem with the service pages and Service unavailable pages, and the wording is up to date.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Notification banner" (Telling the user about a problem that affects the whole service).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Notification banner > Telling the user about something that’s happening elsewhere
title: Notification banner: Telling the user about something that’s happening elsewhere
statement: Use a ‘neutral’ notification banner if the user needs to know about something that’s happening elsewhere in the service. For example: - in a case working system, the user might need to know that there are new cases waiting for their attention - in an account-type service, you might need to tell the user that there’s a deadline approaching or that a payment is overdue
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Notification banner" (Telling the user about something that’s happening elsewhere).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Pagination
title: Pagination
statement: Help users navigate forwards and backwards through a series of pages. For example, search results or guidance that's divided into multiple website pages.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Pagination" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Pagination > When to use this component
title: Pagination: When to use this component
statement: Consider using pagination when: - showing all the content on a single page makes the page take too long to load - most users will only need the content on the first page or first few pages
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Pagination" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Pagination > When not to use this component
title: Pagination: When not to use this component
statement: Only break up content onto separate pages if it improves the performance or usability of your service. Avoid using the 'infinite scroll' technique to automatically load content when the user approaches the bottom of the page. This causes problems for keyboard users. Do not use this Pagination component for linear journeys – for example, where you’re asking the user to complete a form. Instead, use the Button component (usually a 'Continue' button) to let the user move to the next page – and a Back link component to let them move to the previous page.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Pagination" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Pagination > How it works
title: Pagination: How it works
statement: Add the pagination component after the content on each page that you're paginating. View an example of Pagination in a standard GOV.UK page template. Do not show pagination if there's only one page of content. Redirect users to the first page if they enter a URL of a page that no longer exists.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Pagination" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Pagination > For navigating between content pages
title: Pagination: For navigating between content pages
statement: Use the 'block' style of pagination to let users navigate through related content that has been split across multiple pages. Stack the links vertically, so they’re more obvious to screen magnifier users when they’re zoomed in. You can use link labels to give context on what the neighbouring pages are about.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Pagination" (For navigating between content pages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Pagination > For navigating between pages of items
title: Pagination: For navigating between pages of items
statement: Use a list-type layout if users need to navigate through pages of similar items. For example, a list of search results or a list of cases in a case working system. Show the page number in the page so that screen reader users know they’ve navigated to a different page. For example, 'Search results (page 1 of 4)'. Show an appropriate number of pages to fit the horizontal space available. For smaller screens, show page numbers for: - the current page - previous and next pages - first and last pages For larger screens, show page numbers for: - the current page - at least one page immediately before and after the current page - first and last pages Use ellipses (…) to replace any skipped pages. For example: - [1] 2 … 100 - 1 [2] 3 … 100 - 1 2 [3] 4 … 100 - 1 2 3 [4] 5 … 100 - 1 … 4 [5] 6 … 100 - 1 … 97 [98] 99 100 - 1 … 98 [99] 100 - 1 … 99 [100]
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Pagination" (For navigating between pages of items).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Pagination > For navigating between pages of items > First and last pages
title: Pagination: First and last pages
statement: Do not show the previous page link on the first page – and do not show the next page link on the last page.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Pagination" (For navigating between pages of items > First and last pages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Pagination > For navigating between pages of items > Filtering and sorting
title: Pagination: Filtering and sorting
statement: Consider adding filtering or sorting options if it helps users to find what they need in a long list of pages. For example, the business support finder on GOV.UK has filtering options. If the user filters or sorts the list of pages, apply this to the whole list (not just the current page) and redirect them back to the first page of the new results. Set defaults to minimise how many pages most users have to click through to find what they need.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Pagination" (For navigating between pages of items > Filtering and sorting).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Panel
title: Panel
statement: The Panel component is a visible container used to highlight important content.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Panel" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Panel > When to use this component
title: Panel: When to use this component
statement: Use the Panel component to display important information within: - Confirmation pages, which tell the user they’ve successfully completed the transaction - Interruption pages, which pause the user journey to give important information
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Panel" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Panel > When not to use this component
title: Panel: When not to use this component
statement: Never use the Panel component to highlight any other information.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Panel" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Panel > How it works
title: Panel: How it works
statement: There are 2 ways to use the panel component. You can use HTML or, if you are using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Panel" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Panel > How it works > Confirmation panel
title: Panel: Confirmation panel
statement: The confirmation panel is part of a Confirmation page and tells the user the outcome of their journey as a heading. You might also give more detailed information as description text.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Panel" (How it works > Confirmation panel).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Panel > How it works > How to write confirmation panel text
title: Panel: How to write confirmation panel text
statement: Keep your panel text brief, as it's only meant for a high-level explanation of what has happened. Aim to use short words and phrases to make sure highlighted information is easy to read at different screen sizes. For example, shorter amounts of information are less likely to wrap around the panel, which can happen when using the zoom function on mobiles.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Panel" (How it works > How to write confirmation panel text).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Panel > Interruption panel
title: Panel: Interruption panel
statement: The interruption panel is part of an Interruption page and shows the user important information that they’d miss if shown any other way. Within the panel is a button that the user must interact with to resume their journey. The information itself is usually shown as heading with some description text, possibly with bullet points and numbered steps.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Panel" (Interruption panel).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Password input > When to use this component
title: Password input: When to use this component
statement: Use this component whenever you need users to create or enter a password. Before using this component, you should also read the guidance on the Ask users for passwords pattern and Creating user accounts pattern.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Password input" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Password input > When not to use this component
title: Password input: When not to use this component
statement: Do not use this component to ask for any information other than a password. Use a Text input component to ask for other security information, such as: - multi-factor authentication codes - answers to security questions - other personally identifiable information Also see the Confirm a phone number pattern.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Password input" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Password input > How it works
title: Password input: How it works
statement: This component allows users to enter a password, with an option to show what they’ve entered as plain text. This allows users to visually check their password before they submit it, which helps them reduce errors and choose passwords that are more unique and secure.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Password input" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Password input > How it works > Error messages
title: Password input: Error messages
statement: If the user enters their account details incorrectly, do not reveal whether they got the username or password wrong. Clear any information entered into the password input. Revealing the source of the error can help fraudsters break into people’s accounts. See how to handle incorrect login attempts and help users who forget their password in the Ask users for passwords pattern.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Password input" (How it works > Error messages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Password input > How it works > Showing and hiding passwords
title: Password input: Showing and hiding passwords
statement: Hide passwords by default until the user chooses to show it using the ‘show’ button. Users might not be in a private space when entering or creating a password, so you should hide passwords by default. If you do choose to include two or more password inputs on a page, the ‘show’ and ‘hide’ toggles and labels for each password input must be different. For example, you can label: - the first input as 'Password' with a toggle of 'show password' - the second input as 'Re-enter password' with a toggle of 'show re-entered password'
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Password input" (How it works > Showing and hiding passwords).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Password input > How it works > Avoid adding a ‘confirm password’ field
title: Password input: Avoid adding a ‘confirm password’ field
statement: It’s not necessary to add a second password field, also known as a ‘confirm password’ field, particularly as this component allows users to show and hide passwords. See Research on this component and why we decided having a second field is not helpful for users.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Password input" (How it works > Avoid adding a ‘confirm password’ field).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Password input > How it works > Define the input’s type as ‘password’
title: Password input: Define the input’s type as ‘password’
statement: When the form is submitted, the password input should automatically change its type to password, if it has not already done so. This is to prevent browsers from remembering it as a previously-provided value and potentially displaying it as an autofill option on non-password inputs.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Password input" (How it works > Define the input’s type as ‘password’).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Password input > How it works > Use the autocomplete attribute
title: Password input: Use the autocomplete attribute
statement: Use the autocomplete attribute on password inputs to help users complete forms faster. Autocomplete indicates to browsers and password managers what kind of password is needed so it can be entered for the user. Set the autocomplete attribute to new-password if the user is creating a password. Otherwise, use current-password. Many browsers will autofill password inputs, even when the autocomplete attribute is missing or set to off.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Password input" (How it works > Use the autocomplete attribute).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Password input > How it works > Allow copy and paste
title: Password input: Allow copy and paste
statement: Always allow users to copy and paste in password fields. People may have very good reasons why they want to do this, for example if they’re using a password manager.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Password input" (How it works > Allow copy and paste).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Password input > How it works > Copying text from password fields
title: Password input: Copying text from password fields
statement: Users can copy any text from a password field when it’s set on ‘show’ – this is a feature of browser behaviour and cannot be overridden. This can be useful for users, such as to save a password that the browser has suggested into a separate password manager.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Password input" (How it works > Copying text from password fields).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Password input > How it works > Avoid restricting the user's input
title: Password input: Avoid restricting the user's input
statement: See the Ask users for passwords pattern to see how to help users choose strong passwords. Support all the characters users may need to enter a password, including numbers and symbols. If you must place password restrictions on users, such as for technical or security reasons, be clear and consistent. Any restrictions must be identical wherever the user creates or enters a password. If you change the restrictions over time, you must continue to support existing user passwords or ask them to set a new one.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Password input" (How it works > Avoid restricting the user's input).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Password input > How it works > Do not use maxlength to restrict password length
title: Password input: Do not use maxlength to restrict password length
statement: Users will not get any feedback when they’ve reached the maxlength and their text input has been truncated. This happens when a user has pasted text from elsewhere or it’s been autofilled by a password manager. If you must restrict the length of a password, show an error message instead using the Validation pattern.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Password input" (How it works > Do not use maxlength to restrict password length).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Phase banner
title: Phase banner
statement: Use the phase banner component to show users your service is still being worked on.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Phase banner" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Phase banner > When to use this component
title: Phase banner: When to use this component
statement: Services hosted on a service.gov.uk domain must use the phase banner until they pass a live assessment.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Phase banner" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Phase banner > How it works
title: Phase banner: How it works
statement: There are 2 ways to use the phase banner component. You can use HTML or, if you are using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro. Use an alpha banner when your service is in alpha, and a beta banner if your service is in private or public beta. Show the Phase banner inside the element, directly after either: - the Service navigation component - the GOV.UK header component (if your service does not use the Service navigation component) If you use Nunjucks, use the headerEnd block to place the Phase banner on your page. See 'Add extra content at the start or end of the element' in 'Page template: Blocks and options'. Phase banners are shown across all pages of a service, so users should understand it as a service-level message. You can choose to place the Phase banner in a more appropriate place for your service, however you’ll need to customise the component and provide your own CSS code to make it show correctly.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Phase banner" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Phase banner > How it works > Collect feedback from users
title: Phase banner: Collect feedback from users
statement: Use the Feedback component to ask users to give feedback about your service and provide them with a link to a feedback page. Find out what feedback you need to collect at each phase in the GOV.UK Service Manual.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Phase banner" (How it works > Collect feedback from users).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Radios > When to use this component
title: Radios: When to use this component
statement: Use the radios component when users can only select one option from a list.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Radios" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Radios > When not to use this component
title: Radios: When not to use this component
statement: Do not use the radios component if users might need to select more than one option. In this case, you should use the Checkboxes component instead.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Radios" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Radios > How it works
title: Radios: How it works
statement: Always position radios to the left of their labels. This makes them easier to find, especially for users of screen magnifiers. Unlike with checkboxes, users can only select one option from a list of radios. Do not assume that users will know how many options they can select based on the visual difference between radios and checkboxes alone. If needed, add a hint explaining this, for example, 'Select one option'. Do not pre-select radio options as this makes it more likely that users will: - not realise they've missed a question - submit the wrong answer Users cannot go back to having no option selected once they have selected one, without refreshing their browser window. Therefore, you should include 'None of the above' or 'I do not know' if they are valid options. Order radio options alphabetically by default. In some cases, it can be helpful to order them from most-to-least common options. For example, you could order options for 'Where do you live?' based on population size. However you should do this with extreme caution as it can reinforce bias in your service. If in doubt, order alphabetically. Group radios together in a with a that describes them, as shown in the examples on this page. This is usually a question, like ‘Where do you live?’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Radios" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Radios > How it works > If you’re asking one question on the page
title: Radios: If you’re asking one question on the page
statement: If you are asking just one question per page in your service as recommended, you can set the contents of the as the page heading. This is good practice as it means that users of screen readers will only hear the contents once. Read more about why and how to set legends as headings. There are 2 ways to use the radios component. You can use HTML or, if you are using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Radios" (How it works > If you’re asking one question on the page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Radios > How it works > If you’re asking more than one question on the page
title: Radios: If you’re asking more than one question on the page
statement: If you're asking more than one question on the page, do not set the contents of the as the page heading. Read more about asking multiple questions on Question pages.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Radios" (How it works > If you’re asking more than one question on the page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Radios > How it works > Inline radios
title: Radios: Inline radios
statement: In some cases, you can choose to display radios 'inline' beside one another (horizontally). Only use inline radios when: - the question only has two options - both options are short Remember that on small screens such as mobile devices, the radios will still be 'stacked' on top of one another (vertically).
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Radios" (How it works > Inline radios).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Radios > How it works > Radio items with hints
title: Radios: Radio items with hints
statement: You can add hints to radio items to provide additional information about the options. Keep each hint to a single short sentence, without any full stops. Screen readers will read out the entire text when users interact with an item. This could frustrate users if the text is long. Do not use links in hint text. While screen readers will read out the link text when describing the item, they usually do not tell users the text is a link.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Radios" (How it works > Radio items with hints).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Radios > How it works > Radio items with a text divider
title: Radios: Radio items with a text divider
statement: If one or more of your radio options is different from the others, it can help users if you separate them using a text divider. The text is usually the word ‘or’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Radios" (How it works > Radio items with a text divider).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Radios > How it works > Smaller radios
title: Radios: Smaller radios
statement: Use standard-sized radios in nearly all cases. However, smaller versions work well on pages where it’s helpful to make them less visually prominent. For example, on a page of search results, the primary user need is to see the results. Using smaller radios lets users see and change search filters without distracting them from the main content. Small radios can work well on information dense screens in services designed for repeat use, like caseworking systems. In services like these, the risk that they will not be noticed is lower because users return to the screen multiple times.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Radios" (How it works > Smaller radios).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Radios > How it works > Error messages
title: Radios: Error messages
statement: Display an error message if the user has not: - selected any radios - answered a conditionally revealed question Error messages should be styled like this: Make sure errors follow the guidance in the Error message component and have specific error messages for specific error states.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Radios" (How it works > Error messages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Radios > How it works > If it’s a ‘yes’ or ‘no’ question
title: Radios: If it’s a ‘yes’ or ‘no’ question
statement: Say ‘Select yes if [whatever it is is true]’. For example, ‘Select yes if Sarah normally lives with you’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Radios" (How it works > If it’s a ‘yes’ or ‘no’ question).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Radios > How it works > If it's a conditionally revealed question
title: Radios: If it's a conditionally revealed question
statement: Include an Error message component that is clearly related to the initial question.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Radios" (How it works > If it's a conditionally revealed question).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Select > When to use this component
title: Select: When to use this component
statement: The select component should only be used as a last resort in public-facing services because research shows that some users find selects very difficult to use.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Select" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Select > When not to use this component
title: Select: When not to use this component
statement: The select component allows users to choose an option from a long list. Before using the select component, try asking users questions which will allow you to present them with fewer options. Asking questions means you’re less likely to need to use the select component, and can consider using a different solution, such as a Radios component.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Select" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Select > How it works
title: Select: How it works
statement: If you use the component for settings, you can make an option pre-selected by default when users first see it. If you use the component for questions, you should not pre-select any of the options in case it influences users' answers. There are 2 ways to use the select component. You can use HTML or, if you’re using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Select" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Select > How it works > Select with hint
title: Select: Select with hint
statement: You can add hint text to help the user understand the options and choose one of them. Keep hint text to a single short sentence, without any full stops. Do not use links in hint text. While screen readers will read out the link text, they usually do not tell users the text is a link.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Select" (How it works > Select with hint).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Select > How it works > Error messages
title: Select: Error messages
statement: Display an error message if the user has not selected an option. Style error messages as shown in the example:
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Select" (How it works > Error messages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Service navigation
title: Service navigation
statement: Service navigation helps users understand that they’re using your service and lets them navigate around your service. If you use the page template, you'll also get the Service navigation without having to add it, as it's included by default. However, if you want to customise the default Service navigation, read the page template guidance about customising components.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Service navigation" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Service navigation > When to use this component
title: Service navigation: When to use this component
statement: Use the Service navigation to help users understand that they’re using your service. To decide when to use navigation links in your service, see the Help users to navigate a service pattern.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Service navigation" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Service navigation > How it works
title: Service navigation: How it works
statement: Together, the GOV.UK header component and Service navigation component ensure users get a consistent experience on GOV.UK. This also assures users that they’re in the right place to use your service and to understand that GOV.UK functions as one website. For guidance on how to plan your header and navigation, see the Help users navigate a service pattern.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Service navigation" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Service navigation > How it works > Showing your service name only
title: Service navigation: Showing your service name only
statement: Use the Service navigation component to show your service name.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Service navigation" (How it works > Showing your service name only).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Service navigation > How it works > Showing service name and navigation links
title: Service navigation: Showing service name and navigation links
statement: Show navigation links to let users navigate to different parts of your service and find useful links and tools. See when and how to show navigation links in the Help users navigate a service pattern.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Service navigation" (How it works > Showing service name and navigation links).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Service navigation > Brand refresh of the Service navigation component
title: Service navigation: Brand refresh of the Service navigation component
statement: In June 2025, we updated this component to support a wider refresh of the GOV.UK brand. You should now use the refreshed GOV.UK branding. If your service has updated to GOV.UK Frontend v6.0.0 or later, you no longer need to use the govukRebrand feature flag and should remove it.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Service navigation" (Brand refresh of the Service navigation component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Skip link
title: Skip link
statement: Use the skip link component to help keyboard-only users skip to the main content on a page. If you use the page template, you'll also get the skip link without having to add it, as it's included by default. However, if you want to customise the default skip link, read the page template guidance about customising components.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Skip link" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Skip link > When to use this component
title: Skip link: When to use this component
statement: All GOV.UK pages must include a skip link. Usually, you should place the skip link immediately after the opening tag. However, if you're using a Cookie banner component, place the skip link immediately after the cookie banner. Some automated accessibility testing tools may warn that the skip link element is not inside a landmark. This warning does not apply to skip links, so you can ignore it. Do not wrap the skip link in a region, or move it inside the header.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Skip link" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Skip link > How it works
title: Skip link: How it works
statement: Some people use the tab key on their keyboard to navigate through the links and form elements on a web page. Including the skip link component gives users the option to bypass the top-level navigation links and jump to the main content on a page. The skip link component is visually hidden until a keyboard press activates it. There are 2 ways to use the skip link component. You can use HTML or, if you are using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Skip link" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Summary list
title: Summary list
statement: Use a summary list to summarise information, for example, a user’s responses at the end of a form.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Summary list" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Summary list > When to use this component
title: Summary list: When to use this component
statement: Use a summary list to show information as a list of key facts. You can use it to display metadata like ‘Last updated’ with a date like ‘22 June 2018’, or to summarise a user’s responses at the end of a form like the Check answers pattern. Summary cards are a variant within this component. You can use summary cards to show multiple summary lists that describe the same type of thing, such as people. You can also add card actions that apply to the entire summary list.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Summary list" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Summary list > When not to use this component
title: Summary list: When not to use this component
statement: The summary list uses the description list ( ) HTML element, so only use it to present information that has a key and at least one value. Do not use it for tabular data or a simple list of information or tasks, like a Task list component. For those use a , or .
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Summary list" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Summary list > How it works
title: Summary list: How it works
statement: Each row of a summary list is made up of a: - ‘key’ that’s a description or label of a piece of information, like “Name” - ‘value’ which is the piece of information itself, such as “John Smith” You can show a single or multiple summary lists on a page. If you’re showing multiple summary lists on a page, you can add structure by using headings or summary cards. There are 2 ways to use the summary list component. You can use HTML or, if you’re using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Summary list" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Summary list > How it works > Adding actions to each row
title: Summary list: Adding actions to each row
statement: You can add ‘row actions’ to a summary list. For example, you can help users go back and edit an answer by adding a ‘change’ link. When navigating visually, the borders above and below each row help to show which row action is tied to which piece of information. Assistive technology users, including those who use a screen reader, might hear a row action link out of context and might not know what it will do. To give more context, add visually hidden text to the links. This means a screen reader user will hear the row action and the ‘key’ label for the information it will affect, like ‘Change name’ or ‘Change date of birth’. If a user decides to go back to a previous answer through a card or row action, make sure information they've already entered is pre-populated.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Summary list" (How it works > Adding actions to each row).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Summary list > How it works > Showing rows with and without actions
title: Summary list: Showing rows with and without actions
statement: If you’re showing a mix of rows (where some rows include actions and some do not), add the govuk-summary-listrow--no-actions modifier class to the rows without actions. This is to ensure the bottom border is drawn correctly in some browsers.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Summary list" (How it works > Showing rows with and without actions).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Summary list > How it works > Removing the borders
title: Summary list: Removing the borders
statement: The summary list includes separating borders to help users by joining the information on each row and its action together. Think carefully before you remove row borders. Borders help many users find and read information that’s laid out in rows, especially users who zoom in on pages or use assistive technologies to magnify their screen. If your summary list does not have any actions, you can choose to remove the separating borders with the govuk-summary-list--no-border class. To remove borders on a single row, use the govuk-summary-listrow--no-border class.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Summary list" (How it works > Removing the borders).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Summary list > How it works > Showing missing information
title: Summary list: Showing missing information
statement: In some contexts, you might need to show rows that have missing information. This can happen when: - a user returns to an incomplete journey - you've added or changed the questions in a service. Show a link to the appropriate question page in the value column so the user can enter the missing information, instead of showing a 'change' link on that row.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Summary list" (How it works > Showing missing information).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Summary list > Summary cards
title: Summary list: Summary cards
statement: If you’re showing multiple summary lists on a page, you can show each list within a summary card. This lets you visually separate each summary list and give each a title and some actions. Use summary cards when you need to show: - multiple summary lists that all describe the same type of thing, such as people - actions that will apply to all the items in a list Summary cards are often used in case working systems to help users quickly view a set of information and related actions. Do not use summary cards if you only need to show a small amount of related information. Use summary lists instead, and structure them with headings if needed. If you’re showing summary cards at the end of a longer journey, you might want to familiarise the user with them earlier on – such as when the user reviews individual sections.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Summary list" (Summary cards).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Summary list > Summary cards > Card titles
title: Summary list: Card titles
statement: Use the summary card’s header area to give each summary list a title. Each title must be unique and help identify what the summary list describes. For example, this could be the name of a specific person, organisation or professional qualification. Try to keep titles short and relevant. You can use one or two important values in the summary list – such as the first and last name of a person.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Summary list" (Summary cards > Card titles).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Summary list > Summary cards > Adding card actions
title: Summary list: Adding card actions
statement: You can add card actions in the header, which will be shown after the summary card's title. For example, if you have multiple rows with "change" actions that all take the user to the same place, you can show a single “change” card action instead. This helps avoid repeating the same row action on every row. Card actions are shown in bold text to make them visually distinct from row actions – and help alert the user that the card action will affect the entire summary card. Write link text for card actions to tell the user what the card action will do and that it will apply to the entire summary card. It should also be as short as possible, usually 2 words. Example card actions include: - Remove tenant - Edit qualification - Update issue - Approve application - Cancel order Keep it short and do not add more than 2 to 3 actions in a header. If a card action cannot easily be undone or might have serious consequences, consider adding a warning or asking the user for confirmation.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Summary list" (Summary cards > Adding card actions).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Table
title: Table
statement: Use the table component to make information easier to compare and scan for users.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Table" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Table > When to use this component
title: Table: When to use this component
statement: Use the table component to let users compare information in rows and columns.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Table" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Table > When not to use this component
title: Table: When not to use this component
statement: Never use the table component to layout content on a page. Instead, use the grid system.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Table" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Table > How it works > Table captions
title: Table: Table captions
statement: Use the element to describe a table in the same way you would use a heading. A caption helps users find, navigate and understand tables. There are other styling options for table captions. You can use govuk-tablecaption--s, govuk-tablecaption--m, govuk-tablecaption--l and govuk-tablecaption--xl classes to make them larger or smaller from the default.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Table" (How it works > Table captions).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Table > How it works > Table headers
title: Table: Table headers
statement: Use table headers to tell users what the rows and columns represent. Use the scope attribute to help users of assistive technology distinguish between row and column headers. There are 2 ways to use the table component. You can use HTML or, if you are using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Table" (How it works > Table headers).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Table > Numbers in a table
title: Table: Numbers in a table
statement: When comparing columns of numbers, align the numbers to the right in table cells.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Table" (Numbers in a table).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Table > Custom column widths
title: Table: Custom column widths
statement: You can use the width override classes to set the width of table columns. If the width override classes do not meet your needs you can create your own width classes and apply them to the cells in the table head. These can be added using the classes option in the Nunjucks macro or adding the class directly to the individual cells within govuk-tablehead as below. To learn more about this, read guidance on extending and modifying components in production.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Table" (Custom column widths).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Table > Tables with a lot of data
title: Table: Tables with a lot of data
statement: If possible, you should aim to have less data in your tables. If you have a lot of data, try to organise it into multiple tables or multiple pages. If you cannot split your data, you can use the CSS class govuk-table--small-text-until-tablet. This class reduces the size of the text on small screens so large amounts of data has more empty space around it. This makes it easier to visually differentiate between each piece of data when read on small screens. The CSS class govuk-table--small-text-until-tablet is only available in version 5.2 of GOV.UK Frontend and later. Read about updating your service to use the new type scale . You should not use this class on tables unless your table has a lot of data, because a smaller amount of data is easier to read if the text is larger.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Table" (Tables with a lot of data).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tabs
title: Tabs
statement: The tabs component lets users navigate between related sections of content, displaying one section at a time.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tabs" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tabs > When to use this component
title: Tabs: When to use this component
statement: Tabs can be a helpful way of letting users quickly switch between related information if: - your content can be usefully separated into clearly labelled sections - the first section is more relevant than the others for most users - users will not need to view all the sections at once Tabs can work well for people who use a service regularly, for example, users of a caseworking system. Their need to perform tasks quickly may be greater than their need for simplicity of first-time use.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tabs" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tabs > When not to use this component
title: Tabs: When not to use this component
statement: Do not use the tabs component if the total amount of content the tabs contain will make the page slow to load. For this reason, do not use the tabs component as a form of page navigation. Tabs hide content from users and not everyone will notice them or understand how they work. Do not use tabs if your users might need to: - read through all of the content in order, for example, to understand a step-by-step process - compare information in different tabs - having to memorise the information and switch backwards and forwards can be frustrating and difficult Test your content without tabs first. Consider if it’s better to: - simplify and reduce the amount of content - split the content across multiple pages - keep the content on a single page, separated by headings - use a table of contents to let users navigate quickly to specific sections of content
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tabs" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tabs > Decide between using tabs, accordion and details
title: Tabs: Decide between using tabs, accordion and details
statement: The Tabs component, Accordion component, and Details component all hide sections of content which a user can choose to reveal. If you decide to use one of these components, consider if: - the user does not need to view more than one section at a time – consider using tabs - the user needs to switch quickly between sections – tabs can show content without pushing other sections down the page, unlike accordions - there are many pieces of content – tabs can fit fewer sections as they’re arranged horizontally, unlike accordions which are arranged vertically - there’s only one or two pieces of short, less important content – the details component is more suitable as it’s visually smaller and less prominent than an accordion or tabs
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tabs" (Decide between using tabs, accordion and details).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tabs > How it works
title: Tabs: How it works
statement: There are 2 ways to use the tabs component. You can use HTML or, if you’re using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro. The tabs component uses JavaScript. When JavaScript is not available, users will see the tabbed content on a single page, in order from first to last, with a table of contents that links to each of the sections. This is also how the component currently behaves on small screens, though more research is needed on this.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tabs" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tabs > How it works > The current tab gets stored in the URL
title: Tabs: The current tab gets stored in the URL
statement: When moving between tabs, the URL gets updated with a fragment (id-of-the-tab) corresponding to the current tab's id attribute's value. If the tab's name is "United Kingdom" then the fragment could be tabunited-kingdom. Because of this feature, pressing the browser's 'back' button should navigate back to the previous tab.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tabs" (How it works > The current tab gets stored in the URL).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tabs > How it works > Use clear labels
title: Tabs: Use clear labels
statement: Tabs hide content, so the tab labels need to make it very clear what they link to, otherwise users will not know if they need to click on them. If you struggle to come up with clear labels, it might be because the way you’ve separated the content is not clear.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tabs" (How it works > Use clear labels).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tabs > How it works > Order the tabs according to user needs
title: Tabs: Order the tabs according to user needs
statement: The first tab should be the most commonly-needed section. Arrange the other tabs in the order that makes most sense for your users.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tabs" (How it works > Order the tabs according to user needs).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tabs > How it works > Do not disable tabs
title: Tabs: Do not disable tabs
statement: Disabling elements is normally confusing for users. If there is no content for a tab, either remove the tab or, if that would be confusing for your users, explain why there is no content when the tab is selected.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tabs" (How it works > Do not disable tabs).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tabs > How it works > Avoid tabs that wrap over more than one line
title: Tabs: Avoid tabs that wrap over more than one line
statement: If you use too many tabs or they have long labels then they may wrap over more than one line. This makes it harder for users to see the connection between the selected tab and its content.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tabs" (How it works > Avoid tabs that wrap over more than one line).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tabs > How it works > Add headings to tab content
title: Tabs: Add headings to tab content
statement: Include a heading at the beginning of each tab that duplicates the information in the tab label. Providing a heading improves navigation on smaller screen sizes and for screen reader users.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tabs" (How it works > Add headings to tab content).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tabs > Research and testing
title: Tabs: Research and testing
statement: This component has not yet been tried in research with users. The design, code and guidance here are based on recommendations from Inclusive Components and the Nielsen Norman Group as well as user research findings and examples of tabs in the following services: - Manage bereavement support payment (DWP) - Support for check your state pension (DWP) - Access to work integrated system (DWP) - Bank holidays (GDS) - Universal Credit (DWP) - Criminal Justice Services (CPP) - Judiciary UI internal systems (HMCTS) - Rural Payments (Defra)
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tabs" (Research and testing).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tag
title: Tag
statement: Use the Tag component to show users the status of something.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tag" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tag > When to use this component
title: Tag: When to use this component
statement: Use the Tag component when it’s possible for something to have more than one status and it’s useful for the user to know about that status. For example, you can use a tag to show whether an item in a Task list component has been ‘completed’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tag" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tag > How it works
title: Tag: How it works
statement: There are two ways to use the Tag component. You can use HTML or, if you are using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro. Tags are only used to indicate a status. Do not make a tag interactive by making it into a link or button. Use adjectives (descriptive words) and not verbs (action words) for the names of your tags. Using a verb might make a user think that clicking on them will do something. Do not use tags to create links, buttons or other interactive elements, as users: - are unlikely to identify the tags as something they’re meant to interact with - would see no visual difference between interactive and non-interactive tags
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tag" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tag > Showing one or two statuses
title: Tag: Showing one or two statuses
statement: Sometimes a single status is enough. For example if you need to tell users which parts of an application they’ve finished and which they have not, you may only need a ‘Completed’ tag. Because the user understands that if something does not have a tag, that means it’s incomplete. The Complete multiple tasks pattern has an example of how to show one status using tags. Or it can make sense to have two statuses. For example you may find that there’s a need to have one tag for ‘Active’ users and one for ‘Inactive’ users.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tag" (Showing one or two statuses).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tag > Showing multiple statuses
title: Tag: Showing multiple statuses
statement: Tags should be helpful to users. The more you add, the harder it is for users to remember them. So start with the smallest number of statuses you think might work, then add more if your user research shows there’s a need for them.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tag" (Showing multiple statuses).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tag > Using colour with tags
title: Tag: Using colour with tags
statement: You can use colour to help distinguish between different tags – or to help draw the user’s attention to a tag if it’s especially important. For example, it probably makes sense to use govuk-tag--red for a tag that reads ‘Urgent’. Do not use colour alone to convey information, because it’s not accessible. If you use the same tag in more than one place, make sure you keep the colour consistent. This is to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.1 Use of colour.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tag" (Using colour with tags).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Tag > Using colour with tags > Additional colours
title: Tag: Additional colours
statement: If you need more tag colours, you can use the following colours.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Tag" (Using colour with tags > Additional colours).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Task list
title: Task list
statement: The task list component displays all the tasks a user needs to do, and allows users to easily identify which ones are done and which they still need to do.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Task list" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Task list > When to use this component
title: Task list: When to use this component
statement: Use the task list to give users more control over how they complete long, complex services. Only use the task list if there’s evidence that users: - do not want to, or cannot, complete all the tasks in one sitting - need to be able to choose the order they complete the tasks in
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Task list" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Task list > When not to use this component
title: Task list: When not to use this component
statement: Try to simplify the service before you use a task list. If you’re able to reduce the number of tasks or steps involved, you might not need one. Do not use the task list for a long service that needs to be completed in a specific order. If it needs to be completed over multiple sessions, consider allowing users to save their progress, and then to continue where they left off when they return. Use the start page to explain what users will be expected to do during the service. The task list should not be used as a way of showing users their answers. For this, you should use a Summary list component instead.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Task list" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Task list > How it works
title: Task list: How it works
statement: There are 2 ways to use the task list component. You can use HTML or, if you’re using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro. Users should be able to complete tasks in whatever order they like. The status alongside the task indicates whether they can start it. Users can select a task to start completing it. Once they have completed it and returned to the task list, the status for that task will have changed to ‘Completed’. Users can only move on from the task list when all tasks are shown as ‘Completed’. Read the Complete multiple tasks pattern guidance for more information on how to use the task list within a service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Task list" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Task list > How it works > Tasks
title: Task list: Tasks
statement: Tasks are usually actions that the user needs to take to complete a service. In a task list, the user should be able to choose to complete tasks in any order that works for them. Each task within a task list includes a task name and a status. It can also include hint text if you decide this is needed. The whole row is linked, allowing users to select anywhere within it to start the task.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Task list" (How it works > Tasks).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Task list > How it works > Write clear task descriptions
title: Task list: Write clear task descriptions
statement: The task name gives users a reasonable expectation of what that task is about. For example, ‘Your contact details’ or ‘Upload evidence’. Use sentence case, and keep it short. Users of screen readers might find it difficult to navigate the task list if the task names are too long. If you’re finding it difficult to come up with a clear and concise task name, it might be because the task itself is too complex and may need to be separated into smaller tasks. Group questions and actions into tasks in a way that makes sense to users, based on their needs.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Task list" (How it works > Write clear task descriptions).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Task list > How it works > Adding hint text
title: Task list: Adding hint text
statement: Only use hint text if there is evidence that the user needs more information about what the task will include. Keep hint text to a single short sentence, without any full stops. Screen readers will read out the entire text when users interact with the task link. This could frustrate users if the text is long. Do not include links within the hint text. The whole task row links users to the task itself, so any links within the hint text will not work.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Task list" (How it works > Adding hint text).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Task list > How it works > Grouping tasks
title: Task list: Grouping tasks
statement: If there are a lot of tasks to complete, you might find that grouping them makes it easier for users to understand and plan what they need to do. Tasks can be grouped into separate task lists on a page. Give each task list a short heading that clearly explains the grouping. Read the Complete multiple tasks pattern guidance for more information on grouping tasks.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Task list" (How it works > Grouping tasks).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Task list > How it works > Statuses
title: Task list: Statuses
statement: Statuses use colour and a short descriptor to give users a quick overview of how much of the task list they have completed, and how much is left to do. Read the Complete multiple tasks pattern guidance for more information on status colours and text.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Task list" (How it works > Statuses).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > When to use this component
title: Text input: When to use this component
statement: Use the text input component when you need to let users enter text that’s no longer than a single line, such as their name or phone number.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > When not to use this component
title: Text input: When not to use this component
statement: Do not use the text input component if you need to let users enter longer answers that might span multiple lines. In this case, you should use the Textarea component.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works
title: Text input: How it works
statement: All text inputs must have labels, and in most cases the label should be visible. You should align labels above the text input they refer to. They should be short, direct and written in sentence case. Do not use colons at the end of labels.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > Avoid placeholder text
title: Text input: Avoid placeholder text
statement: Do not use placeholder text in place of a label, or for hints or examples, as: - it vanishes when the user starts typing, which can cause problems for users with memory conditions or when reviewing answers - not all screen readers read it out - its browser default styles often do not meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (minimum)
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > Avoid placeholder text).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > If you're asking one question on the page
title: Text input: If you're asking one question on the page
statement: If you’re asking just one question per page in your service as recommended, you can set the contents of the as the page heading. This is good practice as it means that users of screen readers will only hear the contents once. Read more about why and how to set legends as headings. There are 2 ways to use the text input component. You can use HTML or, if you’re using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > If you're asking one question on the page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > If you’re asking more than one question on the page
title: Text input: If you’re asking more than one question on the page
statement: If you're asking more than one question on the page, do not set the contents of the as the page heading. Read more about asking multiple questions on Question pages.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > If you’re asking more than one question on the page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > Use appropriately-sized text inputs
title: Text input: Use appropriately-sized text inputs
statement: Help users understand what they should enter by making text inputs the right size for the content they’re intended for. By default, the width of text inputs is fluid and will fit the full width of the container they are placed into. If you want to make the input smaller, you can either use a fixed width input, or use the width override classes to create a smaller, fluid width input.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > Use appropriately-sized text inputs).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > Fixed width inputs
title: Text input: Fixed width inputs
statement: Use fixed width inputs for content that has a specific, known length. Postcode inputs should be postcode-sized, phone number inputs should be phone number-sized. The widths are designed for specific character lengths and to be consistent across a range of browsers. They include extra padding to fit icons that some browsers might insert into the input (for example to show or generate a password). On fixed width inputs, the width will remain fixed on all screens unless it is wider than the viewport, in which case it will shrink to fit.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > Fixed width inputs).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > Fluid width inputs
title: Text input: Fluid width inputs
statement: Use the width override classes to reduce the width of an input in relation to its parent container, for example, to two-thirds. Fluid width inputs will resize with the viewport.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > Fluid width inputs).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > Hint text
title: Text input: Hint text
statement: Use hint text for help that’s relevant to the majority of users, like how their information will be used, or where to find it. Keep hint text to a single short sentence, without any full stops. Do not use links in hint text. While screen readers will read out the link text when describing the field, they usually do not tell users the text is a link.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > Hint text).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > When not to use hint text
title: Text input: When not to use hint text
statement: Do not use hint text to explain anything that's longer than a short, simple sentence. Screen readers read out the entire text when users interact with the form element. This could frustrate users if the text is long. If you’re asking a question that needs a detailed explanation, see asking complex questions without using hint text.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > When not to use hint text).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > Avoid links
title: Text input: Avoid links
statement: Do not include links within hint text. While screen readers will read out the link text when describing the field, they will not tell users that the text is a link.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > Avoid links).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > Asking for whole numbers
title: Text input: Asking for whole numbers
statement: If you're asking the user to enter a whole number, set the inputmode attribute to numeric to use the numeric keypad on devices with on-screen keyboards. See how to do this by opening the HTML and Nunjucks tabs in this example: There is specific guidance on: - how to ask for dates - how to ask for phone numbers
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > Asking for whole numbers).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > Asking for decimal numbers
title: Text input: Asking for decimal numbers
statement: If you're asking the user to enter a number that might include decimal places, set inputmode to decimal. Similar to numeric, this will show a numeric keypad to users on devices with on-screen keyboards, including a decimal separator. Some devices do not allow users to enter negative values using the on-screen keypad. If you want to give users the option to enter a negative number, use input type="text" without the inputmode attribute.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > Asking for decimal numbers).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > Avoid using inputs with a type of number
title: Text input: Avoid using inputs with a type of number
statement: Do not use unless your user research shows that there’s a need for it. With there’s a risk of users accidentally incrementing a number when they’re trying to do something else - for example, scroll up or down the page. And if the user tries to enter something that’s not a number, there’s no explicit feedback about what they’re doing wrong.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > Avoid using inputs with a type of number).
