author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > Prefixes and suffixes
title: Text input: Prefixes and suffixes
statement: Use prefixes and suffixes to help users enter things like currencies and measurements. Prefixes and suffixes are useful when there's a commonly understood symbol or abbreviation for the type of information you're asking for. Do not rely on prefixes or suffixes alone, because screen readers will not read them out. If you need a specific type of information, say so in the input label or hint text as well. For example, put 'Cost, in pounds' in the input label and use the '£' symbol in the prefix. Position prefixes and suffixes so that they're outside of their input. This is to avoid interfering with some browsers that might insert an icon into the input (for example to show or generate a password). Some users may miss that the input already has a suffix or prefix, and enter a prefix or suffix into the input. Allow for this in your validation and do not show an error.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > Prefixes and suffixes).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > Use the autocomplete attribute
title: Text input: Use the autocomplete attribute
statement: Use the autocomplete attribute on text inputs to help users complete forms more quickly. This lets you specify an input's purpose so browsers can autofill the information on a user's behalf if they’ve entered it previously. For example, to enable autofill on a postcode field, set the autocomplete attribute to postal-code. See how to do this in the HTML and Nunjucks tabs in the following example. If you are working in production and there is a relevant input purpose, you'll need to use the autocomplete attribute to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.3.5 Identify input purpose, level AA. You will not normally need to use the autocomplete attribute in prototypes, as users will not generally be using their own devices.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > Use the autocomplete attribute).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > Do not disable copy and paste
title: Text input: Do not disable copy and paste
statement: Users often need to copy and paste information into a text input, so do not stop them from doing this.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > Do not disable copy and paste).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > Avoid restricting the length of a user's input
title: Text input: Avoid restricting the length of a user's input
statement: Using the maxlength attribute means there is no feedback to users that their text input is truncated. This is especially true where the text has been copied and pasted from elsewhere. This can cause users to accidentally provide incorrect or incomplete information. A restrictive maximum length can stop users from formatting information in their usual way. For example, putting spaces in a postcode or commas in a large number. Some assistive technologies do not tell users if an input has a maxlength set or if the user has passed the limit. Voice control software may insert additional spaces into the input. If you must enforce a maximum length for technical reasons, inform the user of the limit in the hint, but allow them to provide more information. Only return an error if the value is longer than allowed after normalisation. For longer values, consider using the Character count component instead.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > Avoid restricting the length of a user's input).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > How and when to spellcheck a user’s input
title: Text input: How and when to spellcheck a user’s input
statement: Sometimes, browsers will spellcheck the information a user puts into a text input. If a user enters something which is recognised as a spelling error, sighted users will see a red line under the word. If you are asking users for information which is not appropriate to spellcheck, like a reference number, name, email address or National Insurance number, disable the spellcheck. To do this set the spellcheck attribute to false as shown in this example. Browsers do not consistently spellcheck user’s input by default. If you are asking a question where spellcheck would be useful, set the spellcheck attribute to true.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > How and when to spellcheck a user’s input).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > If the input has a prefix or a suffix
title: Text input: If the input has a prefix or a suffix
statement: Make sure errors follow the guidance in the Error message component and have specific error messages for specific error states.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > If the input has a prefix or a suffix).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > If the input is empty
title: Text input: If the input is empty
statement: Say ‘Enter [whatever it is]’. For example, ‘Enter your first name’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > If the input is empty).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > If the input is too long
title: Text input: If the input is too long
statement: Say ‘[whatever it is] must be [number] characters or less’. For example, ‘Address line 1 must be 35 characters or less’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > If the input is too long).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > If the input is too short
title: Text input: If the input is too short
statement: Say ‘[whatever it is] must be [number] characters or more’. For example, ‘Full name must be 2 characters or more’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > If the input is too short).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > If the input has both a minimum and maximum length
title: Text input: If the input has both a minimum and maximum length
statement: Say ‘[whatever it is] must be between [number] and [number] characters’. For example, ‘Last name must be between 2 and 35 characters’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > If the input has both a minimum and maximum length).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > If the input uses characters that are not allowed and you know what the characters are
title: Text input: If the input uses characters that are not allowed and you know what the characters are
statement: Say ‘[whatever it is] must not include [characters]’. For example, ‘Town or city must not include è and £’. Support all the characters the user might need to enter, including numbers and symbols.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > If the input uses characters that are not allowed and you know what the characters are).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > If the input uses characters that are not allowed and you do not know what the characters are
title: Text input: If the input uses characters that are not allowed and you do not know what the characters are
statement: Say ‘[whatever it is] must only include [list of allowed characters]’. For example, ‘Full name must only include letters a to z, and special characters such as hyphens, spaces and apostrophes’. Support all the characters the user might need to enter, including numbers and symbols.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > If the input uses characters that are not allowed and you do not know what the characters are).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > If the input is not a number
title: Text input: If the input is not a number
statement: Say ‘[whatever it is] must be a number [optional example]’. For example, ‘Hours worked a week must be a number, like 30’. If the input requires a decimal, use a decimal in the example. If the input allows both whole numbers and decimals, use both in the example.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > If the input is not a number).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > If the input is not a whole number
title: Text input: If the input is not a whole number
statement: Say ‘[whatever it is] must be a whole number [optional example]’. For example, ‘Hours worked a week must be a whole number, like 30’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > If the input is not a whole number).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > If the number is too low
title: Text input: If the number is too low
statement: Say ‘[whatever it is] must be [lowest] or more’. For example, ‘Hours worked a week must be 16 or more’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > If the number is too low).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > If the number is too high
title: Text input: If the number is too high
statement: Say ‘[whatever it is] must be [highest] or fewer’. For example, ‘Hours worked a week must be 99 or fewer’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > If the number is too high).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > If the input must be between 2 numbers
title: Text input: If the input must be between 2 numbers
statement: Say ‘[whatever it is] must be between [lowest] and [highest]’. For example, ‘Hours worked a week must be between 16 and 99’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > If the input must be between 2 numbers).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > If the input is an amount of money that needs decimals
title: Text input: If the input is an amount of money that needs decimals
statement: Say ‘[whatever it is] must include pence, like 123.45 or 156.00’. For example, ‘How much you earn a week must include pence, like 123.45 or 156.00’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > If the input is an amount of money that needs decimals).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Text input > How it works > If the input is an amount of money that must not have decimals
title: Text input: If the input is an amount of money that must not have decimals
statement: Say ‘[whatever it is] must not include pence, like 123 instead of 123.45’. For example, ‘How much you earn a week must not include pence, like 123 instead of 123.45’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Text input" (How it works > If the input is an amount of money that must not have decimals).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Textarea > When to use this component
title: Textarea: When to use this component
statement: Use the textarea component when you need to let users enter an amount of text that’s longer than a single line.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Textarea" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Textarea > When not to use this component
title: Textarea: When not to use this component
statement: Users can find open-ended questions difficult to answer. It might be better to break up one complex question into a series of simple ones, for example where users can select from options using a Radios component.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Textarea" (When not to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Textarea > When not to use this component > If you need to ask an open question
title: Textarea: If you need to ask an open question
statement: Do not use the textarea component if you need to let users enter shorter answers no longer than a single line, such as a phone number or name. In this case, you should use the Text input component.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Textarea" (When not to use this component > If you need to ask an open question).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Textarea > How it works
title: Textarea: How it works
statement: You must label textareas. Placeholder text is not a suitable substitute for a label, as it disappears when users click inside the textarea. Labels must be aligned above the textarea they refer to. They should be short, direct and written in sentence case. Do not use colons at the end of labels. There are 2 ways to use the textarea component. You can use HTML or, if you’re using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Textarea" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Textarea > How it works > Use appropriately-sized textareas
title: Textarea: Use appropriately-sized textareas
statement: Make the height of a textarea proportional to the amount of text you expect users to enter. You can set the height of a textarea by specifying the rows attribute.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Textarea" (How it works > Use appropriately-sized textareas).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Textarea > How it works > Do not disable copy and paste
title: Textarea: Do not disable copy and paste
statement: Users will often need to copy and paste information into a textarea, so do not stop them from doing this.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Textarea" (How it works > Do not disable copy and paste).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Textarea > How it works > If you’re asking more than one question on the page
title: Textarea: If you’re asking more than one question on the page
statement: If you're asking more than one question on the page, do not set the contents of the as the page heading. Read more about asking multiple questions on Question pages.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Textarea" (How it works > If you’re asking more than one question on the page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Textarea > How it works > Limiting the number of characters
title: Textarea: Limiting the number of characters
statement: If there’s a good reason to limit the number of characters users can enter, you can use the Character count component.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Textarea" (How it works > Limiting the number of characters).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Textarea > How it works > Error messages
title: Textarea: Error messages
statement: Error messages should be styled like this: Make sure errors follow the guidance in the Error message component and have specific error messages for specific error states.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Textarea" (How it works > Error messages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Textarea > How it works > If the input is too long
title: Textarea: If the input is too long
statement: Say ‘[whatever it is] must be [number] characters or less’. For example, ‘Summary must be 400 characters or less’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Textarea" (How it works > If the input is too long).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Textarea > How it works > If the input is too short
title: Textarea: If the input is too short
statement: Say ‘[whatever it is] must be [number] characters or more’. For example, ‘Summary must be 10 characters or more’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Textarea" (How it works > If the input is too short).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Textarea > How it works > If the input is too long or too short
title: Textarea: If the input is too long or too short
statement: Say ‘[whatever it is] must be between [number] and [number] characters’. For example, ‘Summary must be between 10 and 400 characters’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Textarea" (How it works > If the input is too long or too short).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Textarea > How it works > If the input uses characters that are not allowed and you know what the characters are
title: Textarea: If the input uses characters that are not allowed and you know what the characters are
statement: Say ‘[whatever it is] must not include [characters]’. For example, ‘Summary must not include è and £’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Textarea" (How it works > If the input uses characters that are not allowed and you know what the characters are).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Textarea > How it works > If the input uses characters that are not allowed and you do not know what the characters are
title: Textarea: If the input uses characters that are not allowed and you do not know what the characters are
statement: Say ‘[whatever it is] must only include [list of allowed characters]’. For example, ‘Summary must only include letters a to z, hyphens, spaces and apostrophes.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Textarea" (How it works > If the input uses characters that are not allowed and you do not know what the characters are).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Warning text > When to use this component
title: Warning text: When to use this component
statement: Use the warning text component when you need to warn users about something important, such as legal consequences of an action, or lack of action, that they might take.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Warning text" (When to use this component).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Warning text > How it works
title: Warning text: How it works
statement: There are 2 ways to use the warning text component. You can use HTML or, if you are using Nunjucks or the GOV.UK Prototype Kit, you can use the Nunjucks macro. You might need to rewrite the hidden text (‘Warning’ in the example) to make it appropriate for your context.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Warning text" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addresses
title: Addresses
statement: This guidance is for government teams that build online services. To find information and services for the public, go to GOV.UK. Help users provide an address using one of the following: - address lookup - multiple text inputs - textarea
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addresses" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addresses > Address lookup
title: Addresses: Address lookup
statement: An address lookup helps users find a full address from partial information such as a postcode.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addresses" (Address lookup).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addresses > Address lookup > When to use an address lookup
title: Addresses: When to use an address lookup
statement: Use an address lookup to collect UK addresses where possible.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addresses" (Address lookup > When to use an address lookup).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addresses > Address lookup > When not to use an address lookup
title: Addresses: When not to use an address lookup
statement: Address lookups generally only work for UK addresses. If you expect both UK and international addresses, give users the option to either search for a UK address or manually enter an international address.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addresses" (Address lookup > When not to use an address lookup).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addresses > Address lookup > How an address lookup works
title: Addresses: How an address lookup works
statement: An address lookup lets users specify a UK address by entering their postcode and selecting their address from a list. There is also an option to enter a street name or number. When using an address lookup, you should: - make it clear that it will only work for UK addresses - provide a manual option for people with international addresses or addresses that are missing or not properly listed in the address lookup - let people enter their postcodes in upper or lower case and with or without spaces
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addresses" (Address lookup > How an address lookup works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addresses > Address lookup > Identify and match addresses with UPRN identifiers
title: Addresses: Identify and match addresses with UPRN identifiers
statement: Use an address lookup that can identify addresses with Unique Property Reference Numbers (UPRNs). UPRNs are 12-digit unique identifiers for every addressable location across the UK. Open standards for government mandate that services that store property information must use UPRN identifiers. Using UPRN identifiers helps users enter addresses accurately. This helps your service by making address data more consistent and easier to handle, which reduces errors and removes the need for manual address matching in the future. See a post on The power of UPRNs in linking data on the Geospatial Insights blog. Your address lookup should only use data from a single API. One option for this is the Ordnance Survey Places API. Public sector organisations can get access to OS Places API as part of the Public Sector Geospatial Agreement (PSGA).
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addresses" (Address lookup > Identify and match addresses with UPRN identifiers).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addresses > Multiple text inputs > When to use multiple text inputs
title: Addresses: When to use multiple text inputs
statement: Only use multiple text inputs to offer users a manual input option when you both: - know which countries the addresses will come from - can find a format that supports them all – this can be difficult to know if you’re asking for addresses outside of the UK Using multiple text inputs means: - you can easily extract and use specific parts of an address - you can give help for individual text inputs - you can validate each part of the address separately - users can complete the form using their browser’s autocomplete function The disadvantages of using multiple text inputs are that: - it’s hard to find a single format that works for all addresses - there’s no guarantee that users will use the text inputs the way you think they will - users cannot easily paste addresses from their clipboards
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addresses" (Multiple text inputs > When to use multiple text inputs).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addresses > Multiple text inputs > How multiple text inputs work
title: Addresses: How multiple text inputs work
statement: If you use multiple text inputs, you should: - only make individual text inputs mandatory if you really need the information - make the text inputs the appropriate length for the content – it helps people understand the form, for example, make postcode text inputs shorter than street text inputs - let users enter postcodes in different formats Make sure there are enough text inputs to accommodate longer addresses if you know your users will need them. For example, allow users to include a company name or flat number. Make it optional for users to enter their county (such as Berkshire or Cumbria). It’s not part of a correct UK address, according to Royal Mail, and it’s not used to deliver post. Remove the county field if you’re sure your users will not need it, and your service will not use it.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addresses" (Multiple text inputs > How multiple text inputs work).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addresses > Multiple text inputs > Use the autocomplete attribute on multiple address fields
title: Addresses: Use the autocomplete attribute on multiple address fields
statement: Use the autocomplete attribute on each individual address field to help users enter their address more quickly. This lets you specify each input’s purpose so browsers can autofill the information on a user’s behalf if they’ve entered it previously. Check which input purpose to use for each field. In production, you’ll need to do this to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.3.5 Identify input purpose. You will not normally need to use the autocomplete attribute in prototypes, as users will not generally be using their own devices.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addresses" (Multiple text inputs > Use the autocomplete attribute on multiple address fields).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addresses > Multiple text inputs > Error messages
title: Addresses: Error messages
statement: Error messages should be styled like this: If a postcode entered is not a real postcode, use a message like this: Make sure errors follow the guidance in the Error message component and have specific error messages for specific error states.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addresses" (Multiple text inputs > Error messages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addresses > Textarea > When to use a textarea
title: Addresses: When to use a textarea
statement: Use a textarea to offer users a manual option to enter an address, such as for international addresses or when users cannot find their address using an address lookup. A textarea is useful when you expect a broad range of address formats and you do not need to format the address for print or use specific sub-parts of the address (for example, street or postcode).
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addresses" (Textarea > When to use a textarea).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addresses > Textarea > When not to use a textarea
title: Addresses: When not to use a textarea
statement: You should not use a textarea if you need to separate an address into accurate sub-parts (for example, street or postcode).
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addresses" (Textarea > When not to use a textarea).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addresses > Textarea > How a textarea works
title: Addresses: How a textarea works
statement: Textareas let users enter an address in any format and make it easy to copy and paste addresses from their clipboard.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addresses" (Textarea > How a textarea works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Addresses > Textarea > Use the autocomplete attribute on a textarea
title: Addresses: Use the autocomplete attribute on a textarea
statement: Use the autocomplete attribute on the textarea component when you're asking for an address. This lets browsers autofill the information on a user's behalf if they’ve entered it previously. To do this, set the autocomplete attribute to street-address as shown in the HTML and Nunjucks tabs in the textarea example above. If you are working in production you’ll need to do this to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.3.5 Identify input purpose. You will not normally need to use the autocomplete attribute in prototypes, as users will not generally be using their own devices.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Addresses" (Textarea > Use the autocomplete attribute on a textarea).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Bank details
title: Bank details
statement: This guidance is for government teams that build online services. To find information and services for the public, go to GOV.UK.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Bank details" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Bank details > When to use this pattern
title: Bank details: When to use this pattern
statement: Follow this pattern if you need users to provide their bank details so you can pay them. Only ask for bank details securely within your service. For example, do not ask users to send their bank details by email. This pattern does yet not cover asking users for bank details so they can pay by Direct Debit. If your service lets users set up Direct Debit payments, first check if you can use GOV.UK Pay.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Bank details" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Bank details > How it works
title: Bank details: How it works
statement: Include extra fields if your payment service provider needs additional information.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Bank details" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Bank details > How it works > Do not ask users for their account type
title: Bank details: Do not ask users for their account type
statement: Do not ask users if they have a bank account or building society account as not all users know this. If your service does not support building society accounts, remove building society from the content and do not ask for a roll number.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Bank details" (How it works > Do not ask users for their account type).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Bank details > How it works > Asking for building society roll numbers
title: Bank details: Asking for building society roll numbers
statement: Roll numbers are only used by some building societies for certain types of account, so make this field optional. However, you need a user’s roll number when they have one. This is why the label says ‘(if you have one)’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Bank details" (How it works > Asking for building society roll numbers).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Bank details > How it works > Use a branching question if users can choose how to get paid
title: Bank details: Use a branching question if users can choose how to get paid
statement: Not everyone has a bank account or wants to share their account details online. Let users choose to get paid by an alternative method. Adapt this question depending on what payment options your users need and what your service can support.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Bank details" (How it works > Use a branching question if users can choose how to get paid).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Bank details > How it works > International bank account details
title: Bank details: International bank account details
statement: If you expect your users will have a non-UK bank account, you’ll need to: - use different fields to sort code and account number - usually BIC code (also known as 'SWIFT code') and IBAN - do research on other fields you may need to add for the countries your service supports - only show the fields for the country your user selects If you expect your users to have a non-UK bank account, give them an option to select this. International bank accounts require different fields to sort code and account number. Different countries ask for additional details. This guidance does not cover all possibilities. You will need to research what information is needed by the countries your service supports. Only show the fields that relate to that country. Most countries need the IBAN and BIC, sometimes known as the SWIFT code.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Bank details" (How it works > International bank account details).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Bank details > How it works > Error messages
title: Bank details: Error messages
statement: Error messages should be styled like this: Make sure errors follow the guidance in the Error message component and have specific error messages for specific error states.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Bank details" (How it works > Error messages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Bank details > How it works > If the building society roll number is too long
title: Bank details: If the building society roll number is too long
statement: Say 'Building society roll number must be between 1 and 18 characters'.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Bank details" (How it works > If the building society roll number is too long).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Bank details > How it works > If the building society roll number uses characters that are not allowed
title: Bank details: If the building society roll number uses characters that are not allowed
statement: Say 'Building society roll number must only include letters a to z, numbers, hyphens, spaces, forward slashes and full stops'.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Bank details" (How it works > If the building society roll number uses characters that are not allowed).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Check a service is suitable
title: Check a service is suitable
statement: Ask users questions to help them work out if they can or should use your service. Doing this helps users save time as it tells them upfront whether they are eligible to use it and if they need it. It can also help reduce time and money spent processing queries from users confused about whether they’re eligible to use your service, or if it’s suitable for them.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Check a service is suitable" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Check a service is suitable > When to use this pattern
title: Check a service is suitable: When to use this pattern
statement: If you have complicated eligibility requirements you should follow this pattern. This will save users from having to read through large amounts of documentation outside of your service to work out if they can use it. Use this pattern to help users work out: - if they’re eligible to use your service - how much it will cost them to use - how much money they will get - how long it will take to get something Read guidance about designing your service so you give users information at the point they need it in the GOV.UK Service Manual.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Check a service is suitable" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Check a service is suitable > When not to use this pattern
title: Check a service is suitable: When not to use this pattern
statement: Do not use this pattern if you can reasonably include information users need to know about your service and its eligibility requirements on a start page.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Check a service is suitable" (When not to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Check a service is suitable > How it works
title: Check a service is suitable: How it works
statement: You should help people find out whether your service is right for them as soon as you can. When using this pattern you need to: - ask a series of simple questions - automatically work out what a user needs to know - present the user with a ‘results’ page If there are general rules about whether a service can or cannot be used such as an age limit or fixed deadline, include these on the start page. Avoid asking questions the user will need to provide again when using your service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Check a service is suitable" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Check a service is suitable > How it works > Presenting results
title: Check a service is suitable: Presenting results
statement: Your results page should show the user if they’re eligible to use it. Where applicable, it should also show them: - if they have to use your service - how much it will cost them to use it - how much money they’ll get from using it - how long the whole process will take If a user is not eligible to use your service, explain why and, if possible, tell them what they should do instead. Here’s an example of a results page:
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Check a service is suitable" (How it works > Presenting results).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Check answers
title: Check answers
statement: Let users check their answers before submitting information to a service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Check answers" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Check answers > When to use this pattern
title: Check answers: When to use this pattern
statement: Show a single check answers page immediately before the confirmation screen for small to medium-sized transactions. When designing a very large transaction with multiple sections, it may help to include a check answers pages at the end of each section. This can be valuable for services where different users might be completing each section. You should test this approach with your users to find out if it’s helpful. Use the Summary card component when users need to check multiple things of the same type. For example to review a series of interview appointments or application choices.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Check answers" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Check answers > How it works
title: Check answers: How it works
statement: Check answers pages help to: - increase users’ confidence as they can clearly see that they have completed all the sections and that their data has been captured - reduce error rates as users are given a second chance to notice and correct errors before submitting data
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Check answers" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Check answers > How it works > Choose the right layout for the page
title: Check answers: Choose the right layout for the page
statement: Many services ask users for short answers, which are suitable for a layout that takes up two-thirds of the screen on desktop devices. For example, the 'Check your answers before submitting your application' page included in this guidance. Using a two-thirds layout stops lines of text getting so long that the page becomes difficult to read. To learn more about line length, see 'Layout'. It also means the action links are closer to the other content on the page. Users with screen magnifiers are less likely to miss them. However, if your service asks users for longer or more detailed answers, a full width layout may be more suitable.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Check answers" (How it works > Choose the right layout for the page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Check answers > How it works > Make the page easy to understand
title: Check answers: Make the page easy to understand
statement: Use the page title to tell the user what they need to do – otherwise, they might miss the 'submit' button at the end of the page. On the page, you should also: - make it clear the transaction will not be complete until a user confirms their information is correct - break the content up into sections when you can - only show sections that are relevant to users – for example, if they’ve said they’re from the UK, do not show sections for questions they have not answered about locations outside of the UK - rephrase questions if you need to – for example, you do not need to label every individual line of an address, and you can rewrite long questions as shorter statements - make sure the 'submit' button clearly shows the action it performs – for example, ‘Change your tax details’ or ‘Send your claim form’
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Check answers" (How it works > Make the page easy to understand).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Check answers > How it works > Let users go back and change their answers
title: Check answers: Let users go back and change their answers
statement: You should provide a ‘Change’ link next to each section on your check answers page so that users can add or change the information. 'Change' links contain hidden text to make them accessible to screen reader users. Update the hidden text to describe what each 'change' link is for. If a user decides to go back to a previous answer, make sure information they've already entered is pre-populated. The answers pages should look the same way they did when the user last used them. When they’ve finished, the ‘Continue’ button should return them to the check answers page. They should not need to go through the rest of the transaction again. If a user changes their response in a way that means you need to ask them more questions, do this before returning them to the check answers page. If you have questions that are optional, let users know that they've skipped it without giving an answer by showing their response as ‘Not provided’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Check answers" (How it works > Let users go back and change their answers).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Complete multiple tasks
title: Complete multiple tasks
statement: Help users understand: - the tasks involved in completing a transaction - the order they should complete tasks in - when they've completed tasks Complete multiple tasks pages use a Task list component for each group of tasks on the page.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Complete multiple tasks" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Complete multiple tasks > When to use this pattern
title: Complete multiple tasks: When to use this pattern
statement: Only use a complete multiple tasks page for longer transactions involving multiple tasks that users may need to complete over a number of sessions. Try to simplify the transaction before you use a complete multiple tasks page. If you’re able to reduce the number of tasks or steps involved, you might not need one.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Complete multiple tasks" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Complete multiple tasks > How it works
title: Complete multiple tasks: How it works
statement: You should show a complete multiple tasks page: - at the start of the transaction - at the start of each returning session If you use a complete multiple tasks page in your service, you'll need to: - group related actions into tasks - show the status of the tasks If there are lots of tasks to complete, you might also need to group them further into steps.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Complete multiple tasks" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Complete multiple tasks > How it works > Show the status of the tasks
title: Complete multiple tasks: Show the status of the tasks
statement: Make it clear to users which tasks they’ve completed and which still need their attention, by labelling them using statuses. Statuses should be helpful to users. The more you add, the harder it is for users to remember them. Start with the smallest number of different statuses you think might work, for example ‘Completed’ and ‘Incomplete’, then add more if your user research shows there’s a need for them. Once the user has completed the task, the status should show as ‘Completed’ and be black text with no background colour. This will draw more attention to tasks that require action.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Complete multiple tasks" (How it works > Show the status of the tasks).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Complete multiple tasks > How it works > Tasks that are in progress
title: Complete multiple tasks: Tasks that are in progress
statement: You may find you need additional statuses if your user research shows that users want to be able to distinguish between the tasks they haven’t started at all, and those they’ve started but not completed. In this instance, instead of ‘Incomplete’, you may want to use ‘Not yet started’ to show which tasks they are yet to start. You should then use ‘In progress’ for tasks they have started but are yet to complete. Different colours may be used to further differentiate between tags.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Complete multiple tasks" (How it works > Tasks that are in progress).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Complete multiple tasks > How it works > Tasks that cannot yet be started
title: Complete multiple tasks: Tasks that cannot yet be started
statement: If the user cannot start the task yet, for example because another task must be completed first, use the ‘Cannot start yet’ status. This should be grey text with no background colour, and the ‘task row’ should not be linked.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Complete multiple tasks" (How it works > Tasks that cannot yet be started).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Complete multiple tasks > How it works > Tasks containing an error
title: Complete multiple tasks: Tasks containing an error
statement: You should avoid tasks having an error status by using the Error summary component and Error message component displayed at the point that the error is made, so that the user can fix it straight away. If it is unavoidable that a task may end up saved but containing an error, use the status text ‘There is a problem’ and a red background. Do not use the red background colour for any status text except errors.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Complete multiple tasks" (How it works > Tasks containing an error).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Complete multiple tasks > How it works > Status text
title: Complete multiple tasks: Status text
statement: Although we recommend using consistent wording across task lists, you can change it if research shows that different text is more suitable to your service or users. If you are creating your own statuses, use adjectives rather than verbs. Use sentence case, and keep it short, so that it can be easily read and understood.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Complete multiple tasks" (How it works > Status text).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Complete multiple tasks > How it works > Additional statuses
title: Complete multiple tasks: Additional statuses
statement: If your user research shows that there is a need for additional status tags, you can use other colours to help distinguish between them.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Complete multiple tasks" (How it works > Additional statuses).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Complete multiple tasks > How it works > Group tasks into steps
title: Complete multiple tasks: Group tasks into steps
statement: If your transaction involves lots of tasks, make it manageable by splitting it up into steps that represent stages in the process. For example, you could group all tasks which help users find out if your service is right for them in a step called ‘Check before you start’. Where possible, allow users to complete tasks in any order. This will help them plan their time and complete sections as and when they can.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Complete multiple tasks" (How it works > Group tasks into steps).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Complete multiple tasks > How it works > Marking tasks as completed
title: Complete multiple tasks: Marking tasks as completed
statement: Sometimes, it’s better to let the user decide when a task is completed. This can be helpful when a task involves: - some questions that are optional - writing a long answer (such as in a Textarea component) - looking up information, such as details about previous jobs - answers that need to be checked carefully with someone else Do this by asking a radio question at the end of the task – either as the last question (if the task is a single page) or on the Check answers page (if the task involves more than one page). Ask ‘Have you completed this section?’ with the radio options ‘Yes, I’ve completed this section’ or ‘No, I’ll come back later’. If the user selects ‘No, I’ll come back to it later,’ mark the task as 'Incomplete' or 'In progress'. If the user selects ‘Yes, I’ve completed this section,’ mark the task as 'Completed'. Always allow users to go back into a task to change their answer.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Complete multiple tasks" (How it works > Marking tasks as completed).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Complete multiple tasks > How it works > Error messages
title: Complete multiple tasks: Error messages
statement: If the user does not select an option, show an Error message component to say: 'Select whether you’ve completed this section'.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Complete multiple tasks" (How it works > Error messages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Confirm a phone number
title: Confirm a phone number
statement: Check that a user has access to a specific mobile phone number using a security code sent by text message.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Confirm a phone number" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Confirm a phone number > When to use this pattern
title: Confirm a phone number: When to use this pattern
statement: Ask the user to enter a security code when they need to sign in or complete a higher-risk task, such as changing a password. Asking the user to enter a security code sent to their mobile phone gives a second layer of security over only asking for a password. You can ask for a security code every time a user signs in or only once per device, depending on the risk level of your service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Confirm a phone number" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Confirm a phone number > How it works
title: Confirm a phone number: How it works
statement: Send and ask the user for the security code when they: - create an account - sign in later
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Confirm a phone number" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Confirm a phone number > How it works > When the user creates an account
title: Confirm a phone number: When the user creates an account
statement: When the user creates an account, ask for their password and mobile phone number at the same time. Make it clear if you'll only use the mobile number for sending security codes, or if you'll also use it for other purposes. After saving the user’s password and mobile phone number, verify their mobile phone number by sending them a text message with a 5 digit code in this format: 12345 is your [service name] security code Then ask the user to enter this code: Let the user enter the code in whatever format is familiar to them. Allow additional spaces, hyphens and dashes. Give a time limit of 15 minutes for the user to enter the code – the code should expire after this time limit. If the user enters an expired code that was sent more than: - 15 minutes ago, show a ‘code has expired’ error message and send the user a new code - 2 hours ago, show an ‘incorrect security code’ message, even if the code was correct If the user follows the ‘Not received a text message?’ link, allow them to check which mobile number they entered, and to change it if necessary. This prevents the user becoming stuck if they entered a mobile number incorrectly. Do not allow the user to change the number when they're signing in. When the user requests a new code, send them a new one. The new code should have its 15 minute time limit. The previous code should remain valid within its original time limit.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Confirm a phone number" (How it works > When the user creates an account).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Confirm a phone number > How it works > When the user signs in
title: Confirm a phone number: When the user signs in
statement: When the user returns to your service, verify their password first. Once they have entered this correctly, send a text message to their mobile phone with a 5 digit code in this format: 12345 is your [service name] security code Ask the user to enter this code. Use the same pattern and time limit as when creating an account. If they follow the ‘Not received a text message?’ link, show them a page allowing them to request a new code. Do not reveal the mobile number you sent it to. You should tell the user what to do if they no longer have access to the phone used to sign up. For example, you might tell them to contact a support address.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Confirm a phone number" (How it works > When the user signs in).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Confirm a phone number > How it works > Error messages
title: Confirm a phone number: Error messages
statement: Style error messages like this: If the user does not enter enough digits: Say ‘You've not entered enough numbers, the code must be 5 numbers’. If the user enters too many digits: Say ‘You’ve entered too many numbers, the code must be 5 numbers’. If the user enters non-numeric characters, other than spaces: Say ‘The code must be 5 numbers’. If the code has expired, show this message: If the code was sent more than 2 hours ago, show the 'incorrect security code' message.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Confirm a phone number" (How it works > Error messages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Confirm a phone number > How it works > Technical security measures
title: Confirm a phone number: Technical security measures
statement: Use technical measures to prevent automated attacks. For example, add a time delay after 10 incorrect number entries. Set up monitoring for potentially malicious behaviour, such as activity from unexpected geographical areas.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Confirm a phone number" (How it works > Technical security measures).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Confirm an email address
title: Confirm an email address
statement: This guidance is for government teams that build online services. To find information and services for the public, go to GOV.UK. Check that a user has access to a specific email account using an email confirmation loop.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Confirm an email address" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Confirm an email address > When to use this pattern
title: Confirm an email address: When to use this pattern
statement: Only use email confirmation loops if: - critical functionality in the service is only available via email, for example, a password reset - accidentally using the wrong email address would give someone else access to sensitive information about the user Remember that confirmed emails do not prove a person’s identity, just that they have access to that email address at the time they confirmed.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Confirm an email address" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Confirm an email address > How it works
title: Confirm an email address: How it works
statement: Email confirmation loops can be disruptive because they force users to switch from your service to their email account and back again. Common problems with email confirmation include: - confusing users about the journey outside the service - assuming users have an email account and access to it - taking too long to send the confirmation email - not taking steps to prevent emails from being marked as spam You must design your service to reduce these issues for users. If you use email confirmation loops you must consider: - any expiry conditions you set on the email link - letting users resend their email - whether to use a blocking or non-blocking loop - the design of the ‘activate your account’ page Most email confirmation loops will send the user a link and ask them to click it to return to the service. Another approach is to send the user a security code, similar to the Confirm a phone number pattern, and ask the user to enter it.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Confirm an email address" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Confirm an email address > How it works > Set expiry conditions
title: Confirm an email address: Set expiry conditions
statement: You must set an expiry date on the email you send so that the link cannot be used after a certain period of time. You should also set the link to expire when: - it’s been used once - it’s superseded by a new link - the user has changed the email address on their account If a user attempts to use an expired link or a link that’s already been used then you should explain that it’s expired, and why.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Confirm an email address" (How it works > Set expiry conditions).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Confirm an email address > How it works > Let users resend the email
title: Confirm an email address: Let users resend the email
statement: You should let users resend the email confirmation link in case they entered the wrong email address previously or the email did not arrive.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Confirm an email address" (How it works > Let users resend the email).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Confirm an email address > How it works > Blocking or non-blocking loops
title: Confirm an email address: Blocking or non-blocking loops
statement: There are 2 versions of the email confirmation loop: blocking and non-blocking. In a blocking loop, the user cannot use the service until they’ve confirmed their email address. In the non-blocking version, they can continue to use the service, but will be reminded regularly that they need to confirm their email. Some functionality may not be available until they’ve done this. Blocking loops have a simpler flow, but if a user cannot complete the loop then they’re unable to use the service at all. It’s important that you send the emails instantly if you use blocking loops. Non-blocking loops need more careful design because you cannot guarantee that all users will confirm their email. This could stop people from accessing your service. You can also use a combination of both, by starting users on a non-blocking loop initially and then change to a blocking loop.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Confirm an email address" (How it works > Blocking or non-blocking loops).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Confirm an email address > How it works > Designing the ‘activate your account’ page
title: Confirm an email address: Designing the ‘activate your account’ page
statement: This page should explain what the user needs to do to activate their account. You should show this page immediately after the user provides their email address or if they try to sign in before confirming their email. The page should: - show the user the email address that you sent their activation email to - explain that they need to click the link in the email to proceed - let them resend the activation email to a different email address if necessary For blocking loops this should be the only page the user sees if they try to sign in before activating their account. For non-blocking loops, if a user signs in before activating their account then you should: - let them use the service - remind them that they need to activate their account - tell them where the activation email has been sent - let them resend the activation email - let them change their email address and confirm that instead When a user clicks on the link in the activation email, send them to a page that confirms they’ve activated their account. You may or may not require them to sign in at this stage, depending on where in the flow the ‘activate your account’ screen appears.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Confirm an email address" (How it works > Designing the ‘activate your account’ page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Confirmation pages
title: Confirmation pages
statement: Use this pattern to let users know they’ve completed a transaction. Include a link to the GOV.UK feedback page to allow users to tell you what they think of your transaction.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Confirmation pages" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Confirmation pages > When to use this pattern
title: Confirmation pages: When to use this pattern
statement: You should use a confirmation page at the end of a transaction.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Confirmation pages" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Confirmation pages > How it works
title: Confirmation pages: How it works
statement: Confirmation pages reassure users that they have completed a transaction and helps them understand what to expect next. Your confirmation page must include: - a reference number, if there is one - details of what happens next and when - contact details for the service - links to information or services that users are likely to need next - a link to your feedback page - a way for users to save a record of the transaction, for example, as a PDF If you choose to add links, buttons or other interactive elements in the green confirmation panel, they will not be accessible. You'll need to make changes to the panel or focus state style to make them accessible and meet a minimum contrast ratio of 3:1.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Confirmation pages" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Confirmation pages > How it works > Help users who bookmark the page
title: Confirmation pages: Help users who bookmark the page
statement: Some users will bookmark the confirmation page as a form of receipt. You should allow them to return to the page, whenever possible. If you cannot, make sure your service responds in a helpful way when users return using a bookmarked link. For example, if people use your service to make an application you could provide links to information on: - tracking an application - starting a new application - what to do or who to contact if they have a problem with their application
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Confirmation pages" (How it works > Help users who bookmark the page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Contact a department or service team > When to use this pattern
title: Contact a department or service team: When to use this pattern
statement: Use this pattern whenever you need to help users contact your team or department. Carry out contextual user research to decide exactly where to use this pattern in a page or service. Read about how and why to set up user support in the GOV.UK Service Manual.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Contact a department or service team" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Contact a department or service team > How it works
title: Contact a department or service team: How it works
statement: Order contact channels based on what research shows your users need, and what your service or department can best support. Show contact channels in the same order throughout your service. This helps users to find what they need more easily.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Contact a department or service team" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Contact a department or service team > How it works > Social media
title: Contact a department or service team: Social media
statement: If you have social media channels, list these channels last. Tell users not to share personal information where others can see it.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Contact a department or service team" (How it works > Social media).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Contact a department or service team > How it works > Explain any charges
title: Contact a department or service team: Explain any charges
statement: Tell users if they might have to pay to use any of your contact channels. For phone call charges, link to the GOV.UK page on call charges. Include the link after the contact channels list and opening hours.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Contact a department or service team" (How it works > Explain any charges).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Contact a department or service team > How it works > Give opening hours
title: Contact a department or service team: Give opening hours
statement: Follow the GOV.UK style guide format for time ranges and date ranges. Explain any exceptions, like bank holidays, or days of the week when your opening hours are different. For example, ‘Monday to Friday, 9am to midday and 2pm to 4:30pm (closed on bank holidays)’ or ‘24-hour service’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Contact a department or service team" (How it works > Give opening hours).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Contact a department or service team > How it works > Tell users how long they’ll have to wait
title: Contact a department or service team: Tell users how long they’ll have to wait
statement: Tell users when you'll respond to them. This helps users choose which contact channel to use. For example, tell users how long it'll usually take to: - receive a response to their email - get to the front of your webchat queue
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Contact a department or service team" (How it works > Tell users how long they’ll have to wait).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Contact a department or service team > How it works > Inset contact information
title: Contact a department or service team: Inset contact information
statement: Use the Inset text component to display contact information when you want to differentiate it from the content that surrounds it.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Contact a department or service team" (How it works > Inset contact information).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Contact a department or service team > How it works > Expanding contact information
title: Contact a department or service team: Expanding contact information
statement: If contact information is less important than other content on a page, you can enclose contact information inside the Details component to avoid distracting users. For example, if you need to provide contact information at the bottom of a form page for users who need help completing the form. Only do this when there’s a lot of contact information to display. When there are only 1 or 2 lines, include the contact information within the body of the page.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Contact a department or service team" (How it works > Expanding contact information).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookies page
title: Cookies page
statement: Tell users about the cookies you’re setting on their device and let them accept or reject different types of non-essential cookies.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookies page" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookies page > When to use this pattern
title: Cookies page: When to use this pattern
statement: Use a cookies page to tell the user about any cookies your service uses - or any other technologies that work in a similar way and store information on the user’s device. For example, HTML5 local storage or service workers.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookies page" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookies page > How it works
title: Cookies page: How it works
statement: A cookies page helps you to be transparent about the cookies you’re using. The Service Manual has guidance on how and when to use cookies.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookies page" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookies page > Preparing your cookies page
title: Cookies page: Preparing your cookies page
statement: You must publish a cookies page by the time your service goes into public beta. The cookies page must be unique to your service: do not link to the cookie policy for the main GOV.UK website. Follow the steps below to create a cookie policy. 1. Audit your cookies. 2. Categorise your cookies. 3. Write your cookies page.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookies page" (Preparing your cookies page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookies page > Auditing and categorising your cookies
title: Cookies page: Auditing and categorising your cookies
statement: List all the cookies you’re using in the service. Divide the list into: - essential cookies - these are cookies you need to set so the service will work - functional cookies - the service will work without them, but the user will not be able to take advantage of some functionality (for example, remembering the settings they’ve chosen between different visits) - analytics cookies - cookies that let you collect analytics data to use within your own organisation - any other types of cookie you’re using You should also identify if each cookie is set on the server or client. The result of your audit will guide your cookie policy and how the service should use a cookies page and cookie banner. The Cookie banner component shows several options for using a cookie banner for services that: - only set essential cookies - sets non-essential cookies on the server - including services that also set non-essential cookies on the client - sets non-essential cookies - but only on the client
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookies page" (Auditing and categorising your cookies).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookies page > Writing your cookies page
title: Cookies page: Writing your cookies page
statement: Work with your organisation’s privacy expert to write the cookies page. Cookie policy must be written in clear language. List the cookies individually on the cookies page, under the relevant category. For each cookie, give: - the cookie name - a brief description of what the cookie does - for third party cookies, who is setting the cookie (for example, social media websites may require users to accept their cookies in order to provide their functionality as part of your service) - when the cookie will expire You can see an example on the GOV.UK Notify cookies page. Do not bury your cookie policy in a ‘terms and conditions’ page. Have an agreed process for updating the cookie policy when you add or remove a cookie. Make sure the relevant people on your team know what the process is.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookies page" (Writing your cookies page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookies page > Which cookies you need consent for
title: Cookies page: Which cookies you need consent for
statement: You do not need the user’s consent to set essential or ‘strictly necessary’ cookies. A cookie is ‘strictly necessary’ if the service will not work without it. The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has guidance on what types of cookie are likely to be considered ‘strictly necessary’. For example, load balancing cookies are likely to be strictly necessary - but cookies that collect analytics data are not. You must get the user’s consent before you set any cookies that are not strictly necessary. You can get the user’s consent: - by using a Cookie banner component - by letting the user change and save their settings on the cookies page
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookies page" (Which cookies you need consent for).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookies page > Publishing your cookies page
title: Cookies page: Publishing your cookies page
statement: Link to the cookies page from the Footer component and from the Cookie banner component.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookies page" (Publishing your cookies page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookies page > Letting users accept or reject cookies on the cookies page
title: Cookies page: Letting users accept or reject cookies on the cookies page
statement: Use a Radios component and a Button component to let users accept or reject non-essential cookies. Load the page with the radios set to ‘no’ on the user’s first visit. If they’ve previously used the service and set their preferences, load the page with those preferences selected. When the user sets or changes their cookie preferences, use a green Notification banner component to confirm that the service has updated the user’s cookie settings. This is so they can get back to the page they were looking at.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookies page" (Letting users accept or reject cookies on the cookies page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookies page > If you depend on JavaScript to ask users to accept or reject cookies
title: Cookies page: If you depend on JavaScript to ask users to accept or reject cookies
statement: If you depend on JavaScript to ask about cookie preferences and the user’s device is not running JavaScript, show them a different version of the cookies page. Replace the radios with a section of text explaining what the user needs to do in order to change their cookie settings.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookies page" (If you depend on JavaScript to ask users to accept or reject cookies).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Cookies page > Keeping your cookies page up to date and asking for new consent
title: Cookies page: Keeping your cookies page up to date and asking for new consent
statement: Update your cookies page when you change the cookies you’re using. Check with your organisation’s privacy expert: - how you should classify the new cookie - whether you’ll need to ask for new consent from all users (including those who’ve already consented to the cookies you were previously using) It’s likely you’ll need to ask for new consent if: - you start using a type of non-essential cookie you have not used before (for example, if you start using functional cookies for the first time) - you start using cookies which could be considered intrusive (for example because they collect sensitive information which could be associated with an individual, like health information) - you start doing something with the data you’re collecting through cookies which is significantly different to what the user originally consented to Do not set any new non-essential cookies until the user has given their consent again.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Cookies page" (Keeping your cookies page up to date and asking for new consent).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Create a username
title: Create a username
statement: Help users to create a unique and memorable username to sign into a service with.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Create a username" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Create a username > When to use this pattern
title: Create a username: When to use this pattern
statement: Before using this pattern, you should consider whether you really need users to create accounts in your service in the first place.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Create a username" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Create a username > How it works
title: Create a username: How it works
statement: Where possible, use email addresses for usernames because they are: - memorable - unique - often required by the service anyway However, not everyone has or wants to use an email address. The number of users without access to email will differ from service to service. You should do research to understand this group and have a plan for helping them to use your service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Create a username" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Create a username > How it works > Custom usernames
title: Create a username: Custom usernames
statement: You should only ask users to create their own custom usernames if your service contains user-generated content that requires attributing, for example, a blog with comments. Allowing custom usernames lets users hide their identity if they want to. User-generated usernames are harder to create and easier to forget than email addresses.
