You need to: - tell the user whether their proposed username is unique - suggest a unique username for them, in some cases - make sure the user can retrieve or reset their username - ignore letter case when accepting usernames - for example, if the actual username is ‘Mary @example.com’, the user can still sign in with ‘mary @example.com’
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Create a username" (How it works > Custom usernames).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Create a username > How it works > Always let people make changes
title: Create a username: Always let people make changes
statement: Whatever approach to usernames you take, make sure you let people change their email address or username.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Create a username" (How it works > Always let people make changes).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Create accounts > When to use this pattern
title: Create accounts: When to use this pattern
statement: Provide user accounts if your users will need to regularly access or update their data in your service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Create accounts" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Create accounts > When not to use this pattern
title: Create accounts: When not to use this pattern
statement: Do not create user accounts if you can provide a usable service without them. This is because user accounts are: - a barrier for many users and make it more likely they will drop out - difficult to build and maintain If you want to let users check the status of a one-off transaction, give them a unique reference number they can use along with their name or email address. Unique references are hard to remember so you should send them in an email or text message to the user.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Create accounts" (When not to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Create accounts > How it works
title: Create accounts: How it works
statement: If a user needs an account as part of your service: - let them use as much of your service as possible before they need to create an account - use clear and consistent language - create a simple user journey - make the sign-up process clear
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Create accounts" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Create accounts > How it works > Use clear and consistent language
title: Create accounts: Use clear and consistent language
statement: For consistency with other GOV.UK services, use the phrase ‘Create an account’ instead of ‘Register’, ‘Sign up’ or something else. Use labels like ‘Create a username’ and ‘Create a password’ rather than ‘Username’ and ‘Password’. This helps users to understand that they’re not being asked to enter an existing username or password.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Create accounts" (How it works > Use clear and consistent language).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Create accounts > How it works > Create a simple user journey
title: Create accounts: Create a simple user journey
statement: Make it clear what you need users to do when they create an account. Show a clear difference between creating an account and signing in. Presenting the options side by side is not enough because users might miss one of them or not understand the difference.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Create accounts" (How it works > Create a simple user journey).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Create accounts > How it works > Make the sign-up process clear
title: Create accounts: Make the sign-up process clear
statement: If a user fails to create an account they might not be able to use your service at all. Make sure the account creation screen is solely about that task. Do not add any distracting content or links. Make sure users do not need to enter the same information more than once when creating an account.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Create accounts" (How it works > Make the sign-up process clear).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Create accounts > How it works > Avoid using security measures such as CAPTCHAs
title: Create accounts: Avoid using security measures such as CAPTCHAs
statement: CAPTCHAs and similar tests require users to recognise words or pictures. These are tests of cognitive function, which might be difficult for some users. Users can also struggle to recognise specific words or pictures due to differences in culture and locale. See more about using CAPTCHAs and why they’re problematic in the Service Manual. WCAG lists some other security measures you can implement to prevent misuse and automated abuse in your service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Create accounts" (How it works > Avoid using security measures such as CAPTCHAs).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Create accounts > How it works > Never use National Insurance numbers to verify a user’s identity
title: Create accounts: Never use National Insurance numbers to verify a user’s identity
statement: If you currently use National Insurance numbers to verify identity, find out how to protect your service against fraud.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Create accounts" (How it works > Never use National Insurance numbers to verify a user’s identity).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Dates > When to use this pattern
title: Dates: When to use this pattern
statement: Follow this pattern whenever you need users to provide or select a date as part of your service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Dates" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Dates > How it works
title: Dates: How it works
statement: The way you should ask users for dates depends on the types of date you’re asking for. Dates you may need users to provide include: - memorable dates, like a date of birth or marriage - dates from documents or cards, like a passport or credit card - approximate dates, like ‘December 2017’ - relative dates, like ‘4 days from today’ In some cases you might need users to pick a date from a given selection.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Dates" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Dates > How it works > Asking for memorable dates
title: Dates: Asking for memorable dates
statement: Ask for memorable dates, like dates of birth, using the Date input component component.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Dates" (How it works > Asking for memorable dates).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Dates > How it works > Asking for dates from documents and cards
title: Dates: Asking for dates from documents and cards
statement: When asking for a date exactly as it’s shown on a passport, credit card or other document, make the fields match the format of the original. This makes it easier for users to copy the date across accurately.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Dates" (How it works > Asking for dates from documents and cards).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Dates > How it works > Asking for approximate dates
title: Dates: Asking for approximate dates
statement: Allow users to enter an approximate date when you are asking them for information they may not know or may struggle to remember. For example, allow users to enter ‘December 2017’ for a field that says ‘the date you lost your passport’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Dates" (How it works > Asking for approximate dates).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Dates > How it works > Asking for relative dates
title: Dates: Asking for relative dates
statement: You may need to ask for dates that are relative to today’s date or another date - this is common if a user is setting a reminder. To do this let users enter or select relative dates like ‘tomorrow’ or ‘1 day before’. If the day of the week is important, show this as well.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Dates" (How it works > Asking for relative dates).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Dates > How it works > Helping users to pick a date
title: Dates: Helping users to pick a date
statement: Users might need to pick a date from a selection, for example, to book an appointment. To do this, you can present dates in a calendar format using a calendar control. Users are typically shown one month’s worth of dates at a time, and can skip through months and years. Only use a calendar control if users need to: - pick a date in the near future or recent past - know the day of the week, or the week of the month, as well as the date - be able to see dates in relation to other dates Never make a calendar control that depends on JavaScript as the only input option. Allow users to enter the date into a text input as well as use the control.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Dates" (How it works > Helping users to pick a date).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Dates > How it works > How to write dates
title: Dates: How to write dates
statement: See the GOV.UK style for writing dates and date ranges. If you give an example date, use 13 or more for the day and 9 or less for the month - for example ‘27 3 2007’. This helps users enter the date in the correct order and shows them they do not need to include leading zeroes.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Dates" (How it works > How to write dates).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Email addresses
title: Email addresses
statement: This guidance is for government teams that build online services. To find information and services for the public, go to GOV.UK.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Email addresses" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Email addresses > When to use this pattern
title: Email addresses: When to use this pattern
statement: Follow this pattern whenever you need to capture an email address.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Email addresses" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Email addresses > How it works
title: Email addresses: How it works
statement: When asking users for their email address, you must: - make it clear why you’re asking - make sure the field works for all of your users - help users to enter a valid email address You may also need to check that users have access to the email account they give you.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Email addresses" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Email addresses > How it works > Tell users why you want the email address
title: Email addresses: Tell users why you want the email address
statement: Make it clear what the email address will be used for so that: - users feel confident that you’re not going to abuse it - users with multiple email addresses can choose which one to give you If the email address field is part of a sign-in box, you do not need to say ‘We need your email so we can sign you in’.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Email addresses" (How it works > Tell users why you want the email address).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Email addresses > How it works > Make sure the field works for all of your users
title: Email addresses: Make sure the field works for all of your users
statement: Make sure the field can accommodate up to 254 characters, which is the longest an email address can be.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Email addresses" (How it works > Make sure the field works for all of your users).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Email addresses > How it works > Help users to enter a valid email address
title: Email addresses: Help users to enter a valid email address
statement: Help your users to enter a valid email address by: - checking they have entered the correct format - allowing users to paste the email address - setting the type attribute to email so that devices display the correct keyboard - setting the spellcheck attribute to false so that browsers do not spellcheck the email address - confirming their address back to them so they can check and change it You should also set the autocomplete attribute to email. This lets browsers autofill the email address on a user's behalf if they’ve entered it previously. If you are working in production you’ll need to do this to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.3.5 Identify input purpose. You will not normally need to use the autocomplete attribute in prototypes, as users will not generally be using their own devices. The field should be wide enough for most users to see their entire email address once they have entered it. A good rule of thumb is to make sure you can see at least 30 characters at once. You can analyse your user data to refine this. You can check for common misspellings of popular email providers, for example ‘homtail.com’ instead of ‘hotmail.com’. Warn users if you detect one, but allow them to proceed in case it’s a genuine email address. Some services ask users to repeat their email address. Only do this if your user research shows it to be effective.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Email addresses" (How it works > Help users to enter a valid email address).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Email addresses > How it works > Check the user has access to their email account
title: Email addresses: Check the user has access to their email account
statement: If email is an essential part of your service - for example to send a password reset - you can confirm whether the user has access to the email address they give you using an email confirmation loop. However, these are disruptive and should be avoided as far as possible.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Email addresses" (How it works > Check the user has access to their email account).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Email addresses > How it works > Error messages
title: Email addresses: Error messages
statement: Error messages should be styled like this: Make sure errors follow the guidance in the Error message component and have specific error messages for specific error states.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Email addresses" (How it works > Error messages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Equality information
title: Equality information
statement: Public sector organisations have a duty to consider the need to avoid discrimination and advance equality of opportunity as part of what they do. This is part of what’s called the public sector equality duty. Public sector bodies often collect equality information about service users to help them meet this duty.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Equality information" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Equality information > When to use this pattern
title: Equality information: When to use this pattern
statement: These patterns are based on the harmonised standards developed by the Government Statistical Service. Collecting equality information in a consistent way across the public sector makes the data more useful. For example, an organisation can benchmark its own services against other public sector services or the population in general. And it can adjust its approach if it finds a particular group is under-represented. Do not use this pattern to collect information for operational reasons - especially if you’re legally required to ask for the information in a particular way.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Equality information" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Equality information > How it works
title: Equality information: How it works
statement: When asking users for equality information, make it clear: - that the questions are different from other questions in the service - why you’re asking the questions, and what you’ll do with the information - that the questions are optional
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Equality information" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Equality information > How it works > Where to place equality questions
title: Equality information: Where to place equality questions
statement: For a service that people are likely to use on a one-off basis: - place equality questions between your service's Check your answers page and your Confirmation page - show the user a screen explaining why you’re asking the questions and what you’ll do with the information they provide, like the one below
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Equality information" (How it works > Where to place equality questions).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Equality information > How it works > Longer term services
title: Equality information: Longer term services
statement: With a service that you expect users to return to multiple times, you’ll need to decide where to place the equality questions. For example, with an account-type service with tasks that need to be completed at different times, you might choose to make answering the equality questions an optional task. You’ll also need to give users the option to update their equality information in case anything changes.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Equality information" (How it works > Longer term services).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Equality information > How it works > Updating equality information
title: Equality information: Updating equality information
statement: Some categories of equality information can change over time, including changes to: - marriage or partnership status - disability - religion - sexual orientation - gender identity When possible, offer users the option to update their equality information. Users should be able to update their equality information through an online account, a change request form, or other contact methods. Integrating the option to update equality information directly into your service or user account system is often the most usable and efficient method. Updating equality information is especially relevant for longer term services and services that use the same equality information multiple times.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Equality information" (How it works > Updating equality information).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Equality information > Get specialist privacy or data protection advice
title: Equality information: Get specialist privacy or data protection advice
statement: Some or all of the equality information you collect is likely to be what’s called ‘special category personal data’, meaning it has special legal protections. So before you start collecting equality information, it’s important to get advice and approval from your organisation’s privacy or data protection expert on how to collect and process the information. You’ll also need to update the service’s privacy notice.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Equality information" (Get specialist privacy or data protection advice).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Equality information > What information to collect
title: Equality information: What information to collect
statement: Public sector organisations will have someone who is responsible for making sure the organisation is meeting its obligations under the public sector equality duty. They can help you work out what equality information to collect. This pattern covers: - age - disability - ethnic group - marital or partnership status - religion - sex and gender identity - sexual orientation
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Equality information" (What information to collect).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Equality information > What information to collect > Collecting more detailed information
title: Equality information: Collecting more detailed information
statement: Start with the harmonised standards, keeping the categories of responses in the same order. Break them down into subcategories if necessary. For example if your service is aimed at a disabled people in particular, you may want to collect more detailed information about their disability. But make sure any categories you use map back to a ‘parent’ category in the harmonised standard.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Equality information" (What information to collect > Collecting more detailed information).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Equality information > What information to collect > Collecting other types of equality information
title: Equality information: Collecting other types of equality information
statement: See the full list of Government Statistical Service harmonised standards if you want to collect other types of equality information. For example, about income or employment status.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Equality information" (What information to collect > Collecting other types of equality information).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Equality information > What information to collect > Asking about disability
title: Equality information: Asking about disability
statement: Use this approach to ask about disability. If the user answers ‘yes’, ask about the impact of their condition or illness.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Equality information" (What information to collect > Asking about disability).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Equality information > What information to collect > Asking about ethnic group
title: Equality information: Asking about ethnic group
statement: The ethnic groups used here are for England. The Government Statistical Service harmonised standard uses different categories for ethnicity data collected in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. This is to reflect differences in local populations. If your service covers more than one of England, Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland, you should accommodate these differences in your design. For example, by changing the ethnic groups shown depending on where the user is based. Where this is not possible, use the English categories. First ask about the user’s broad ethnic group. Then ask for a more detailed category, depending on which broad ethnic group the user selects. Always give the user the option to enter their own description of their background.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Equality information" (What information to collect > Asking about ethnic group).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Equality information > What information to collect > Asking about marriage or civil partnership status
title: Equality information: Asking about marriage or civil partnership status
statement: Use this approach to ask about marriage or civil partnership status.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Equality information" (What information to collect > Asking about marriage or civil partnership status).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Equality information > What information to collect > Asking about religion
title: Equality information: Asking about religion
statement: The categories used here are for England. The Government Statistical Service harmonised standard uses different categories for religion data collected in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. This is to reflect differences in local populations. If your service covers more than one of England, Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland, you should accommodate these differences in your design. For example, by changing the categories shown depending on where the user is based. Where this is not possible, use the English categories.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Equality information" (What information to collect > Asking about religion).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Equality information > What information to collect > Validation and error messages
title: Equality information: Validation and error messages
statement: If a user enters information that’s valid but incomplete, accept it. For example, they might just enter their year of birth without the day or month. Error messages should be styled like this -
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Equality information" (What information to collect > Validation and error messages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Ethnic groups
title: Ethnic groups
statement: In March 2021, we published a new pattern to ask users for equality information, based on data standards set by the Government Statistical Service (GSS). To meet these standards, we’ve retired the ethnic groups pattern, which has been replaced by parts of the new pattern.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Ethnic groups" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Exit a page quickly
title: Exit a page quickly
statement: Give users a way to quickly and safely exit a service, website or application. Use this pattern to add the Exit this page component to your service and keep users safe by helping them to protect their privacy.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Exit a page quickly" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Exit a page quickly > When to use this pattern
title: Exit a page quickly: When to use this pattern
statement: Use this pattern to help the user protect their privacy when your service contains sensitive information that could: - put someone at risk of abuse or retaliation - reveal someone’s plans to avoid or escape from harm For example, a potential victim using a service to help them leave domestic abuse. Other situations and topics where sensitive information could put users at risk might include: - rape or sexual assault - child abuse and neglect - any other type of abuse - stalking and harassment - reporting crime or fraud (whistleblowing)
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Exit a page quickly" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Exit a page quickly > When not to use this pattern
title: Exit a page quickly: When not to use this pattern
statement: You should not use this pattern for standalone content pages, such as dashboards and guidance. In these cases, use the Exit this page component on its own.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Exit a page quickly" (When not to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Exit a page quickly > How it works
title: Exit a page quickly: How it works
statement: First, you’ll need to add the Exit this page component to your service and decide how it should work within your service. The component has several parts, including: - a button, that when activated, will take the user to another website - a secondary link, to give people that use assistive technologies another way to activate the component - a loading overlay, to immediately clear any content off the browser until the next website loads Next, you’ll need to create new content pages in your service. The purpose of these pages are to: - tell the users how to use ‘Exit this page’ to protect their privacy (this called the interruption page) - give users information they need to stay safe online (this is called the safety content page) This pattern is not a complete solution to eliminating all possible risk to the user. Perpetrators can monitor potential victims through other methods, such as malicious software.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Exit a page quickly" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Exit a page quickly > Interruption page
title: Exit a page quickly: Interruption page
statement: Create a page to explain Exit this page to users. You must show this page after the start point of your service, but before the page where the user will see the Exit this page button for the first time. On longer services, you might need more than one interruption page. The page should tell the user: - about the Exit this page button and what it’s for - what happens when they press it - they can also activate Exit this page by pressing shift 3 times or by using the secondary link The page should also tell the user that: - their internet browsing history will not be erased, which can still put them at risk - any information they’ve entered will not be saved, depending on what you’ve decided to do with your service's user session data - to return to the service, they can search for the site they were using, or find it in their internet browsing history - there are other things they can do to stay safe online (include a link to a ‘safety content page’ where the user can learn more)
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Exit a page quickly" (Interruption page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Exit a page quickly > Safety content page
title: Exit a page quickly: Safety content page
statement: Create a page to give users important information they need to stay safe online. Generally, this page should tell the user other steps they can take to protect their privacy. What you include will depend on your service and who uses it. But wherever practical, you should recommend the user takes some basic steps such as: - only using your service on a public device, such as in a library - using private browsing - clearing their internet browsing history and cookies
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Exit a page quickly" (Safety content page).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Gender or sex
title: Gender or sex
statement: For up to date information, see the ask users for equality information pattern.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Gender or sex" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Interruption pages
title: Interruption pages
statement: Use Interruption pages to pause the user’s journey and give them important information.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Interruption pages" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Interruption pages > When to use this pattern
title: Interruption pages: When to use this pattern
statement: Think carefully before you choose to use an Interruption page, as doing this might get in the way of the user completing their task. Use Interruption pages to warn the user before they: - do something unusual that’s probably a mistake - do something that cannot be undone (so you can ask the user “Are you sure?”) - give an answer that conflicts with existing information You can also use Interruption pages: - instead of Confirmation pages to show more varied journey outcomes (that are different to a straightforward success, rejection or completion) - to show the user important information ahead of a task
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Interruption pages" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Interruption pages > When not to use this pattern
title: Interruption pages: When not to use this pattern
statement: Do not use Interruption pages unless you're confident that both: - there’s evidence of a clear need to pause the user journey - it's the only way to give the user information and that they’d otherwise miss it Read guidance in the Service Manual, particularly to Map and understand a user's whole problem, to find ways to improve the user journey and the organisational processes behind them.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Interruption pages" (When not to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Interruption pages > How it works
title: Interruption pages: How it works
statement: Interruption pages pause the user journey to show important information. Use Interruption pages sparingly, as they get less effective the more often users see them. All important information on the page is shown within an Interruption panel, to help ensure the user does not miss it. The panel includes a button that the user must interact with to continue their journey. Information within the panel is usually shown as a heading with some description text, possibly with bullet points and numbered steps. Keep information within the panel short. Do not place any other components or form elements inside the panel.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Interruption pages" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Interruption pages > How it works > Back links and cancel buttons
title: Interruption pages: Back links and cancel buttons
statement: The Interruption page includes a back link at the top of a page, to allow users to go back to the previous page they were on. If it’s helpful for users to jump back to another point in the journey, such as the start of a section, add a link and group it alongside the continue button. Write link text that describes the action it performs or the page it will take the user.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Interruption pages" (How it works > Back links and cancel buttons).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Names > When to use this pattern
title: Names: When to use this pattern
statement: You should follow this pattern whenever you need to ask for a user’s name as part of your service. Only ask for people’s names if you need that information to deliver a service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Names" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Names > How it works > Make sure the fields work for most of your users
title: Names: Make sure the fields work for most of your users
statement: Fields must be long enough to accommodate the names of your users. You should use population data or data about your existing users to do this. Support all the characters users may need to enter, including numbers and symbols.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Names" (How it works > Make sure the fields work for most of your users).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Names > How it works > Single or multiple name fields
title: Names: Single or multiple name fields
statement: Use single or multiple fields depending on your user’s needs. Not everyone’s name fits the first-name, last-name format. Using multiple name fields mean there’s more risk that a person’s name will not fit the format you’ve chosen and that it is entered incorrectly. A single name field can accommodate the broadest range of name types, but means you cannot reliably extract parts of a name.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Names" (How it works > Single or multiple name fields).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Names > How it works > Labelling name fields
title: Names: Labelling name fields
statement: Label single name fields: - ‘Full name’ For multiple name fields, use: - ‘First name’ - ‘Last name’ If users are from outside the UK, use the labels: - ‘Given names’ - ‘Family name’ Make it clear whether you need someone’s common name, or their name as it's written on official documents such as a passport or driving licence.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Names" (How it works > Labelling name fields).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Names > How it works > Middle names
title: Names: Middle names
statement: Only ask for middle names if your service requires them. Use the label: - ’Middle names‘ Make sure middle names are optional, as not everyone has them. The label should not include (optional). Users will enter their middle names if they have them and skip the field if they do not.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Names" (How it works > Middle names).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Names > How it works > Use the autocomplete attribute on name fields
title: Names: Use the autocomplete attribute on name fields
statement: Use the autocomplete attribute on the text input component when you're asking for a user's name. This lets browsers autofill the information on a user's behalf if they’ve entered it previously. If you are asking for a user's full name in a single field, set the autocomplete attribute to name. If you are asking users to enter their name in multiple fields, set the autocomplete attribute on both fields using: - given-name for fields labelled 'First name' or 'Given name' - family-name for fields labelled 'Last name' or 'Family name' If you are working in production you’ll need to do this to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.3.5 Identify input purpose. You will not normally need to use the autocomplete attribute in prototypes, as users will not generally be using their own devices.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Names" (How it works > Use the autocomplete attribute on name fields).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Names > How it works > Do not spellcheck user's names
title: Names: Do not spellcheck user's names
statement: Sometimes, browsers will spellcheck the information a user enters into a text input. To make sure user's names will not be spellchecked, set the spellcheck attribute to false as shown in this example.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Names" (How it works > Do not spellcheck user's names).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Names > How it works > Avoid asking for a person’s title
title: Names: Avoid asking for a person’s title
statement: Avoid asking users for their title. It’s extra work for them and you’re asking them to potentially reveal their gender and marital status, which they may not want to do. It’s also hard to predict the range of titles your users will have. If you have to ask for someone’s title, use an optional Text input component not a Select component. Remember to correctly use people’s names in any resulting correspondence.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Names" (How it works > Avoid asking for a person’s title).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Names > How it works > Allow users to change their name
title: Names: Allow users to change their name
statement: If your service stores personal information, you should allow users to update their details, including their name. Allowing users to change their name helps your service respect their personal identity. It also means they can continue using your service without having to start over. People change their name for many reasons. For example, because of a change in marital status, family situation or gender. Avoid making it hard for users to change their name. As well as causing them distress, it may make them reluctant to use your service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Names" (How it works > Allow users to change their name).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Names > How it works > Error messages
title: Names: Error messages
statement: Error messages should be styled like this: Make sure errors follow the guidance in the Error message component and have specific error messages for specific error states.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Names" (How it works > Error messages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: National Insurance numbers
title: National Insurance numbers
statement: This guidance is for government teams that build online services. To find information and services for the public, go to GOV.UK. Ask users to provide their National Insurance number.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "National Insurance numbers" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: National Insurance numbers > When to use this pattern
title: National Insurance numbers: When to use this pattern
statement: Follow this pattern whenever you need to ask for a National Insurance number.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "National Insurance numbers" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: National Insurance numbers > When not to use this pattern
title: National Insurance numbers: When not to use this pattern
statement: Never use National Insurance numbers to verify a user’s identity. If you currently use National Insurance numbers to verify identity, find out how to protect your service against fraud.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "National Insurance numbers" (When not to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: National Insurance numbers > How it works
title: National Insurance numbers: How it works
statement: Use a single Text input component labelled ‘National Insurance number’. Write it out in full and never use abbreviations such as ‘NINO’ or ‘NI Number’. Show a National Insurance number using the format ‘QQ 12 34 56 C’ – the spaces will break up the number to make it easier to read, particularly for screen reader users. When asking for a National Insurance number: - allow for 13 characters as National Insurance numbers are spaced in pairs followed by a single letter - let users enter upper and lower case letters, additional spaces and punctuation - ignore any unwanted characters before validating - avoid using ‘AB 12 34 56 C’ as an example because it belongs to a real person and use ‘QQ 12 34 56 C’ instead - set the spellcheck attribute to false so that browsers do not spellcheck the National Insurance number
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "National Insurance numbers" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: National Insurance numbers > How it works > Error messages
title: National Insurance numbers: Error messages
statement: Error messages should be styled like this: Make sure errors follow the guidance in the Error message component and have specific error messages for specific error states.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "National Insurance numbers" (How it works > Error messages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service
title: Navigate a service
statement: Help users know they’re using your service and navigate around it. Use this pattern to plan and design your navigation header using the GOV.UK header component and Service navigation component. Check the ‘When to use this component’ sections in each of these components to make sure they’re right for your service. This pattern also includes guidance on how to add other elements commonly used alongside navigation that are not in the GOV.UK Design System. We’ve included this guidance to help service teams make navigation headers more consistent across government.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service > When to use this pattern
title: Navigate a service: When to use this pattern
statement: Navigation links usually appear in services that: - are used repeatedly by some users - involve multiple tasks - do not have a clear order of tasks or end-to-end journey Simplify the user journey as much as possible first. This might remove the need for users to navigate around your service.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service > When not to use this pattern
title: Navigate a service: When not to use this pattern
statement: If your service does have a clear end-to-end journey, avoid using navigation links. Use a Task list component instead, as they’re better for helping users understand: - the tasks involved in completing a transaction - the order they should complete tasks in - when they’ve completed tasks See how to do this in the Help users to complete multiple tasks pattern.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" (When not to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service > How it works
title: Navigate a service: How it works
statement: Together, the GOV.UK header component and Service navigation component work together to assure users that they’re in the right place to use your service. They also help users understand that GOV.UK functions as one website. The GOV.UK header (blue background) includes space to show: - the GOV.UK logo, which links to the GOV.UK homepage - GOV.UK-wide tools such as GOV.UK One Login The Service navigation (light blue background) includes space to show: - the service name, which links to the homepage of your service (or closest page) - a navigation menu for your service - service-level tools, such as a search within your service
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service > How it works > Plan your GOV.UK header
title: Navigate a service: Plan your GOV.UK header
statement: The GOV.UK header component should only be used to show the GOV.UK logo and any GOV.UK-wide tools used in your service, such as GOV.UK One Login. If you need to show your service name or add navigation links, use the Service navigation component.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" (How it works > Plan your GOV.UK header).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service > How it works > Do not show GOV.UK topic links
title: Navigate a service: Do not show GOV.UK topic links
statement: To help users focus on completing your service, do not add the menu of GOV.UK topic links to your service’s GOV.UK header. The menu bar used in the GOV.UK homepage and mainstream guidance pages are designed to help users explore topics and find government services and information. Once users enter your service, they should have all the information they need to complete it from your service's Start page. If you need to refer to specific information as part of your service’s journey, use links within your pages.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" (How it works > Do not show GOV.UK topic links).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service > How it works > Plan your Service navigation
title: Navigate a service: Plan your Service navigation
statement: Use the Service navigation component to show your service name, navigation links and other service-level tools.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" (How it works > Plan your Service navigation).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service > How it works > Show the service name as a link
title: Navigate a service: Show the service name as a link
statement: Show your service name in the Service navigation. Make the service name a link to the homepage of your service. If your service does not have a homepage, link to either: - your service’s GOV.UK start page - the first question of your service
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" (How it works > Show the service name as a link).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service > How it works > Choosing and writing navigation links
title: Navigate a service: Choosing and writing navigation links
statement: You can use the rest of the space in the Service navigation component to show links, such as to help users: - navigate around your service - get in touch - manage their accounts Links within your service must go to the most important top-level sections that are the most useful to the user. This gives the user an idea of what your service does and what they can find within it. Navigation is not a site map and does not need to list every part of your service. In November 2021, the GOV.UK homepage introduced a menu bar that avoids obscuring content by shifting the page down.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" (How it works > Choosing and writing navigation links).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service > How it works > External links
title: Navigate a service: External links
statement: Links that go outside of your service should usually: - be grouped together, and shown after links within your service - open in a new window – warn the user of this, if possible Consider showing external links in the page body instead.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" (How it works > External links).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service > How it works > GOV.UK One Login
title: Navigate a service: GOV.UK One Login
statement: GOV.UK One Login publishes its own header component for services to give users an easy, consistent route to their GOV.UK One Login and a way to sign out.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" (How it works > GOV.UK One Login).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service > Adding other header and navigation elements
title: Navigate a service: Adding other header and navigation elements
statement: To help maintain consistency across services on GOV.UK, we’ve outlined some guidance on how to use the space in your header, and where to add other components and elements. As a general rule, the ordering of header and navigation elements should start with the most general (GOV.UK-wide) elements at the top, with the more specific (service-level) elements further down.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" (Adding other header and navigation elements).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service > Adding other header and navigation elements > Next, show any important elements that affect your entire service
title: Navigate a service: Next, show any important elements that affect your entire service
statement: You can add space between the GOV.UK header and Service navigation to insert important elements that apply to your entire service. Elements you might add here include ‘organisation switchers’, or similar tools that help users use your service across a set of things See an example of an organisation switcher component in the Ministry of Justice Design System. We’d like to learn more about elements you might place between the GOV.UK header and Service navigation. Tell us in our discussion space.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" (Adding other header and navigation elements > Next, show any important elements that affect your entire service).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service > Adding other header and navigation elements > Then, add any other service-level elements
title: Navigate a service: Then, add any other service-level elements
statement: Most other service-level elements can be added within the Service navigation, after the service name.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" (Adding other header and navigation elements > Then, add any other service-level elements).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service > Adding other header and navigation elements > Language navigation
title: Navigate a service: Language navigation
statement: If you provide your whole service in more than one language, you can place the Language navigation component in the Service navigation.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" (Adding other header and navigation elements > Language navigation).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service > Adding other header and navigation elements > Use ‘slots’ to add custom elements
title: Navigate a service: Use ‘slots’ to add custom elements
statement: The Service navigation component includes ‘slots’ to support adding custom elements. You’ll need to decide on the most appropriate layout and positioning and provide your own styles. For example, you might add a search input, if it only searches within your service. To help users understand what the search input will cover, include ‘Search [your service]’ as placeholder text within the search input.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" (Adding other header and navigation elements > Use ‘slots’ to add custom elements).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service > Adding other header and navigation elements > Phase banners
title: Navigate a service: Phase banners
statement: Show the Phase banner component directly under either: - the Service navigation component - the GOV.UK header (if your service does not use the Service navigation component) Phase banners are shown across all pages of a service, so users should understand it as a service-level message. You can choose to place the Phase banner in a more appropriate place for your service, however you’ll need to customise the component and provide your own CSS code to make it show correctly.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" (Adding other header and navigation elements > Phase banners).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service > Adding other header and navigation elements > Finally, show page-specific elements
title: Navigate a service: Finally, show page-specific elements
statement: Show any elements that only affect the current page after the Service header navigation. If your service uses the Breadcrumbs component, place them just before the element. Placing them here means that the ‘Skip to main content’ link allows the user to skip all navigation links, including breadcrumbs.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" (Adding other header and navigation elements > Finally, show page-specific elements).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Navigate a service > How the GOV.UK header and Service navigation work together
title: Navigate a service: How the GOV.UK header and Service navigation work together
statement: We introduced this pattern and the Service navigation component in August 2024. You can no longer use the GOV.UK header to show service name or navigation links. We made these changes to help users better understand: - the relationship between GOV.UK and services - that GOV.UK functions as one website - the difference between GOV.UK-wide tools with service-level tools To help us further improve, share your research and give us your feedback in our GitHub discussion space.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Navigate a service" (How the GOV.UK header and Service navigation work together).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Page not found pages
title: Page not found pages
statement: A page not found tells someone we cannot find the page they were trying to view. They are also known as 404 pages.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Page not found pages" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Page not found pages > When to use this pattern
title: Page not found pages: When to use this pattern
statement: Use a page not found if someone is trying to view a page that does not exist. This happens if someone: - selects a link or button that takes them to a page that does not exist - types or copies a web address for a page that does not exist - types or copies a web address incorrectly Test all links and buttons to make sure they work. Remember to do the hard work to make it simple. Make sure any web addresses in your service, letters, forms and on GOV.UK are for pages that exist or redirect to pages that exist.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Page not found pages" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Page not found pages > How it works
title: Page not found pages: How it works
statement: The page should have: - ‘Page not found – service name – GOV.UK’ as the page title - ‘Page not found’ as the H1 - contact information, if it exists and helps meet a user need Contact information should either: - be a link to a specific page that includes numbers and opening times - include all numbers and opening times The content should be clear and concise, not blame the user. Do not use: - breadcrumbs - technical jargon like 404 or bad request - informal or humorous words like oops - red text to warn people
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Page not found pages" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Passwords
title: Passwords
statement: Help users to create and enter secure and memorable passwords.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Passwords" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Passwords > When to use this pattern
title: Passwords: When to use this pattern
statement: You should follow this pattern whenever you need users to create or enter a password. Before using this pattern, you should also read the guidance on the User accounts pattern. For technical considerations, you may also want to read the guidance for the Password input component.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Passwords" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Passwords > How it works
title: Passwords: How it works
statement: When using passwords in your service, you should: - help users make strong, unique passwords - let users paste their password - keep them secure, particularly when helping users reset a password
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Passwords" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Passwords > How it works > Helping users choose strong passwords
title: Passwords: Helping users choose strong passwords
statement: Overly strict or confusing constraints can make it harder for people to create strong and memorable passwords. This could mean they: - stop using your service - forget their password and have to reset it - store their password in a non-secure place Choose restrictions that meet the security needs of your service, and be clear and consistent about them. Any restrictions must be identical wherever the user creates or enters a password. If you change the restrictions over time, you must continue to support existing user passwords or ask them to set a new one. If you need additional security, consider adding a second authentication factor rather than extra password restrictions. Make sure you: - set a minimum length of at least 8 characters - do not set a maximum length - explain any restrictions to users - do not allow commonly used passwords
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Passwords" (How it works > Helping users choose strong passwords).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Passwords > How it works > Do not make users keep changing their passwords
title: Passwords: Do not make users keep changing their passwords
statement: Some services force users to change their passwords regularly, for example every month. You should not do this because it means users: - are more likely to forget their passwords - will tend to pick simple variations on their previous password - are more likely to store their password in a non-secure place Usually, you should only force a password change if you suspect an account might be compromised.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Passwords" (How it works > Do not make users keep changing their passwords).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Passwords > How it works > Handling incorrect login attempts
title: Passwords: Handling incorrect login attempts
statement: If a user enters their account details incorrectly, do not reveal whether they got the username or password wrong. Revealing the source of the error can help fraudsters break into people’s accounts. Do not keep any entered password inputs from an incorrect login attempt. Give users between 5 and 10 attempts to enter their password correctly before you lock their account or do any further security checks.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Passwords" (How it works > Handling incorrect login attempts).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Passwords > How it works > Help users who forget their password
title: Passwords: Help users who forget their password
statement: Passwords that are hard to guess can also be hard to remember. When helping users who’ve forgotten their password, you should: - send them a link or code to trigger a password reset - avoid password reset questions - avoid password reminders
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Passwords" (How it works > Help users who forget their password).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Passwords > How it works > Send a link to trigger password resets
title: Passwords: Send a link to trigger password resets
statement: You should never send passwords by email because it’s not a secure channel. Instead, send users a time-limited password-reset link or code to the email address or phone number that they registered with. Always email the user when a password reset has happened, in case it was triggered by someone else trying to get into their account.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Passwords" (How it works > Send a link to trigger password resets).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Passwords > How it works > Avoid password reset questions
title: Passwords: Avoid password reset questions
statement: Some services ask users a ‘password reset question’ when they create a password, and ask users to answer it again when they’ve forgotten their password. You should not use password reset questions because they often ask for information that’s: - too obscure and therefore just as hard to remember as a password - too easy for someone else to find out, for example ‘mother’s maiden name’ - subject to change, for example ‘favourite colour’
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Passwords" (How it works > Avoid password reset questions).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Passwords > How it works > Avoid password reminders
title: Passwords: Avoid password reminders
statement: Some services ask users to provide a ‘password reminder’ when they create a password, and give users the option to show this reminder when they’ve forgotten their password. You should not use password reminders because they: - encourage users to reveal information about their password - do not work for very strong passwords involving random strings of characters
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Passwords" (How it works > Avoid password reminders).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Payment card details
title: Payment card details
statement: This guidance is for government teams that build online services. To find information and services for the public, go to GOV.UK.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Payment card details" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Payment card details > When to use this pattern
title: Payment card details: When to use this pattern
statement: Before using this pattern, check if GOV.UK Pay is suitable for your service. If you cannot use GOV.UK Pay and need to build your own payment service, follow this pattern to collect payment card details from your users.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Payment card details" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Payment card details > How it works > Allow different formats
title: Payment card details: Allow different formats
statement: Let users enter payment card numbers in whatever format is familiar to them. Allow additional spaces, hyphens and dashes.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Payment card details" (How it works > Allow different formats).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Payment card details > How it works > Help users enter valid card information
title: Payment card details: Help users enter valid card information
statement: Present all fields on a single page, in the order in which they appear on a credit or debit card. This makes it easy for users to transcribe the information from their payment card. Show logos for the cards you accept as icons so users can see whether their card is supported. Use Issuer Identification Number (IIN) lookups to validate the card number as the user enters it. Once you’ve been able to identify the user’s card type, leave only the relevant logo highlighted and grey out the others. This video shows the card number validation in practice. It does not have any audio. If JavaScript is not available, display all of the logos anyway, as they still help users to understand which card types you support. When you validate the card number, the card security code information should update according to the type of card being used. For example, if a user enters an American Express card, the hint text and icon should change to match the front of the card. Do not use CVV or other acronyms for the card security code. If you need to ask for a user's name elsewhere in your service, do not assume that the name on their card will be the same.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Payment card details" (How it works > Help users enter valid card information).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Phone numbers
title: Phone numbers
statement: This guidance is for government teams that build online services. To find information and services for the public, go to GOV.UK.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Phone numbers" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Phone numbers > When to use this pattern
title: Phone numbers: When to use this pattern
statement: Only collect phone numbers from people if you genuinely need them. Not everyone has or can use a phone, so make sure you give users a choice about how they can be contacted.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Phone numbers" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Phone numbers > How it works > Allow different formats
title: Phone numbers: Allow different formats
statement: Let users enter phone numbers in whatever format is familiar to them. Allow for additional spaces, hyphens, dashes and brackets, and be able to accommodate country and area codes.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Phone numbers" (How it works > Allow different formats).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Phone numbers > How it works > Validate phone numbers
title: Phone numbers: Validate phone numbers
statement: You should validate phone numbers so you can let users know if they have entered one incorrectly. Google’s libphonenumber library can validate phone numbers from most countries.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Phone numbers" (How it works > Validate phone numbers).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Phone numbers > How it works > Use the autocomplete attribute
title: Phone numbers: Use the autocomplete attribute
statement: Use the autocomplete attribute on phone number inputs. This lets browsers autofill the information on a user's behalf if they’ve entered it previously. To do this, set the autocomplete attribute to tel, as shown in the HTML and Nunjucks tabs in the examples on this page. If you are working in production you’ll need to do this to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.3.5 Identify input purpose. You will not normally need to use the autocomplete attribute in prototypes, as users will not generally be using their own devices.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Phone numbers" (How it works > Use the autocomplete attribute).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Phone numbers > How it works > Error messages
title: Phone numbers: Error messages
statement: Error messages should be styled like this: Make sure errors follow the guidance in the Error message component and have specific error messages for specific error states.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Phone numbers" (How it works > Error messages).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Phone numbers > How it works > Make it clear what type of phone number you need
title: Phone numbers: Make it clear what type of phone number you need
statement: Use the form label or hint text to tell users if you specifically need a UK, international or mobile phone number.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Phone numbers" (How it works > Make it clear what type of phone number you need).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Phone numbers > How it works > Do not display phone numbers as links on devices that cannot make calls
title: Phone numbers: Do not display phone numbers as links on devices that cannot make calls
statement: It’s possible to mark up phone numbers as links, like this: However, doing this will style phone numbers as links, which is confusing on devices that do not support phone calls. It might also not be necessary - some modern mobile browsers automatically detect phone numbers and display them as links anyway. If you do need to mark up your phone numbers as links, for example, to support a device that cannot automatically detect them, make sure they do not display as links on devices that cannot make calls. When you look at your service's user journey, remember that phone numbers as links might behave in unexpected ways for the user. For example, unless the user sets a default app to handle tel: links, some browsers and operating systems will automatically start a setup process.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Phone numbers" (How it works > Do not display phone numbers as links on devices that cannot make calls).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Phone numbers > How it works > Avoid input masking
title: Phone numbers: Avoid input masking
statement: Avoid 'input masking', or showing placeholder answer, because it makes it harder for users to: - type a number in their preferred way - transcribe a number from another place and check that they’ve got it right
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Phone numbers" (How it works > Avoid input masking).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Phone numbers > How it works > Avoid reformatting phone numbers
title: Phone numbers: Avoid reformatting phone numbers
statement: The GOV.UK Notify team have observed some users becoming confused when presented with a reformatted version of a phone number that they provided, for example, with the +44 country code added.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Phone numbers" (How it works > Avoid reformatting phone numbers).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: There is a problem with the service pages
title: There is a problem with the service pages
statement: This guidance is for government teams that build online services. To find information and services for the public, go to GOV.UK. Tell the user there is something wrong with the service. These are also known as 500 and internal server error pages.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "There is a problem with the service pages" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: There is a problem with the service pages > When to use this pattern
title: There is a problem with the service pages: When to use this pattern
statement: Use this page when there is an unexpected problem with the service. Use the same page for all unexpected problems. Log all errors and fix them as quickly as possible. Only display the page for a short time. If a problem cannot be fixed quickly, close the service and use a Service unavailable page.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "There is a problem with the service pages" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: There is a problem with the service pages > How it works
title: There is a problem with the service pages: How it works
statement: These pages should have: - ‘Sorry, there is a problem with the service – service name – GOV.UK’ as the page title - ‘Sorry, there is a problem with the service’ as the H1 - ‘Try again later.’ as a normal paragraph - information about what has happened to their answers if they are in the middle of a transaction - contact information, if it exists and helps meet a user need - a link to another service, if they can use it to do what they came to do Contact information should either be: - a link to a specific page that includes numbers and opening times - include all numbers and opening times Have clear and concise content and do not use: - breadcrumbs - jargon like 500 or bad request - ‘We are experiencing technical difficulties’ - red text to warn people Store previously entered information for a reasonable amount of time so users can resume a journey with re-populated information when the service becomes available again.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "There is a problem with the service pages" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: There is a problem with the service pages > How it works > Showing contact information
title: There is a problem with the service pages: Showing contact information
statement: Contact information should either: - include all numbers and opening times in one place on the page - be a link out to a page that includes numbers and opening times You might choose to link to a ‘contact information’ page, such as one shown in the ‘Contact a department or service team’ pattern.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "There is a problem with the service pages" (How it works > Showing contact information).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Question pages
title: Question pages
statement: This pattern explains when to use question pages and what elements they need to include.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Question pages" ().

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Question pages > When to use this pattern
title: Question pages: When to use this pattern
statement: Follow this pattern whenever you need to ask users questions within your service. You should make sure you know why you’re asking every question and only ask users for information you really need. To help you work out what to ask, you can carry out a question protocol. If you ask for optional information: - in most contexts, add ‘(optional)’ to the labels of optional fields - for Radios components and Checkboxes components, add ‘(optional)’ to the legend Never mark mandatory fields with asterisks. On every question page you should: - make sure it’s clear to users why you’re asking each question - allow users to answer ‘I do not know’ or ‘I’m not sure’ if they are valid responses Read more about designing good questions in the GOV.UK Service Manual.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Question pages" (When to use this pattern).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Question pages > How it works
title: Question pages: How it works
statement: Question pages must include a: - back link - page heading - continue button If research shows it’s helpful for users, you can also include a progress indicator. Make sure to only ask for a piece of information once within a single journey. Whenever possible, do not ask a user to re-enter information they’ve already provided. If the same type of information is needed more than once, make it easier to reuse previously entered answers through one of these methods: - pre-populating the relevant fields - showing carried-forward responses as an option for the user to select
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Question pages" (How it works).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Question pages > How it works > Back link
title: Question pages: Back link
statement: Some users do not trust browser back buttons when they’re entering data. Always include a Back link component at the top of question pages to reassure them it’s possible to go back and change previous answers. However, do not break the browser back button. Make sure it takes users to the previous page they were on, in the state they last saw it. An exception to this is when the user has performed an action they should only do once, like make a payment or complete an application. The browser back button should still work, but show the user a sensible message rather than let them perform the action again.
citation: Government Digital Service (UK). GOV.UK Design System: "Question pages" (How it works > Back link).

author: Government Digital Service (UK)
subcategory: Question pages > How it works > Start by asking one question per page
title: Question pages: Start by asking one question per page
statement: Asking just one question per question page helps users understand what you’re asking them to do, and focus on the specific question and its answer. To help you follow this approach, you can set the contents of a or for a page’s input as the page heading.
